title: Project Management for Engineering Students
text:
Welcome to the Course
This course introduces engineering students to the principles, tools, and practices of professional project management. Whether you are building a bridge, developing software, or managing a manufacturing plant upgrade, the ability to plan, execute, and control projects is one of the most valuable skills an engineer can possess.

title: Project Management for Engineering Students
text:
Note🎯 Course Philosophy



This course is built on a simple idea: Project Management is an engineering discipline. It requires systematic thinking, quantitative analysis, and structured problem solving — the same skills you use in your technical courses, applied to the management of complex, real-world endeavours.

0.0.1 Part I — Foundations

✅ Understand what projects are and why they fail
✅ Analyse projects using the systems view and three-sphere model

✅ Allocate and level resources efficiently

0.0.3 Part III — Execution & Control

✅ Identify, analyse, and respond to risks
✅ Monitor costs using Earned Value Management
✅ Implement quality assurance and control processes

0.0.4 Part IV — Modern Approaches

✅ Apply Agile and Scrum to engineering projects
✅ Lead high-performance project teams

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management
text:
2.1 What Is a Project? 📋 Required
A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result (Project Management Institute 2021).






Note📖 PMI Definition of a Project




“A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result. The temporary nature of projects indicates a beginning and an end to the project work.” — PMBOK® Guide, 7th Edition



The three essential characteristics of every project are:





flowchart TD
    P([🗂️ PROJECT]) --> T
    P --> U
    P --> G
    T["⏱️ TEMPORARY<br/>Has a definite start<br/>and end date"]
    U["🔷 UNIQUE<br/>Produces a unique<br/>output or result"]
    G["🎯 GOAL-ORIENTED<br/>Created to achieve a<br/>specific objective"]

    style P fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
    style T fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e40af
    style U fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534
    style G fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308,color:#854d0e


 The three defining characteristics of any project

2.2 The Project Lifecycle 📋 Required
Every project passes through a series of phases from inception to completion. The PMI recognises five Process Groups:

    C["⚙️ EXECUTING<br/>Do the work<br/>Manage teams<br/>Produce deliverables"]
    D["📊 MONITORING<br/>& CONTROLLING<br/>Track progress<br/>Control changes<br/>Manage issues"]
    E["🏁 CLOSING<br/>Finalise all work<br/>Hand over asset<br/>Lessons learned"]

 The five PMI process groups across the project lifecycle 









Note📖 Key Concept — Process Groups vs. Project Phases



Process Groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) describe what activities are performed.
Project Phases (e.g., Feasibility, Design, Construction, Commissioning) describe how the work is organised in a specific industry or project. Multiple process groups may occur within each phase.

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management
text:
2.3 The Triple Constraint 📋 Required
The Triple Constraint (also known as the Iron Triangle) is the foundation of project management. Every project must be managed within three interrelated constraints:





%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 30, 'rankSpacing': 40}}}%%
graph LR
    S["📐 SCOPE<br/>Deliverables & features<br/>What is included?"]
    T["⏱️ TIME<br/>Deadline & schedule<br/>How long will it take?"]
    C["💰 COST<br/>Budget & resources<br/>How much will it cost?"]
    Q["⭐ QUALITY<br/>at the centre"]

    S --- T
    T --- C
    C --- S
    S --- Q
    T --- Q
    C --- Q

    style S fill:#3b82f6,color:#fff,stroke:#3b82f6
    style T fill:#22c55e,color:#fff,stroke:#22c55e
    style C fill:#f97316,color:#fff,stroke:#f97316
    style Q fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308,color:#854d0e


 The Triple Constraint (Iron Triangle) of project management 









Warning⚠️ The Triple Constraint Trade-off



The golden rule: You cannot change one constraint without affecting at least one other.



If the client wants…
Then you must…




Reduced cost
Reduce scope OR extend time


Shorter time
Increase cost OR reduce scope


Increased scope
Increase cost OR extend time


All three improved
Accept lower quality



As a PM, your job is to manage these trade-offs transparently with your stakeholders.



2.3.1 Extended Constraints (The Six-Sided Diamond)
Modern project management recognises additional constraints beyond the original three:

ScopeTimeCostQualityRiskResources


“What are we building?” - Defines the work to be completed - Includes all deliverables and acceptance criteria - Controlled through a scope management plan - Changes managed via a formal change control process


“When will it be done?” - Total project duration and milestone dates - Drives the schedule and critical path - Measured via Gantt charts and network diagrams - Buffer time (float) must be carefully managed


“How much will it cost?” - Total approved budget for the project - Includes labour, materials, equipment, and overheads - Tracked using Earned Value Management (EVM) - Contingency reserves held for risks


“How good must it be?” - The standard to which deliverables must conform - Defined in specifications and acceptance criteria - Managed through QA (prevention) and QC (inspection) - Cannot be sacrificed to save cost or time


“What could go wrong?” - Uncertainty that can affect objectives - Can be positive (opportunities) or negative (threats) - Managed through identification, analysis, and response planning - Risks increase when other constraints are squeezed


“Who and what do we need?” - Human resources (skills, availability, roles) - Physical resources (equipment, materials, facilities) - Resource constraints often drive schedule changes - Team management is a key PM competency

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management
text:
2.5 Why Projects Fail 📋 Required
Research consistently shows that a large proportion of engineering projects experience cost overruns, schedule delays, or scope issues.






Important🏭 Real-World Data — Project Failure Rates



According to the Standish Group CHAOS Report 2020 (The Standish Group International 2020):

Only 31% of IT projects are delivered on time, on budget, and within scope
52% are challenged (late, over budget, or missing features)
17% are outright failures (cancelled or abandoned)

For large-scale infrastructure projects, Flyvbjerg’s research (Flyvbjerg 2009) found:

9 out of 10 projects have cost overruns
Average cost overrun: 28% for roads, 45% for rail
Average schedule overrun: 17–45% depending on project type




2.5.1 Root Causes of Project Failure

flowchart TD

    F --> R1["📋 Poor Planning<br/>Unrealistic schedules<br/>Incomplete scope"]
    F --> R2["💬 Communication Breakdown<br/>Unclear requirements<br/>Stakeholder misalignment"]
    F --> R3["🔄 Scope Creep<br/>Undocumented changes<br/>No change control"]
    F --> R4["👥 Resource Issues<br/>Skill shortages<br/>Key person dependency"]
    F --> R5["⚠️ Risk Blindness<br/>Risks not identified<br/>No contingency plans"]
    F --> R6["🏛️ Governance Failure<br/>Weak sponsorship<br/>Conflicting priorities"]

 Common causes of engineering project failure 





2.5.2 The Classic PM Triangle — Failure Modes






Warning⚠️ Common Mistake — The “Heroic Engineer” Fallacy



Many engineering projects fail because technical experts underestimate the management component. A brilliant technical solution delivered late, over budget, or with poor stakeholder management is still a failed project.
Studies show that technical problems account for fewer than 20% of project failures. The other 80% are management problems: poor communication, unclear requirements, inadequate planning, or weak leadership.

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management
section: 2.6 How IT Projects Differ from Other Projects ➕ Extended
text:
2.6 How IT Projects Differ from Other Projects ➕ Extended
This book is based on Schwalbe’s IT Project Management framework, which recognises that IT projects have unique characteristics that make them fundamentally different from construction, manufacturing, or infrastructure projects. Understanding these differences explains why IT projects fail more often — and why Agile methods emerged specifically for them.





flowchart LR
    subgraph IT["💻 IT Projects"]
        IT1["Invisible deliverable\n(software, data, systems)"]
        IT2["Requirements change\nfrequently"]
        IT3["Progress hard\nto measure"]
        IT4["Cheap to rework\nbefore release"]
        IT5["High technology\nuncertainty"]
    end
    subgraph OTHER["🏗️ Engineering / Construction Projects"]
        O1["Visible, physical\ndeliverable"]
        O2["Scope changes\nare costly & rare"]
        O3["Progress visible\n(% built)"]
        O4["Rework is\nextremely expensive"]
        O5["Established methods\nand standards"]
    end

    style IT fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6
    style OTHER fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e


 Key differences between IT projects and other project types 




IT vs. Engineering project characteristics







Characteristic
IT Projects
Construction / Engineering




Deliverable
Intangible — software, database, system
Tangible — building, road, plant


Visibility of progress
Difficult — “90% done” is unreliable
Easy — you can see what is built


Requirement changes
Frequent and expected
Rare and expensive


Rework cost
Low before release; very high after
Always very high


Technology risk
High — tools and platforms evolve rapidly
Low — established construction methods


Uniqueness
Almost every project is one-of-a-kind
Some reuse of standard designs


Team skills
Highly specialised, scarce, hard to replace
Broader labour pools available


Failure rate
~52% challenged, ~17% fail (Standish 2020)
Lower, but cost overruns are common









Note📖 Why This Matters for Project Management



These differences explain three important things:

Why Agile was invented for IT — Fixed-scope waterfall planning fails when requirements change every sprint. IT projects need iterative, flexible approaches.
Why IT projects are harder to control — You cannot walk the site and see progress. Earned Value, burndown charts, and demos are used instead.
Why stakeholder involvement is critical in IT — Since the product is invisible until it is built, continuous user feedback is the only way to ensure the final system meets the real need.

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management
text:
2.8 Organisational Structures for Projects 📋 Required
The way an organisation is structured determines who holds authority over the project manager and team. The structure shapes communication paths, resource availability, and ultimately, the project manager’s power to deliver. PMBOK recognises five main types:






Note📖 Key Roles — PM vs. Functional Manager (FM)











Role
Who They Are
What They Control




Project Manager (PM)
Leads the project — responsible for scope, schedule, cost, and quality
Project deliverables and outcomes


Functional Manager (FM)
Head of a department (e.g., Head of Engineering, Head of Finance, Head of HR)
People, salaries, technical standards, and departmental resources



The central question in every organisational structure is: between the PM and the FM — who has more power?




2.8.1 1. Functional Structure



Functional organisational structure — PM has little or no authority


In a functional structure, the organisation is divided into specialised departments (Engineering, Finance, Manufacturing, etc.), each led by a director. It is the classic hierarchy seen in government, military, and traditional manufacturing.






Warning⚖️ PM Authority: Very Low — Acts as Coordinator Only



The PM cannot directly assign tasks to other departments. Every request must pass up to the department head, who then delegates it down. Results travel back up the same chain. The PM holds accountability without matching authority.






Functional




PM Authority
Little or none


Resource Control
Functional managers own resources


PM Role
Part-time coordinator


Budget Control
Functional manager


Best For
Stable, repetitive work; single-department projects



✅ Advantages - Clear career paths and deep technical specialisation - Efficient use of shared resources across multiple projects - Strong departmental expertise and quality control
❌ Disadvantages - Extremely poor horizontal communication - PM lacks authority to drive cross-department coordination - Slow decision-making — everything travels up and down the chain - Team loyalty is to the department, not the project



2.8.2 2. Divisional Structure
In a divisional structure, the organisation is split into self-contained units — each division has its own functional departments (Engineering, Finance, HR, etc.) and operates semi-independently. Divisions are typically organised by:

Product (e.g., Infrastructure Division, Buildings Division, Energy Division)
Geography (e.g., Middle East Division, Europe Division)
Customer/Market (e.g., Government Clients Division, Private Sector Division)






flowchart TD
    CEO["🏢 CEO / Head Office"]
    CEO --> D1["🏗️ Infrastructure\nDivision"]
    CEO --> D2["🏢 Buildings\nDivision"]
    CEO --> D3["⚡ Energy\nDivision"]

    D1 --> D1E["Engineering"]
    D1 --> D1F["Finance"]
    D1 --> D1P["Projects"]

    D2 --> D2E["Engineering"]
    D2 --> D2F["Finance"]
    D2 --> D2P["Projects"]

    D3 --> D3E["Engineering"]
    D3 --> D3F["Finance"]
    D3 --> D3P["Projects"]

    style CEO fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff
    style D1 fill:#0f766e,color:#fff
    style D2 fill:#15803d,color:#fff
    style D3 fill:#b45309,color:#fff


 Divisional organisational structure — each division is a mini-organisation 









Note⚖️ PM Authority: Medium — Authority Within the Division



The PM operates within the division and reports to the Division Head. Authority is stronger than in a functional structure but limited to the division’s resources — cross-division collaboration requires executive-level approval.










Divisional




PM Authority
Medium (within division)


Resource Control
Division manager


PM Role
Full-time within division


Budget Control
Division manager


Best For
Large organisations with distinct product lines or regional operations



✅ Advantages - Each division is focused and accountable for its own results - Faster decision-making within the division - Clear ownership of divisional projects and budgets - Easier to measure divisional performance
❌ Disadvantages - Duplication of functions across divisions (each has its own HR, Finance, etc.) - Poor collaboration and resource sharing between divisions - Potential for divisions to compete against each other internally - Inconsistent PM practices across divisions unless a central PMO exists



2.8.3 3. Weak Matrix Structure



Weak matrix organisational structure — PM has limited authority


The weak matrix resembles the functional structure on an org chart, but horizontal communication is slightly improved. Employees from other departments will at least listen, though the PM still cannot assign tasks or change plans without department head approval. The PM often emerges from among the performers (e.g., a developer on an IT project).






Warning⚖️ PM Authority: Low — Plans Require Department Head Approval



Employees have dual reporting lines — to both their department head and the PM — but the department head’s word takes precedence. Part-time involvement is common.










Weak Matrix




PM Authority
Low


Resource Control
Mostly functional managers


PM Role
Part-time


Budget Control
Functional manager


Best For
Manufacturing environments adding new capacity with minimal PM change



✅ Advantages - Slightly better cross-department collaboration than pure functional - Low disruption to existing structure - Flexible — employees remain in home departments
❌ Disadvantages - PM still lacks real authority to drive the project - Dual reporting creates confusion and conflict - Difficult to get employee time committed to project work



2.8.4 4. Balanced Matrix Structure



Balanced matrix organisational structure — shared authority


The balanced matrix is common in IT companies and engineering firms. A real project manager exists with genuine responsibility and authority. Employees clearly understand they have two supervisors — their department head and the PM — and they respect both equally.






Tip⚖️ PM Authority: Medium — Shared Equally with Functional Managers



The PM can influence task priorities and may have input into hiring/firing decisions. Decisions are made collaboratively between the PM and department heads. The department head focuses on employee development; the PM focuses on deadlines and deliverables.






Balanced Matrix




PM Authority
Medium


Resource Control
Shared


PM Role
Full-time


Budget Control
Mixed (PM and functional manager)


Best For
IT projects, product development, engineering firms



✅ Advantages - Efficient resource sharing across multiple projects - Strong communication between functional expertise and project needs - PM has real influence over project outcomes - Employees maintain professional development through home department
❌ Disadvantages - Dual authority can create conflict over priorities - Requires skilled negotiation between PM and department heads - More complex to manage than pure functional or projectised



2.8.5 5. Strong Matrix Structure



Strong matrix organisational structure — PM has high authority


In a strong matrix, the PM’s authority is dominant. A dedicated Project Management Office (PMO) exists as its own department. The PM handles hiring, firing, task assignment, and priority setting decisively. This person is a full-time project management professional with no other technical role.






Tip⚖️ PM Authority: High — PM Leads; Functional Managers Support



The PM can unilaterally adjust plans, assign resources, and make staffing decisions. The PMO is a recognised power centre within the organisation.










Strong Matrix




PM Authority
High


Resource Control
Primarily PM


PM Role
Full-time


Budget Control
Project manager


Best For
Large complex projects, companies running many concurrent projects



✅ Advantages - Clear PM authority enables fast decision-making - Enhanced cross-functional communication - Projects aligned with strategic objectives - Best balance of specialisation and project focus
❌ Disadvantages - Functional managers may feel their authority is undermined - Risk of conflict between PMO and functional departments - Requires mature PM professionals



2.8.6 6. Projectised (Flat) Structure



Projectised (flat) organisational structure — PM has full authority


In a projectised (or flat) structure, there are no permanent departments — only a resource pool and project managers. When a project is launched, the PM selects team members from the pool, builds the team, and leads them to completion. Unused staff remain in the pool awaiting the next project. This is common in large outsourcing and consultancy firms.






Important⚖️ PM Authority: Full — Absolute Authority Over the Project



The PM does not consult with anyone else. They are fully responsible for hiring, firing, scheduling, and budget. There is no functional manager counterpart.










Projectised

Budget Control

Best For
Large outsourcing firms, defence contractors, construction megaprojects



✅ Advantages - Maximum PM authority — fastest decision-making - Team fully dedicated to the project (no split loyalties) - Clearest accountability
❌ Disadvantages - No home base for employees — loss of career development and mentoring - Resources may sit idle between projects (costly) - Duplication of specialist roles across projects - When the project ends, the team disperses

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management
section: Case Study — Rawabi New City, Palestine
text:
Case Study — Rawabi New City, Palestine






Important🏭 Case Study: Rawabi — Palestine’s First Planned City



Background:
Rawabi (رواب، “hills” in Arabic) is the first planned Palestinian city, built on the hills north of Ramallah in the West Bank. Developed by Bayti Real Estate Investment Company (founder: Bashar Masri) with approximately $1 billion investment from Qatari Diar, Rawabi represents one of the most challenging and inspiring project management achievements in the Arab world — a city built against extraordinary political, logistical, and financial obstacles.
Original Plans (2009): - Budget: Approximately $1 billion (Phase 1) - Duration: 3 years — first residents targeted for 2012 - Scope: 6,000 housing units, 40,000 residents, commercial district, schools, amphitheatre
Actual Outcome: - First residents moved in: February 2016 (4 years late) - Continued expansion through 2020s despite ongoing constraints - Phase 1 delivered; city operational and growing
Key Challenges Unique to this Project:







Factor
What Happened




Access Road Blocked
The only viable construction access road required Israeli Civil Administration approval — denied for 2+ years, halting heavy equipment deliveries entirely


Import Permit Restrictions
Cement, steel, and crushed stone required import permits via Israeli-controlled crossings; strategic 6-month stockpiles were maintained


Financing Uncertainty
Qatari Diar payments were tied to political developments; phased construction aligned with available cash


Unproven Market
First market-rate housing project in Palestine — no historical price data; pre-sales of 3,000+ units carried out before construction started


Skilled Labour Scarcity
Specialist MEP trades unavailable locally; training programmes for Palestinian youth were launched on site



Lessons Learned: 1. Political and external constraints are real risks — a 2-year access road delay was foreseeable and must appear in the risk register with a mitigation plan 2. Stakeholder management beyond the project boundary (foreign governments, approval authorities) is sometimes more important than managing construction 3. Cash-flow planning under politically uncertain financing requires 12+ months of reserve capacity 4. Phased delivery maintains credibility — delivering housing blocks sequentially built buyer trust during delays 5. Scope discipline under adversity: when deadlines slipped, the temptation to add unplanned features was resisted
What Worked: Despite facing constraints that would have ended most projects, Rawabi delivered a functional city of 6,000 homes, a thriving commercial street, schools, a 15,000-seat amphitheatre, and a technology park — demonstrating that strong leadership, community stakeholder engagement, and financial resilience can overcome extraordinary external constraints.
Discussion Questions: 1. Which of the PMBOK knowledge areas was most severely impacted by the political constraints on this project? 2. How would you conduct a stakeholder analysis when a non-traditional “stakeholder” (a foreign government with approval authority) is in scope? 3. If you were preparing the business case for Rawabi in 2008, what risk contingency would you have recommended for the access road issue?
Sources: Masri (2010); Flyvbjerg (2009)

1.9 Exercises






Caution✏️ Exercise 1.1 — Project vs. Operation Classification



Classify each of the following as either a Project or an Operation. For each project, identify the three constraints (scope, time, cost):

Building a new highway interchange
Weekly maintenance of a water treatment plant

Developing a new structural analysis software tool
Operating a production line to manufacture steel beams
Designing and installing a solar power system for a hospital
Conducting annual safety inspections of an offshore platform
Relocating a factory to a new site
Running daily quality checks on concrete samples

Reflection: What criteria did you use to distinguish projects from operations?








Caution✏️ Exercise 1.2 — Triple Constraint Analysis



An engineering consulting firm is contracted to design a bridge. The original contract states:

Scope: Full structural design, drawings, and specifications
Time: 8 months
Cost: $450,000 fixed price

After 3 months, the client requests: - Inclusion of seismic analysis (not in original scope) - Deadline brought forward by 6 weeks (client’s new funding deadline) - No increase in fee
Using the Triple Constraint model:

Analyse the impact of each change request
What trade-offs would you propose to the client?
Draft a brief response (2-3 sentences) for each change request
Which request would you consider most unreasonable, and why?









Caution✏️ Exercise 1.3 — PM Knowledge Areas Mapping



For the following engineering project — “Construction of a 50 MW Solar Farm” — identify at least TWO specific activities or deliverables for FIVE of the ten PMBOK knowledge areas.
Present your answer in a table with columns: Knowledge Area | Activity 1 | Activity 2
Bonus: Identify which two knowledge areas you think will be MOST challenging for this project and explain why.








Caution✏️ Exercise 1.4 — Root Cause Analysis



Read the following scenario and identify the root causes of the project failure:

“A major city council contracted an engineering firm to install a new smart traffic control system across 200 intersections. The project had an 18-month deadline and a $12M budget. After 24 months and $18M spent, the system was still not operational. The software contractor delivered code 6 months late, which meant hardware installation had to start before software testing was complete. The council kept adding intersections to the scope. Three project managers resigned during the project. The final handover revealed that 40 intersections were wired incorrectly.”


List all the root causes you can identify (minimum 5)
For each root cause, state which PMBOK knowledge area was at fault
Propose one preventive action for each root cause

title: 3  The Project Management and Engineering Context
section: 3.1 A Systems View of Project Management 📋 Required
text:
3.1 A Systems View of Project Management 📋 Required
Engineering projects do not exist in isolation — they operate inside complex systems of people, technology, organisations, and regulations. A systems approach means looking at the whole rather than individual parts.






Note📖 Key Concept — Systems Thinking



Systems thinking is a holistic approach to analysis that focuses on how a system’s individual components interrelate and work together over time within the context of larger systems. In project management, it means recognising that a project’s success depends on its environment — not just the work inside the project.


A project manager who ignores the organisational context, technology constraints, or business strategy is like a structural engineer who designs a beam without considering the building it sits in.

3.1.1 The Three-Sphere Model
The Three-Sphere Model for Systems Management recognises that every project operates at the intersection of three domains:





%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#dbeafe'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    P(["🗂️ PROJECT"])

    B["💼 BUSINESS<br/>• Strategy & goals<br/>• Financial viability<br/>• Market context<br/>• Return on investment"]
    O["🏢 ORGANISATION<br/>• Culture & structure<br/>• Processes & governance<br/>• People & skills<br/>• Change management"]
    T["⚙️ TECHNOLOGY<br/>• Engineering methods<br/>• Tools & platforms<br/>• Technical standards<br/>• Innovation & risk"]

    B --> P
    O --> P
    T --> P

    style P fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
    style B fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308,color:#854d0e
    style O fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534
    style T fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e40af


 The Three-Sphere Model — every project sits at the intersection of business, organisation, and technology 









Important⚠️ Common Mistake



Focusing exclusively on the technology sphere — getting the engineering right — while neglecting the business justification or organisational readiness. Many technically excellent projects fail because the organisation was not prepared to adopt the result.


Engineering Example — A Smart Grid Upgrade:

Three-sphere analysis of a smart grid upgrade






Sphere
Considerations




Business
Does the investment reduce long-term energy costs? Is there regulatory pressure?


Organisation
Are utility operators trained to manage the new system? Will unions resist automation?


Technology
Are the chosen IoT sensors reliable in harsh weather? Do they meet IEC 61850 standards?

title: 3  The Project Management and Engineering Context
text:
3.2 Understanding Organisations 📋 Required
Projects are performed within organisations, and the organisation’s characteristics profoundly shape how projects are managed — for better or worse.

3.2.1 The Four Frames of Organisations
Bolman and Deal’s Four Frames Model provides four different lenses to view organisations. Effective project managers learn to see their environment through all four frames, not just one:





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
quadrantChart
    title Four Organisational Frames
    x-axis "Focus on People" --> "Focus on Structure"
    y-axis "Internal" --> "External"
    quadrant-1 Political Frame
    quadrant-2 Symbolic Frame
    quadrant-3 Human Resources Frame
    quadrant-4 Structural Frame


 Bolman and Deal’s Four Frames of Organisations 




🏗️ Structural Frame👥 Human Resources Frame🎭 Political Frame✨ Symbolic Frame



Focuses on rules, roles, policies, hierarchy, and procedures
The organisation as a machine — efficiency through clear structure
PM implication: Clear reporting lines, defined processes, formal change control
Best for: Stable environments, well-defined projects, compliance-heavy industries




Focuses on people, relationships, skills, and motivation
The organisation as a family — invest in people and they invest in you
PM implication: Team development, training, motivation, conflict resolution, communication
Best for: Knowledge-intensive projects, cross-functional teams




Focuses on power, coalitions, competition, and scarce resources
The organisation as a jungle — success depends on building alliances
PM implication: Stakeholder management, negotiation, navigating competing agendas
Best for: Large organisations with multiple departments, government projects




Focuses on culture, rituals, values, vision, and meaning
The organisation as a theatre — symbols and stories drive behaviour
PM implication: Project vision, team identity, celebrating milestones, organisational culture
Best for: Innovative projects, transformational change, multi-cultural environments










Tip💡 Practical Tip



When a project is struggling, try analysing the situation through each of the four frames. Often, a problem that seems purely structural (e.g., “we need a better process”) is actually political (e.g., “two departments are competing for budget”) or human resources (e.g., “the team is demotivated”).




3.2.2 Organisational Structures
The organisational structure determines who has authority over the project manager and team members. The five main types — Functional, Weak Matrix, Balanced Matrix, Strong Matrix, and Projectised — are covered in detail in Chapter 1 (Section 1.7), including the images, authority levels, and advantages/disadvantages of each.
As a quick recap for context, the key principle is:

The more project-oriented the structure, the more authority the PM holds — ranging from none (Functional) to full (Projectised).







Note📖 Key Concept — Matrix Variants



Most engineering organisations operate in some form of matrix:

Weak Matrix: Functional managers retain most authority; PM is more of a coordinator
Balanced Matrix: PM and functional manager share authority; common in mid-size engineering firms
Strong Matrix: PM has more authority than functional managers; resembles projectised

The choice depends on how many projects the organisation runs, how critical projects are to revenue, and how specialised the staff are.




3.2.3 Organisational Culture
Organisational culture is the set of shared assumptions, values, and behaviours that determine “how things are done here.” Culture affects every aspect of project management:

How organisational culture impacts project management






Cultural Dimension
Impact on Projects




Risk tolerance
Conservative cultures resist innovative designs; entrepreneurial cultures embrace them


Decision-making
Hierarchical cultures slow down approvals; flat cultures empower PMs


Communication style
Formal cultures require written memos; informal cultures use quick chats


Attitude to failure
Blame cultures hide problems; learning cultures surface them early


Time orientation
Some cultures view deadlines as targets; others as firm commitments









Important⚠️ Common Mistake — Ignoring Culture



A PM who introduces agile stand-ups into a deeply hierarchical government ministry, or imposes rigid waterfall controls onto a fast-moving startup, will face resistance — not because the method is wrong, but because it clashes with the culture.




3.2.4 The Importance of Top Management Commitment
Research consistently shows that executive sponsorship is the #1 predictor of project success. Without it, projects lack:

Authority to acquire resources and resolve conflicts
Legitimacy in the eyes of stakeholders
Funding protection during budget cuts
Strategic alignment with the organisation’s goals

    TM["🏛️ Top Management<br/>Commitment"] --> A["✅ Clear authority<br/>for PM"]
    TM --> B["💰 Adequate &<br/>protected funding"]
    TM --> C["🎯 Strategic<br/>alignment"]
    TM --> D["🗣️ Visible<br/>sponsorship"]
    A --> S(["🏆 PROJECT<br/>SUCCESS"])
    B --> S
    C --> S
    D --> S

    style TM fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
    style S fill:#15803d,color:#fff,stroke:#15803d


 How top management commitment flows down to project success 









Note📖 Key Concept — The Need for Organisational Standards



Organisations that establish PM standards — standard templates, methodologies, reporting formats, and a Project Management Office (PMO) — achieve higher project success rates. A PMO provides:

Governance: Consistent project initiation and approval processes
Methodology: Standard tools and techniques across all projects
Support: Mentoring, training, and administrative support for PMs
Reporting: Portfolio-level visibility for senior management

3.3 Project Phases and the Project Life Cycle 📋 Required

3.3.1 The Project Life Cycle
Every project passes through a series of phases from initiation to closure. The typical engineering project life cycle includes:





flowchart LR
    F["📊 Feasibility<br/>& Concept"] --> D["📐 Design<br/>& Engineering"]
    D --> P["🔨 Procurement<br/>& Construction"]
    P --> C["🔧 Commissioning<br/>& Handover"]
    C --> O["⚙️ Operations<br/>& Maintenance"]

    style F fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff
    style D fill:#0f766e,color:#fff
    style P fill:#15803d,color:#fff
    style C fill:#b45309,color:#fff
    style O fill:#6b7280,color:#fff


 Typical engineering project life cycle phases 









Note📖 Key Concept — Phases vs. Process Groups



Phases are specific to the project type (e.g., Design → Build → Commission). Process Groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) are universal and occur within each phase.
A construction project’s “Design Phase” involves planning activities, executing design work, and monitoring quality — all process groups in action within one phase.




3.3.2 Phase Gates and Kill Points
Between each phase sits a formal review point — the project must pass this review before advancing to the next phase. This review point is known by several names:



Term
Also Known As




Phase Gate
Stage Gate, Phase-End Review


Kill Point
Go/No-Go Decision Point









Important⚠️ Kill Point — Exam Tip



The completion of a project phase review is formally called a Kill Point (or Phase Gate).
The sponsor or steering committee makes one of three decisions:



Decision
Outcome




Go
Advance to the next phase


No-Go (Kill)
Project is stopped or cancelled


Hold / Recycle
Return to current phase to resolve issues first



Advancement is conditional — the project only moves forward if it meets the phase exit criteria.







flowchart LR
    F["📊 Feasibility"] -->|"🚦 Kill Point 1"| D["📐 Design"]
    D -->|"🚦 Kill Point 2"| P["🔨 Construction"]
    P -->|"🚦 Kill Point 3"| C["🔧 Commissioning"]

    style F fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff
    style D fill:#0f766e,color:#fff
    style P fill:#15803d,color:#fff
    style C fill:#b45309,color:#fff


 Kill points sit between each project phase 





3.3.3 The Product Life Cycle
The product life cycle is broader than the project life cycle — it includes the entire lifespan of the deliverable:





flowchart LR
    subgraph ProductLC ["📦 Product Life Cycle (30–50 years for infrastructure)"]
        direction LR
        subgraph ProjLC1 ["🗂️ Original Project"]
            I1["Concept"] --> D1["Design"] --> B1["Build"] --> H1["Handover"]
        end
        subgraph OPS ["⚙️ Operations & Maintenance"]
            O1["Routine O&M"]
        end
        subgraph ProjLC2 ["🗂️ Upgrade Project"]
            I2["Concept"] --> D2["Design"] --> B2["Build"] --> H2["Handover"]
        end
        subgraph RET ["🏚️ Retirement"]
            R1["Decommission"]
        end
        ProjLC1 --> OPS --> ProjLC2 --> RET
    end

    style ProductLC fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155
    style ProjLC1 fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6
    style OPS fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e
    style ProjLC2 fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308
    style RET fill:#fecaca,stroke:#ef4444


 Product life cycle encompasses multiple project life cycles 



Engineering Example:
A highway bridge has a product life cycle of 75 years:

Original project (3 years): Feasibility → Design → Construction → Commissioning
Operations (60+ years): Routine inspection and maintenance
Upgrade project (1 year): Seismic retrofitting to meet new codes
Retirement (1 year): Demolition and replacement planning

The PM manages the project life cycle; the asset owner manages the product life cycle.

title: 3  The Project Management and Engineering Context
section: 3.4 The Nature of Engineering Projects ➕ Extended
text:
3.4 The Nature of Engineering Projects ➕ Extended
Engineering projects have unique characteristics that distinguish them from other project types:

3.4.1 Characteristics of Engineering Projects

Distinguishing characteristics of engineering projects






Characteristic
Description




Physical deliverables
Create tangible infrastructure, buildings, systems, or products


Regulatory compliance
Must meet building codes, environmental regulations, safety standards


Interdisciplinary teams
Require civil, mechanical, electrical, environmental, and other specialists


Long durations
Often span years, not weeks or months


High capital cost
Budgets frequently in millions or billions of dollars


Environmental impact
Construction and operation affect surrounding communities and ecosystems


Safety-critical
Design and construction errors can endanger human life


Geographic constraints
Site conditions, soil, weather, and access profoundly affect execution





3.4.2 Diverse Technologies and Specialisations
Engineering projects often involve multiple technical disciplines working in parallel. A modern building project might require:

Structural engineering (concrete, steel)
Mechanical engineering (HVAC, plumbing)
Electrical engineering (power, lighting, firesafety)
Civil engineering (earthworks, drainage)
Software/controls engineering (BMS, automation)
Telecommunications (networking, security systems)

The PM need not be an expert in every discipline, but must understand enough to coordinate them and recognise when specialist input is needed.

title: 3  The Project Management and Engineering Context
section: 3.5 Recent Trends in Engineering Project Management ➕ Extended
text:
3.5 Recent Trends in Engineering Project Management ➕ Extended
The practice of project management continues to evolve. Several trends are reshaping how engineering projects are delivered:

3.5.1 Building Information Modelling (BIM)
BIM creates a shared digital model of a building or infrastructure asset, enabling all disciplines to work on a single source of truth:

3D Modelling: Visualise the design before construction begins
4D (Time): Link the model to the schedule to simulate construction sequences
5D (Cost): Attach cost data to model elements for real-time budget tracking
6D (Sustainability): Analyse energy performance and environmental impact
7D (Facility Management): Use the model for operations and maintenance after handover







Tip💡 BIM vs. Traditional CAD



Traditional CAD produces 2D drawings that are disconnected from each other. BIM produces an intelligent model where a change in one view automatically updates all others. Clash detection — finding conflicts between structural beams and HVAC ducts, for example — happens before construction, not during.




3.5.2 Globalisation and Virtual Teams
Modern engineering projects increasingly involve global teams:

Design in one country, procurement in another, construction in a third
Virtual teams connected by video conferencing, cloud collaboration, and shared project servers
Challenges: Time zones, language barriers, cultural differences, trust-building without face-to-face contact



3.5.3 Sustainability and Green Engineering
The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) increasingly influence project selection and design:

Net-zero carbon construction targets
Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) for material selection
Green building certifications (LEED, BREEAM, Estidama)
Circular economy principles — design for disassembly and material reuse



3.5.4 Agile and Hybrid Approaches
While traditional plan-driven (waterfall) approaches dominate construction, hybrid approaches are emerging:

Agile methods for the design and engineering phases (iterative design reviews)
Traditional methods for procurement and construction (sequential, safety-critical)
Lean Construction and the Last Planner System for collaborative scheduling







Note📖 Key Concept — Agile in Engineering



Agile does not mean “no planning.” It means adaptive planning — shorter cycles, frequent feedback, and the ability to respond to change. Chapter 11 covers Agile and Scrum in detail.




3.5.5 Artificial Intelligence and Digital Twins
Emerging technologies are transforming project management:

AI-powered scheduling: Predictive analytics for delay risk, automatic schedule optimisation
Digital Twins: A live virtual replica of a physical asset, updated with real-time sensor data
Drones and LiDAR: Automated site surveys, progress monitoring, and safety inspection
Robotic Process Automation: Automating repetitive administrative tasks (document control, reporting)

title: 3  The Project Management and Engineering Context
section: 2.6 Case Study — Neom: The Line, Saudi Arabia
text:
2.6 Case Study — Neom: The Line, Saudi Arabia






Caution🏗️ Case Study — Neom: The Line, Saudi Arabia



The Line is a 170 km linear city in northwestern Saudi Arabia, part of the $500 billion Neom megaproject. Announced in 2021, it aims to house 9 million people in a structure 200 metres wide, 500 metres tall, with zero cars, zero streets, and zero carbon emissions.

3.5.6 Project Context







Attribute
Detail




Location
Tabuk Province, Saudi Arabia


Estimated cost
$500 billion+ (Neom total)


Timeline
Phase 1 target: 2030


Workforce
Peak estimate: 300,000+ workers


Key innovation
Linear urban design — all services within 5-minute walk





3.5.7 Three-Sphere Analysis

💼 Business Sphere🏢 Organisation Sphere⚙️ Technology Sphere



Part of Saudi Vision 2030 — economic diversification away from oil
Funded by the Public Investment Fund (PIF), one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds
Revenue model: tourism, technology, sports, entertainment, advanced manufacturing
Competing globally for talent and investment with established cities




NEOM Company: a new government-backed entity with unprecedented authority
Matrix of international consultants, contractors, and Saudi government agencies
Massive workforce from dozens of countries — cultural integration challenge
Need for new governance structures — no precedent for a project of this scale




Mirror-clad exterior with integrated solar panels
Underground high-speed rail running the full 170 km length
AI-driven city management — energy, waste, transport, security
Modular construction techniques to achieve the unprecedented scale
Vertical farming, desalination, and renewable energy at city scale






3.5.8 Lessons for Project Managers

Systems thinking is essential: The Line cannot succeed with engineering excellence alone — it requires alignment across business (economic model), organisation (governance), and technology (innovation)
Organisational culture matters: Creating a new organisation from scratch means deliberately designing the culture — values, decision-making norms, communication standards
Top management commitment is necessary but not sufficient: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman provides ultimate sponsorship, but execution depends on thousands of middle managers making daily decisions
Product life cycle thinking: The project delivers a city that must operate for centuries — decisions made during design lock in operational costs and capabilities for generations

title: 3  The Project Management and Engineering Context
text:
2.7 Exercises






Warning✏️ Exercise 2.1 — Three-Sphere Analysis



Scenario: Your university is building a new Engineering Innovation Centre — a 5,000 m² building with smart classrooms, fabrication labs, a maker space, and a rooftop solar array.
Tasks:

Identify at least three considerations for each sphere (Business, Organisation, Technology)
For each sphere, identify one risk that could threaten the project
Describe how the three spheres interact — give an example where a decision in one sphere affects the others
Recommend the most appropriate organisational structure (functional, matrix, or projectised) for this project and justify your choice









Warning✏️ Exercise 2.2 — Four Frames Analysis



Scenario: A municipal government has hired an engineering firm to design and build a new wastewater treatment plant. The project is six months behind schedule, and the client is threatening to cancel the contract.
Tasks:

Analyse the situation through each of Bolman and Deal’s four frames — for each frame, suggest one possible root cause of the delay
For each root cause, propose one corrective action
Which frame do you think is most likely to explain the delay in an engineering project context? Justify your answer









Warning✏️ Exercise 2.3 — Organisational Structure Comparison



Scenario: Consider the following three organisations:

Organisation A: A large government roads authority with 2,000 employees and 50+ active projects
Organisation B: A small engineering consultancy with 30 employees and 5 active projects
Organisation C: A defence contractor building a single $2 billion naval vessel over 8 years

Tasks:

Recommend the most appropriate organisational structure for each (functional, weak/balanced/strong matrix, or projectised)
For each recommendation, explain why this structure fits the organisation’s characteristics
For Organisation A, describe how a PMO could add value and what services it should provide









Warning✏️ Exercise 2.4 — Product vs. Project Life Cycle



Scenario: A regional water utility plans to build a new desalination plant with a design capacity of 100,000 m³/day and an expected operational life of 40 years.
Tasks:

Draw the project life cycle — identify 4–5 phases with key deliverables for each
Draw the product life cycle — identify all stages from initial concept through to eventual decommissioning
Identify two decisions made during the project that will significantly impact the product’s long-term operational costs
Explain why a PM should think about the product life cycle even though they are only responsible for the project

4.1 Overview of the Process Groups 📋 Required
The PMI defines five process groups that organise all project management activities. These are not sequential phases — they overlap and interact throughout the project:





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart LR
    I["🚀 INITIATING<br/>Define & authorise<br/>the project"]
    P["📋 PLANNING<br/>Define objectives &<br/>plan the work"]
    E["⚙️ EXECUTING<br/>Do the work &<br/>manage the team"]
    MC["📊 MONITORING<br/>& CONTROLLING<br/>Track, review &<br/>regulate progress"]
    C["🏁 CLOSING<br/>Formalise acceptance<br/>& close the project"]

    I --> P
    P --> E
    E --> C
    P <--> MC
    E <--> MC
    MC --> C

 The five process groups and their interactions 









Note📖 Key Concept — Process Groups vs. Phases



Process Groups are management activities — they happen in every phase. Phases are divisions of work specific to the project type.
In a construction project:

The Design Phase involves initiating (approve the design scope), planning (design schedule), executing (produce drawings), monitoring (design reviews), and closing (design freeze sign-off).
The Construction Phase then repeats all five process groups for the build work.




4.1.1 Level of Activity Across Process Groups
The amount of effort varies across the process groups. Planning and executing overlap significantly, with monitoring & controlling running continuously:

4.2 The Initiating Process Group 📋 Required
The Initiating process group authorises the project (or a new phase) and provides the high-level direction.

4.2.1 Key Activities

    BC --> CH["📜 Develop<br/>Project Charter"]

Activity

Note📖 Key Concept — The Project Charter



The project charter is the document that formally authorises the project and gives the PM the authority to apply organisational resources. Without a signed charter, the project does not officially exist.
Key elements: project purpose, measurable objectives, high-level requirements, summary budget, milestone schedule, PM name and authority level, sponsor name and approval.

4.3 The Planning Process Group 📋 Required
Planning is the largest process group, encompassing 24 of the 49 PMBOK processes. It defines what needs to be done, how, when, and by whom.

4.3.1 Key Activities

    SM["🤝 Plan Stakeholder<br/>Engagement"]

 Planning process group — core planning activities 









Important⚠️ Common Mistake — Rushing to Execute



Many engineers are eager to “start building” and treat planning as bureaucracy. But poor planning is the #1 cause of project failure. The rule of thumb: every hour spent planning saves 3–5 hours during execution.




4.3.2 The Project Management Plan
The Project Management Plan (PMP) is the master document that integrates all subsidiary plans:

Components of the integrated Project Management Plan






Subsidiary Plan
Defines




Scope Management Plan
How scope will be defined, validated, and controlled


Schedule Management Plan
How the schedule will be developed, managed, and controlled


Cost Management Plan
How costs will be estimated, budgeted, and controlled


Quality Management Plan
Quality standards and how they will be assured and controlled


Resource Management Plan
How resources will be identified, acquired, and managed


Communications Management Plan
Who needs what information, when, and in what format


Risk Management Plan
How risks will be identified, analysed, and responded to


Procurement Management Plan
What to procure, how, and from whom


Stakeholder Engagement Plan
How stakeholders will be engaged throughout the project





4.3.3 The Three Baselines
The PMP includes three baselines that serve as the reference points for measuring project performance:

Scope Baseline = Scope Statement + WBS + WBS Dictionary
Schedule Baseline = Approved project schedule
Cost Baseline = Time-phased project budget

Changes to any baseline require formal change control — you cannot simply move the goalposts.

title: 4  The Project Management Process Groups
text:
4.4 The Executing Process Group 📋 Required
Executing is where the actual work gets done. The PM’s focus shifts from planning to coordinating resources, managing the team, and ensuring quality.

4.4.1 Key Activities

Executing process group activities






Activity
Description




Direct and Manage Project Work
Lead the team in producing deliverables according to the plan


Manage Project Knowledge
Capture and share lessons learned and organisational knowledge


Manage Quality
Perform quality assurance — audit processes and standards compliance


Acquire Resources
Obtain the people, equipment, and materials needed


Develop Team
Build team competence and cohesion (training, team-building)


Manage Team
Track performance, resolve conflicts, provide feedback


Manage Communications
Distribute information per the communications plan


Implement Risk Responses
Execute the planned risk response strategies


Conduct Procurements
Select sellers, negotiate contracts, issue purchase orders


Manage Stakeholder Engagement
Work with stakeholders to meet their needs and address issues









Tip💡 Practical Tip — Where Time and Money Are Spent



The executing process group consumes the most time and the most budget of any process group — typically 60–80% of total project resources. Effective planning and monitoring make this investment efficient; poor planning wastes it.

4.5 The Monitoring and Controlling Process Group 📋 Required
This process group runs continuously throughout the project. It tracks performance against the plan and takes corrective action when deviations occur.

4.5.1 Key Activities

    D -->|No| A["🔧 Take Corrective<br/>or Preventive Action"]

Knowledge Area

Note📖 Key Concept — Integrated Change Control



All changes to project baselines (scope, schedule, cost) must go through a formal change control process:

Request — Document the change request (CR)
Evaluate — Assess the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk
Decide — Change Control Board (CCB) approves, defers, or rejects
Implement — If approved, update the plan and baselines
Communicate — Notify all affected stakeholders

Uncontrolled changes are scope creep — the silent killer of projects.




4.5.2 Configuration Management
Configuration Management ensures that the descriptions of project products and deliverables are correct, complete, and consistent at all times — from initial definition through to final handover.






Note📖 What is Configuration Management?



While Integrated Change Control asks: “Should this change be approved?”, Configuration Management asks: “Is what we are building still accurately described in our documents?”
It tracks and controls the physical and functional characteristics of project deliverables, ensuring that: - Product specifications match what is actually being built - All documentation reflects the latest approved version - No unauthorised changes have been made to the product description









Activity
Description




Configuration Identification
Define and document the characteristics of each deliverable


Configuration Control
Ensure product descriptions are correct and complete; prevent unauthorised changes


Configuration Status Accounting
Record and report the status of all configurations


Configuration Audit
Verify that the deliverable matches its documented specification









Important⚠️ Exam Tip — Configuration Management vs. Integrated Change Control












Configuration Management
Integrated Change Control




Focus
Product descriptions & specifications
Change requests to baselines


Question it answers
Are the product descriptions correct and complete?
Should this change be approved?


Managed by
Configuration Manager / PM
Change Control Board (CCB)




“To ensure that the description of project products are correct and complete” → Configuration Management ✅

Closing formalises acceptance of the project’s deliverables and brings the project (or phase) to an orderly end.

4.6.1 Key Activities

 The closing process group — systematic project completion 









Important⚠️ Common Mistake — Skipping Closure



Many projects drift to an end without formal closure. This means:

No lessons learned captured → same mistakes repeated
No formal acceptance → disputes about what was delivered
Resources not released → they remain allocated but idle
Contracts not closed → lingering financial liabilities

section: Case Study — Al-Maktoum International Airport Expansion, Dubai
text:
Case Study — Al-Maktoum International Airport Expansion, Dubai






Caution🏗️ Case Study — Al-Maktoum International Airport Expansion



Al-Maktoum International Airport (DWC) in Dubai South is planned to become the world’s largest airport, with an ultimate capacity of 260 million passengers per year. The expansion programme illustrates all five process groups in action.

4.8.2 Project Overview







Attribute
Detail




Location
Dubai South (Jebel Ali), UAE


Estimated cost
$35+ billion (full build-out)


Phases
Multi-phase over 20+ years


Client
Dubai Aviation Engineering Projects (DAEP)


Key challenge
Phased construction while maintaining existing operations





4.8.3 Process Groups in Action

🚀 Initiating📋 Planning⚙️ Executing📊 Monitoring & Controlling🏁 Closing



Strategic alignment: Part of Dubai’s vision to be the world’s aviation hub, aligning with Dubai 2040 Urban Master Plan
Business case: Forecast demand exceeding Dubai International Airport’s (DXB) 100M passenger capacity
Project charter: Defined scope as a phased expansion — runway, terminals, cargo, ground transportation
Stakeholder identification: UAE General Civil Aviation Authority, airlines, Dubai Tourism, neighbouring Expo 2020/District 2040 developments, 200+ airline customers




Scope: Full WBS developed for each phase — airside (runways, taxiways, ATC tower), landside (terminals, parking, access roads), systems (baggage, security, IT)
Schedule: Primavera P6 master schedule with 50,000+ activities; critical path through terminal foundations and runway construction
Cost: Class 3 estimate progressing to Class 1; Earned Value Management mandated on all packages
Quality: ITP covering all structural, MEP, and ICT systems; BIM Level 2 mandated
Risk: 500+ risks in the register; key risks include ground conditions (sabkha soil), extreme heat (50°C+), supply chain disruptions, interface conflicts between packages




Team management: Peak workforce estimated at 60,000+ workers from 40+ nationalities
Procurement: Multiple design-build packages awarded to international joint ventures
Quality assurance: Third-party inspection agencies; BIM clash detection before every pour
Communications: Weekly dashboards to DAEP leadership; monthly reports to Dubai Executive Council
Stakeholder engagement: Regular coordination with existing DWC operations to minimise disruption




Earned Value: Monthly EVM reporting (CPI, SPI) at programme, package, and activity level
Change control: Programme Change Board meets bi-weekly; all changes assessed for impact on schedule, cost, and interfaces
Schedule monitoring: 4-week lookahead schedules; delay analysis using Time Impact Analysis (TIA) method
Risk monitoring: Monthly risk reviews; risks that materialise become issues tracked in a separate register
Scope control: BIM model frozen at stage gates; any post-freeze changes require formal variation order




Phased handover: Each terminal zone goes through Testing & Commissioning (T&C), Operational Readiness (ORAT), and formal handover
Lessons learned: Captured at the end of each phase; fed into the planning of subsequent phases
Document turnover: As-built BIM models, O&M manuals, and warranty certificates collected per handover zone
Benefits realisation: Passenger capacity and airline satisfaction measured against business case projections






4.8.4 Lessons for Process Groups

All five process groups operate in every phase — initiation happens again when a new terminal phase is authorised; planning is continuous; monitoring never stops
The planning process group is the backbone — 50,000+ scheduled activities require meticulous planning to coordinate
Monitoring & controlling prevents surprises — EVM and schedule analysis catch deviations early
Closing is critical in phased projects — each phase must be formally closed and handed over before the next can fully begin
Integration is the PM’s core job — with hundreds of interfaces between packages, the programme management team’s primary role is integration

section: 5.1 Time Value of Money — The Financial Foundation ➕ Extended
text:
5.1 Time Value of Money — The Financial Foundation ➕ Extended
Before evaluating any project, engineers must understand one key principle: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future. This is the Time Value of Money (TVM) — the foundation of all engineering economics and project financial analysis.






Note📖 Why Does Money Have a Time Value?



Three reasons: 1. Opportunity cost — money available today can be invested to earn returns 2. Inflation — purchasing power erodes over time 3. Risk — future cash flows are uncertain; present cash is certain
An engineering firm offered $1,000,000 today or $1,000,000 in 3 years will always choose today — they can invest it now and have more than $1M in 3 years.



5.1.1 Future Value (FV)
Future Value answers: If I invest $P today at interest rate r, what will it be worth after n periods?
\[\boxed{FV = PV \times (1 + r)^n}\]
Where: - \(PV\) = Present Value (amount today) - \(r\) = Interest (discount) rate per period - \(n\) = Number of periods






Tip💡 Solved Example 2.1 — Future Value



Problem: An engineering company invests $50,000 in a piece of testing equipment that generates a return. If the investment earns 8% per year, what is the future value after 5 years?
Solution:
\[FV = PV \times (1 + r)^n = 50{,}000 \times (1 + 0.08)^5\]

5.1.3 Net Present Value (NPV)
Net Present Value answers the most important question in project selection: Does this project create or destroy value?
\[\boxed{NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}}\]
Where: - \(B_t\) = Benefits (cash inflows) in year \(t\) - \(C_t\) = Costs (cash outflows) in year \(t\) - \(r\) = Discount rate - \(t\) = Time period (year 0 = today)
Decision Rule: - \(NPV > 0\) → Project creates value → Accept - \(NPV < 0\) → Project destroys value → Reject - \(NPV = 0\) → Project breaks even at the discount rate

The answer is that all figures in the NPV table are estimates and forecasts, produced during the Business Case / Feasibility Study phase. Here is where each number typically comes from:

This is the whole point of NPV as a selection tool:

Before committing to execute a project, decision-makers need to know: Is this investment worth it? NPV uses the best available estimates at the time to answer that question — accepting that estimates carry uncertainty.

A good business case always documents the assumptions behind each number (e.g., “Year 1 cost savings assume 20% reduction in manual processing time based on a pilot study”). This makes it clear what must hold true for the NPV to be valid — and what risks could change it.










Note📝 Note on Notation



\(B_t - C_t\) is simply the net cash flow at time \(t\), often written as \(CF_t\). The two forms are identical:
\[\sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t} \equiv \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}\]

\(CF_t > 0\) → net benefit that year (benefits exceed costs)
\(CF_t < 0\) → net cost that year (costs exceed benefits)

Some textbooks separate \(B_t\) and \(C_t\) explicitly for clarity; others combine them into a single \(CF_t\) term. Both mean the same thing.




5.1.4 NPV with Variable Discount Rates
The standard NPV formula assumes a single constant discount rate \(r\) across all years. In practice, however, discount rates often change year by year — due to shifting interest rates, changing risk profiles, or project-specific cost-of-capital adjustments.
When each year has its own discount rate \(r_t\), the simple exponent \((1+r)^t\) no longer works. Instead, you use the cumulative product of all per-period rates up to year \(t\).
\[\boxed{NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1+r_i)}}\]
Where: - \(CF_t\) = Net cash flow in year \(t\) (benefits minus costs) - \(r_i\) = Discount rate applicable to period \(i\) - \(\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1+r_i)\) = Cumulative product of discount factors from period 1 through period \(t\) - Year 0 cash flows are not discounted (they are already in today’s money)
Discount factor for each year:
\[DF_t = \frac{1}{(1+r_1)(1+r_2)\cdots(1+r_t)}\]
Notice how each year’s factor compounds all previous years’ rates — this is the cumulative product method.






Note🔍 Why Cumulative Product and Not Just \((1+r_t)^t\)?



With a constant rate, \((1+r)^t\) is simply shorthand for multiplying \((1+r)\) by itself \(t\) times:
\[(1+r)^t = \underbrace{(1+r)(1+r)\cdots(1+r)}_{t \text{ times}}\]
With variable rates, you replace each identical factor with the actual rate for that period:
\[\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1+r_i) = (1+r_1)(1+r_2)\cdots(1+r_t)\]
The two formulas are identical when all rates are the same. The cumulative product is simply the general form that works in all cases.

5.1.5 Return on Investment (ROI)

العائد على الاستثمار

Return on Investment (ROI) measures how much value a project generates relative to its cost. It answers: For every dollar invested, how much do I get back?
\[\boxed{ROI = \frac{\text{Net Discounted Benefits}}{\text{Discounted Costs}} = \frac{\text{Discounted Benefits} - \text{Discounted Costs}}{\text{Discounted Costs}}}\]
Decision Rule: - \(ROI > 0\%\) → Project returns more than it costs → Accept - \(ROI = 0\%\) → Project breaks even - \(ROI < 0\%\) → Project loses money → Reject - Higher ROI = more efficient use of investment

Interpretation: For every $1 invested (in today’s money), the project returns $1.12 in net benefit — meaning you get your dollar back plus $1.12 on top. The project is 112% efficient on its investment.

5.1.6 Payback Period
Payback Period is the point in time when cumulative discounted benefits first equal or exceed cumulative discounted costs — i.e., when the project recoups its investment.
It is found by tracking the net position (cumulative benefits − cumulative costs) year by year until it turns positive:
\[\text{Net Position}_t = \sum_{i=0}^{t} \text{Discounted Benefits}_i - \sum_{i=0}^{t} \text{Discounted Costs}_i\]
Step 1 — Identify the payback year: the first year where Net Position ≥ 0.
Step 2 — Calculate the exact (fractional) payback to know the precise month:
\[\boxed{\text{Exact Payback} = \text{Last negative year} + \frac{|\text{Net Position at last negative year}|}{\text{Net cash flow in payback year}}}\]
Where Net cash flow in payback year = Discounted Benefits − Discounted Costs for that year.
Multiply the decimal fraction by 12 to convert to months.
Decision Rule: - Shorter payback → less risk, faster return of investment - Compare against a target (e.g., “must pay back within 3 years”)

5.1.7 Break-Even Analysis

هي الحد الأدنى من المبيعات الذي يجب تحقيقه لتغطية جميع التكاليف

Break-even analysis determines the minimum level of sales (units or revenue) that must be achieved to cover all costs — both fixed and variable. At the break-even point, the project neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss. Every unit sold below break-even means a loss; every unit sold above it generates profit.






Note📖 Core Concepts



To perform a break-even analysis, you need to understand three building blocks:








Concept
Definition
Example




Fixed Costs (FC)
Costs that do not change regardless of how many units are produced or sold — you pay them even if output is zero
Rent, equipment purchase, software licences, salaries of permanent staff


Variable Costs (VC)
Costs that increase with every unit produced or sold
Raw materials, packaging, sales commissions, direct labour per unit


Selling Price (SP)
Revenue received per unit sold
Price charged to the customer per item



Contribution Margin (CM) is the amount each unit contributes toward covering fixed costs — and eventually generating profit:
\[CM = \text{Selling Price per Unit} - \text{Variable Cost per Unit}\]
Intuition: Think of it this way — every unit you sell first pays for its own variable cost, and whatever is left over goes toward paying off the fixed costs. Once fixed costs are fully covered, you have reached break-even. After that, every unit sold is pure profit.


Break-Even Point (in units):
\[\boxed{BEP_{\text{units}} = \frac{\text{Fixed Costs}}{CM} = \frac{\text{Fixed Costs}}{\text{Selling Price per Unit} - \text{Variable Cost per Unit}}}\]
Break-Even Point (in revenue $):
\[\boxed{BEP_{\text{revenue}} = BEP_{\text{units}} \times \text{Selling Price per Unit}}\]
Decision Rule:



Actual Sales vs. BEP
Meaning




Sales < BEP
Loss — not enough sales to cover all costs


Sales = BEP
Break-even — all costs covered, profit = $0


Sales > BEP
Profit — every unit beyond BEP earns pure margin

5.1.8 Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
The IRR is the discount rate at which the NPV of a project equals zero. In other words, it is the project’s own internal rate of return — the rate the project earns on every dollar invested.
\[\boxed{\text{Find } r \text{ such that: } NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t} = 0}\]

The Hurdle Rate
The Hurdle Rate (also called the minimum acceptable rate of return, MARR) is the minimum return the organisation requires before it will invest in a project. It typically reflects:



Component
Example




Cost of borrowing money (loan/bond interest)
5%


Expected return from alternative investments
7%


Risk premium for this type of project
2%


Resulting Hurdle Rate
~8–10%



The organisation sets the hurdle rate before evaluating any project. The IRR is then compared to it:
\[\text{IRR} > \text{Hurdle Rate} \Rightarrow \text{Accept} \qquad \text{IRR} < \text{Hurdle Rate} \Rightarrow \text{Reject}\]


How IRR is Calculated (Trial & Error + Interpolation)
There is no direct formula to solve for IRR — you cannot isolate \(r\) algebraically when \(n > 1\). Instead, you use trial and error:

Pick two trial rates — one that gives a positive NPV (too low) and one that gives a negative NPV (too high). The IRR lies between them.
Interpolate linearly to estimate the exact crossing point.

How to choose trial rates: - Start with the hurdle rate (e.g., 8%) — if NPV > 0, the project exceeds the hurdle, so try higher. - Try 5% steps (10%, 15%, 20%) until NPV flips sign. - You need one positive NPV and one negative NPV — the IRR is between those two rates.
\[\boxed{IRR \approx r_L + \frac{NPV_L}{NPV_L - NPV_H} \times (r_H - r_L)}\]
Where: - \(r_L\) = lower trial rate (gives positive NPV) - \(r_H\) = higher trial rate (gives negative NPV) - \(NPV_L\) = NPV at \(r_L\) (positive) - \(NPV_H\) = NPV at \(r_H\) (negative)

Percentage return (%)
Comparing with hurdle rate
Can give misleading results with non-conventional cash flows


Payback
Speed of cost recovery (years)
Risk assessment; cash flow constraints
Ignores time value; ignores cash flows after payback


ROI
Return as % of cost
Quick comparison metric
Doesn’t account for time value or duration



Best practice: Use NPV as primary decision criterion; use IRR and payback as supplementary checks.

5.2 The Initiation Phase 📋 Required
The Initiation Phase is where a project is formally authorised to begin. This phase answers the fundamental questions: Should we do this project? Who is authorised to lead it? Who are the key players?

5.2.1 Project Initiation Triggers
A project does not start on its own — it is always triggered by a need, problem, or external requirement. PMBOK identifies the following common triggers:








Trigger
Description
Example




Market demand
A market opportunity or customer need
Develop a water-saving product due to drought


Business need
Internal organisational requirement
Upgrade ageing IT infrastructure


Customer request
A specific client asks for work
Client commissions a bridge design


Technological advance
New technology requires adoption
Migrate systems to cloud platform


Legal requirement
New law or regulation must be complied with
Build a wastewater plant to meet EPA standards


Ecological/social need
Environmental or community pressure
Remediate a contaminated site


Directive
New requirements imposed by management, government, or external authority
Management orders a safety upgrade across all sites









Important⚠️ Directive — Exam Tip



A directive is a requirement imposed by management, government, or an external authority that the organisation has no choice but to comply with. Unlike market-driven or business-need projects, directive projects are mandatory — they proceed regardless of financial return (e.g., regulatory compliance, safety mandates, government legislation).
Key point: When a project is initiated because of a directive, the business case may still be prepared — but the decision to proceed is not optional.

title: 5  Project Initiation & Selection
text:
5.3 The Business Case 📋 Required
Before any project begins, the organisation must determine whether the project is worth doing. This is the purpose of the Business Case.






Note📖 What is a Business Case?



A Business Case is a documented justification for undertaking a project, showing that the expected benefits outweigh the costs, risks, and effort required. It is the primary decision-making document for project approval.



5.3.1 Elements of a Strong Business Case

1. Problem Statement2. Options Analysis3. Financial Analysis4. Risk Summary5. Recommendation


What problem or opportunity is being addressed?

Current situation (As-Is)
Desired future state (To-Be)
Gap analysis
Urgency and consequence of inaction

Example: “Route 60 (الطريق 60، الطريق الرئيسي القدس-رام الله) currently handles 38,000 vehicles/day — 42% above its designed capacity. This causes an average of 1.8 hours daily congestion, costing the West Bank regional economy an estimated $65M per year in productivity losses and contributing to dangerous road safety conditions…”


What are the possible solutions?
Present at least three options: - Option 0: Do nothing (baseline comparison) - Option 1: Minimum viable solution - Option 2: Recommended solution
- Option 3: Maximum solution
Evaluate each option against criteria: cost, benefit, risk, timeline, feasibility


Does it make financial sense?
Key financial metrics:








Metric
Formula
Good Indicator




Net Present Value (NPV)
\(NPV = \sum \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}\)
NPV > 0


Return on Investment (ROI)
\(ROI = \frac{Benefit - Cost}{Cost} \times 100\%\)
ROI > hurdle rate


Payback Period
Months to recover investment
< threshold period


Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR)
\(BCR = \frac{Benefits}{Costs}\)
BCR > 1





What are the key risks to delivery and benefit realisation?

Top 5 project delivery risks
Top 5 operational/benefit risks
Overall risk rating
Key risk mitigation strategies



What should the decision-maker approve?

Clearly state the recommended option
State total approved budget
State approved timeline
List key conditions and assumptions

title: 5  Project Initiation & Selection
text:
5.4 Project Selection Models 📋 Required
Before a project is formally authorised, organisations must decide which projects to pursue from a pool of competing proposals. Project selection is a strategic decision that balances financial return, strategic fit, risk, and resource availability.






Note📖 Why Project Selection Matters



Organisations always have more candidate projects than available resources. A disciplined selection process ensures that approved projects:

Align with strategic objectives
Deliver an acceptable return on investment
Are technically and operationally feasible
Fit within available resource capacity




5.4.1 Categories of Selection Models
Project selection models fall into two broad categories:





%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 30, 'rankSpacing': 60}}}%%
flowchart TD
    S["PROJECT SELECTION MODELS"] --> N & M
    N["NON-NUMERIC MODELS<br/>No mathematical calculation<br/>Based on judgment & policy"] --> N1 & N2 & N3
    M["NUMERIC MODELS<br/>Quantitative analysis<br/>Objective comparison"] --> M1 & M2
    N1["Sacred Cow<br/>Championed by senior exec<br/>Not challenged formally"]
    N2["Operating Necessity<br/>Required for legal / safety<br/>compliance"]
    N3["Comparative Benefit<br/>Rank projects by<br/>strategic value score"]
    M1["Profitability Models<br/>NPV, IRR, Payback,<br/>BCR"]
    M2["Scoring Models<br/>Weighted criteria<br/>across multiple factors"]

    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style N fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e40af
    style M fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534


 Project selection model categories 






5.4.2 Profitability (Financial) Models
For projects that generate measurable financial returns, these models provide objective comparison:

Financial selection models







Model
Formula
Decision Rule




Net Present Value (NPV)
\(NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}\)
Accept if NPV > 0; higher NPV preferred


Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
Rate where \(NPV = 0\)
Accept if IRR > hurdle rate


Payback Period
\(PP = \frac{\text{Initial Investment}}{\text{Annual Net Cash Flow}}\)
Shorter payback preferred


Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR)
\(BCR = \frac{\text{PV of Benefits}}{\text{PV of Costs}}\)
Accept if BCR > 1.0

5.4.3 Weighted Scoring Model
When projects must be compared on multiple criteria beyond financials, the Weighted Scoring Model provides a structured, transparent process:
Steps:

5.6 Stakeholder Identification and Analysis 📋 Required
Stakeholder management is consistently identified as one of the most critical — and most underestimated — aspects of engineering project management.






Note📖 Definition — Stakeholder



A stakeholder is any individual, group, or organisation that: - May affect the project, OR - May be affected by the project, OR - May perceive themselves to be affected by the project
This includes both positive stakeholders (who benefit) and negative stakeholders (who are disadvantaged).
