title: 5  Project Initiation & Selection
section: Case Study — Dubai Metro: Red Line Project
text:
Case Study — Dubai Metro: Red Line Project






Important🏭 Case Study: Dubai Metro — World’s Longest Fully Automated Metro System



Background:
The Dubai Metro was initiated in 2005 as a response to Dubai’s rapidly growing population and worsening road congestion. The Red Line project was the world’s largest single contract public transport system at the time, valued at USD $7.6 billion.
Initiating the Project:
The project followed a rigorous initiation process:

Business Case — Traffic modelling showed Dubai’s road network would be saturated by 2010. Rail was the only viable mass transit solution.
Feasibility Study — Multiple route options assessed over 18 months before Red Line alignment was chosen.
Project Charter — Government of Dubai issued Decree authorising the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA) as project owner.
Stakeholder Analysis — Over 200 stakeholder groups identified including: Dubai government, RTA, Hitachi-led consortium, 47 sub-contractors, 300,000+ daily users (projected), property owners along alignment, Dubai Metro Authority.

Stakeholder Challenges:








Stakeholder
Issue
How it was Managed




Property Owners
Land acquisition for 52km alignment
Government-mandated acquisition + fair compensation package


Adjacent Businesses
Construction disruption for 3 years
Vibration monitoring, restricted working hours in key areas, compensation scheme


Cultural Groups
Women-only carriages requirement
Dedicated carriages in Gold Class section


Environmental Groups
Coastal construction impacts
Environmental impact assessment + mitigation measures



Outcome:
The Red Line opened in September 2009 — on time for the Dubai World Expo. It now carries over 600,000 passengers per day.
Key Initiation Success Factors: - High-level government sponsorship (Ruler’s office directly involved) - Extremely detailed stakeholder mapping with dedicated relationship managers per group - Clear project charter with unambiguous governance structure - International PM expertise brought in to supplement local capability - Early community engagement, not just at approval stage
Discussion Questions: 1. How did political will and government sponsorship affect the success of this project? 2. What are the risks of having too many stakeholders vs. too few? 3. How would you adapt the stakeholder communication plan for a project of this scale?

Caution✏️ Exercise 2.1 — Business Case Development



Scenario: The West Bank Water Authority is considering replacing 120 km of ageing asbestos-cement water mains installed in the 1970s across the Ramallah governorate. The pipes are causing 180+ leaks per year, losing an estimated 35% of distributed water, and costing ₪8.5 million (~$2.3M) annually in emergency repairs and water loss.
Develop a Business Case Summary that includes:

Three options (Do Nothing / Reactive Emergency Repairs / Full Phased Replacement Programme)
For each option: Estimated cost, estimated benefit, risk rating
A recommendation with justification

Key data provided: - Pipe replacement cost: ~$280K/km (phased over 6 years with donor co-funding from the World Bank) - Each leak event: $13,000 average direct cost (repair + water lost) - Water loss from leakage: ~35% of annual production (valued at $1.4M/yr) - Customer complaints from low pressure and interruptions: 1,800/year - Critical risk: A main failure near Ramallah Government Hospital would trigger a public health emergency

title: 6  Project Integration Management
section: 6.1 What Is Project Integration Management? 📋 Required
text:
6.1 What Is Project Integration Management? 📋 Required
Project integration management involves coordinating all of the other project management knowledge areas throughout a project’s life cycle. It ensures that all elements of a project come together at the right times to complete the project successfully.
The PMBOK® Guide defines six core processes in project integration management:

        P1["Develop\nProject Charter"]
    end
    subgraph PLN["📋 PLANNING"]
        P2["Develop Project\nManagement Plan"]
    end
    subgraph EXE["⚙️ EXECUTING"]
        P3["Direct & Manage\nProject Work"]
    end
    subgraph MC["📊 MONITORING & CONTROLLING"]
        P4["Monitor & Control\nProject Work"]
        P5["Perform Integrated\nChange Control"]
    end
    subgraph CLO["🏁 CLOSING"]
        P6["Close Project\nor Phase"]
    end

    INI --> PLN --> EXE --> CLO
    EXE <--> MC
    PLN <--> MC

    style INI fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff,stroke:#4f46e5
    style PLN fill:#0f766e,color:#fff,stroke:#0f766e
    style EXE fill:#15803d,color:#fff,stroke:#15803d
    style MC fill:#b45309,color:#fff,stroke:#b45309
    style CLO fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c


 Project integration management — six processes mapped to process groups 









Note📖 Key Concept — Why Integration Management Matters



The project manager’s primary responsibility is integration management — coordinating all people, plans, and work so the project succeeds. This includes:

Interface management: identifying and managing points of interaction between project elements
Communication: keeping all stakeholders informed across organizational boundaries
Decision-making: resolving conflicts among project goals and team members
Big-picture focus: steering the entire project toward successful completion

Many project managers make the mistake of focusing on technical work rather than integration. A technically excellent project can still fail if the project manager ignores stakeholder communication, planning, and change control.

title: 6  Project Integration Management
section: 6.2 Strategic Planning and Project Selection 📋 Required
text:
6.2 Strategic Planning and Project Selection 📋 Required
Before managing a project, organisations must decide which projects to pursue. This is where strategic planning and project selection come in.

6.2.1 Strategic Planning
Strategic planning involves determining long-term objectives by:

Analysing the strengths and weaknesses of the organisation
Studying opportunities and threats in the business environment
Predicting future trends and projecting the need for new products and services

A widely used strategic planning tool is SWOT analysis:





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
quadrantChart
    title SWOT Analysis — Four Dimensions
    x-axis Internal --> External
    y-axis Negative --> Positive
    quadrant-1 Opportunities
    quadrant-2 Strengths
    quadrant-3 Weaknesses
    quadrant-4 Threats
    Existing expertise: [0.2, 0.8]
    Technical skills: [0.3, 0.75]
    No marketing plan: [0.2, 0.25]
    Limited budget: [0.3, 0.2]
    Growing market: [0.75, 0.8]
    New client project: [0.8, 0.85]
    Strong competition: [0.75, 0.25]
    Technology risks: [0.85, 0.15]


 SWOT analysis framework for identifying potential projects 





6.2.2 The Four-Stage IT Project Selection Process
Organisations that manage IT projects well typically follow a structured, four-stage process for selecting projects:

Four-stage IT project planning process (Schwalbe, Ch.4)








Stage
Name
Purpose
Key Output




1
IT Strategy Planning
Align IT strategy with organisational mission and vision
Strategic IT goals


2
Business Area Analysis

Business case list


3
Project Planning
Define potential projects — scope, benefits, constraints
Project candidates


4
Resource Allocation
Select projects and assign resources
Approved project list





6.2.3 Categorising IT Projects
Organisations can categorise potential IT projects by their source or nature:

ProblemsOpportunitiesDirectives


Address undesirable situations requiring correction — e.g., a buggy legacy system causing financial reporting errors.


Capitalise on favourable conditions — e.g., developing a mobile app to reach a new customer segment.


Respond to new requirements imposed by management, government regulation, or customers — e.g., a GDPR compliance system.

title: 6  Project Integration Management
text:
6.3 Methods for Selecting Projects
Once potential projects are identified, organisations use financial and scoring methods to compare and rank them.

6.3.1 Net Present Value (NPV) Analysis
NPV discounts all future cash flows back to today’s value, reflecting the time value of money.
\[NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}\]
Where: - \(C_t\) = cash flow at time \(t\) - \(r\) = discount rate (cost of capital) - \(n\) = project duration (years)
Decision rule: Select projects with NPV > 0. A higher NPV indicates greater value created.






Tip💡 Solved Example 4.1 — NPV Analysis



An engineering company is evaluating a new IT system. Initial investment (Year 0): $120,000. Discount rate: 10%.

\[NPV = -120{,}000 + 27{,}270 + 33{,}040 + 37{,}550 + 34{,}150 + 24{,}840 = \mathbf{\$36{,}850}\]
Decision: NPV = $36,850 > 0 → Accept the project




6.3.2 Return on Investment (ROI)
\[ROI = \frac{\text{Total Discounted Benefits} - \text{Total Discounted Costs}}{\text{Total Discounted Costs}} \times 100\%\]






Tip💡 Solved Example 4.2 — ROI



If total discounted benefits = $120,000 and total discounted costs = $100,000:
\[ROI = \frac{120{,}000 - 100{,}000}{100{,}000} \times 100\% = \mathbf{20\%}\]
A positive ROI indicates the project returns more than it costs. Higher ROI is preferred when comparing alternatives.




6.3.3 Payback Analysis
Payback period is the time required to recover the initial investment from project cash flows.
\[\text{Payback Period} = \text{Year before recovery} + \frac{\text{Unrecovered amount at start of year}}{\text{Cash flow during year}}\]

\[\text{Payback Period} = 3 \text{ years}\]
If the organisation’s maximum acceptable payback is 4 years → Project is acceptable




6.3.4 Weighted Scoring Model
When financial analysis alone is insufficient, a weighted scoring model rates each project on multiple criteria using assigned weights.
Steps: 1. Identify evaluation criteria important to the organisation 2. Assign a weight (%) to each criterion (weights sum to 100%) 3. Score each project on each criterion (e.g., 0–100) 4. Calculate weighted score = weight × score for each criterion 5. Sum weighted scores and compare

The balanced scorecard (developed by Kaplan and Norton) converts an organisation’s value drivers into defined metrics across four perspectives:

title: 6  Project Integration Management
text:
6.4 Developing a Project Charter 📋 Required
Once top management selects a project to pursue, the first formal step is to develop the project charter — the document that officially authorises the project.

6.4.1 What Is a Project Charter?
A project charter is a document that:

Formally recognises the existence of a project
Provides direction on the project’s objectives and management
Authorises the project manager to use organisational resources
Should be signed by key stakeholders to acknowledge agreement







Note📖 Key Inputs for Developing a Project Charter










Input
Description




Statement of Work (SOW)
Describes the products/services the project will create; includes business need, requirements, and strategic alignment


Business Case
Justifies the investment; includes objectives, high-level requirements, and financial goals


Agreements/Contracts
Relevant for external projects — contract terms often map to charter content


Enterprise Environmental Factors
Government regulations, industry standards, organisation infrastructure, marketplace conditions


Organisational Process Assets
Policies, templates, lessons learned, historical information from previous projects







6.4.2 Project Charter Contents
Although formats vary, a project charter should include at minimum:

Core ElementsApproach & GovernanceComments & Supporting Docs



Project title and date of authorisation
Project manager name and contact information
Summary schedule — planned start and finish dates; key milestones
Summary budget — total cost estimate or reference to budgetary documents
Project objectives — brief description of goals and business justification




Project success criteria — measurable outcomes; who signs off on acceptance
Management approach summary — stakeholder needs, assumptions, constraints, references to subsidiary plans
Roles and responsibilities matrix — who is responsible for what
Sign-off section — signatures of key project stakeholders




Comments section — space for stakeholder concerns or important notes
References to related plans: communications plan, risk plan, procurement plan










Tip💡 Solved Example 4.5 — Partial Project Charter



Project Title: Campus Network Upgrade Project
Date of Authorisation: 1 September 2026
Project Manager: Eng. Reem Al-Haddad | reem@aaup.edu
Projected Start: 1 October 2026 | Projected Finish: 31 March 2027
Key Milestones:

Project charter milestones


Milestone
Target Date

15 October 2026

15 December 2026

31 January 2027

31 March 2027



Objectives: Upgrade the campus network infrastructure to support gigabit speeds for 2,000 concurrent users across 8 buildings, enabling online learning and administrative applications.
Budget Summary: $450,000 (±20% at charter stage)
Approach: Use a phased rollout building-by-building to minimise disruption. An external network contractor will be engaged for installation. Weekly status reports to the sponsor.
Success Criteria: 99.5% network uptime within 30 days of go-live; all buildings connected; user acceptance confirmed by IT Director.

title: 6  Project Integration Management
section: 6.5 Developing a Project Management Plan 📋 Required
text:
6.5 Developing a Project Management Plan 📋 Required
The project management plan is the central document that integrates and coordinates all other planning outputs. It is far more than a Gantt chart.

6.5.1 Project Management Plan Contents
A comprehensive project management plan includes:

Project management plan subsidiary plans






Section
Content




Scope management plan
How scope will be defined, validated, and controlled


Schedule management plan
How the schedule will be developed and controlled


Cost management plan
How costs will be estimated, budgeted, and controlled


Quality management plan
Quality standards and assurance/control activities


Resource management plan
How physical and human resources will be acquired and managed


Communications management plan
What information is communicated, to whom, when, and how


Risk management plan
How risks will be identified, analysed, and responded to


Procurement management plan
How goods and services will be acquired from outside the project


Stakeholder engagement plan
How stakeholders will be engaged and managed


Change management plan
How changes will be requested, evaluated, and controlled









Note📖 Key Concept — The Purpose of a Project Management Plan




“The main purpose of project plans is to facilitate action.” — Schwalbe

A project management plan is not just documentation for its own sake. It exists to:

Guide the project team in executing the work
Establish baselines against which progress is measured
Provide a basis for communicating with stakeholders
Enable controlled changes when circumstances change

Best practice: Those who will do the work should plan the work. The project manager solicits input from all team members and specialists.




6.5.2 Using Guidelines to Create Project Management Plans
Many organisations provide guidelines and templates to ensure consistency across projects. Notable standards include:

IEEE Standard 1058-1998 — Software Project Management Plan (SPMP): covers overview, project organisation, managerial process plans, technical process plans, and supporting process plans
U.S. DoD Standard 2167 — Software Development Plan for defence projects
PMI PMBOK® Guide — knowledge area plans as subsidiary components

title: 6  Project Integration Management
section: 6.6 Directing and Managing Project Work 📋 Required
text:
6.6 Directing and Managing Project Work 📋 Required
Directing and managing project work is the process of executing the project management plan — actually doing the work to produce the project’s deliverables.

6.6.1 Key Outputs of Execution





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart TD
    PM["📋 Project Management Plan\n(Input)"] --> EXEC["⚙️ Direct & Manage\nProject Work"]
    CR["✅ Approved Change\nRequests (Input)"] --> EXEC
    EXEC --> D["📦 Deliverables"]
    EXEC --> WPI["📊 Work Performance\nInformation"]
    EXEC --> CRQ["🔄 Change Requests"]
    EXEC --> UPD["📝 Plan & Document\nUpdates"]

    style EXEC fill:#15803d,color:#fff,stroke:#15803d


 Outputs of directing and managing project work 





6.6.2 Factors for Successful Execution

Strong LeadershipSupportive CultureBusiness & Technical Knowledge


Project managers must lead by example — if they follow through on their own plans, team members are more likely to do the same.
A project manager must: - Provide clear direction and priorities - Motivate and develop the team - Navigate organisational politics to remove barriers - Break rules when necessary (with good judgement and political skill)


A supportive organisational culture promotes: - Useful guidelines and templates that help (not hinder) getting work done - A culture that uses project plans as the basis for performing work and measuring progress - Clear lines of authority and decision-making


Project managers need to understand: - The application area of the project (the business domain) - The product being created - Enough technical knowledge to guide the team and evaluate options
For large projects: a strong business/domain background often matters more than technical expertise.





6.6.3 Project Execution Tools and Techniques







Tool/Technique
Description




Expert judgment
Consulting specialists on methodology, technology, and approach


Meetings
Face-to-face, phone, and virtual meetings for communication, problem-solving, and relationship-building


Project Management Information Systems (PMIS)
Software for scheduling, tracking, and reporting (e.g., MS Project, Primavera)

title: 6  Project Integration Management
section: 6.7 Monitoring and Controlling Project Work 📋 Required
text:
6.7 Monitoring and Controlling Project Work 📋 Required
Monitoring and controlling project work runs continuously from initiation through closing. It involves:

Comparing actual performance to the project management plan
Identifying variances and taking corrective action
Providing forecasts to update current cost and schedule information
Monitoring implementation of approved changes
Reporting on project status to stakeholders

flowchart LR
    PLAN["📋 Baseline Plan\n(Schedule, Cost, Scope)"]
    EXEC["⚙️ Execute\nProject Work"]
    MEASURE["📊 Measure Actual\nPerformance"]
    COMPARE["🔍 Compare:\nActual vs. Plan"]
    VARIANCE{Variance?}
    CORRECT["🔧 Corrective\nAction"]
    REPORT["📢 Status\nReport"]

    PLAN --> EXEC --> MEASURE --> COMPARE --> VARIANCE
    VARIANCE -->|"Yes"| CORRECT --> EXEC
    VARIANCE -->|"No"| REPORT
    CORRECT --> REPORT

    style PLAN fill:#0f766e,color:#fff
    style CORRECT fill:#b45309,color:#fff


 Monitor and control project work — continuous loop

title: 6  Project Integration Management
text:
6.8 Performing Integrated Change Control 📋 Required
Change is inevitable on projects. The question is not whether changes will occur, but whether they will be managed effectively.

6.8.1 What Is Integrated Change Control?
Integrated change control involves identifying, evaluating, and managing changes throughout the project life cycle. It ensures that:

Changes are formally requested and documented
Impacts on scope, cost, and schedule are assessed before approval
Only approved changes are implemented
All affected plans and documents are updated accordingly



6.8.2 The Change Control System
A formal change control system includes:





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart TD
    REQ["📝 Change Request\nSubmitted"] --> LOG["📋 Log Change\nRequest"]
    LOG --> ASSESS["🔍 Impact Assessment\n(Scope, Cost, Schedule, Risk)"]
    ASSESS --> CCB["👥 Change Control\nBoard (CCB) Review"]
    CCB --> DEC{Decision}
    DEC -->|"Approved"| UPDATE["📝 Update Plans,\nBaselines & Docs"]
    DEC -->|"Rejected"| NOTIFY["📢 Notify\nRequestor"]
    DEC -->|"Deferred"| PEND["⏳ Pending\nReview"]
    UPDATE --> IMPL["⚙️ Implement\nApproved Change"]
    IMPL --> CLOSE["✅ Close Change\nRequest"]

    style CCB fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff
    style DEC fill:#b45309,color:#fff


 Change control process flow 





6.8.3 The Change Control Board (CCB)
A Change Control Board (CCB) is a group of authorised stakeholders who review, evaluate, and approve or reject change requests. The CCB:

Meets regularly (or on-demand for urgent changes)
Reviews all proposed changes against project baselines
Considers cost, schedule, and scope impacts
Has the authority to approve, reject, or defer changes



6.8.4 Configuration Management
Configuration management ensures that the performance and physical characteristics of a product are consistent with its requirements and documentation. On IT projects it involves:

Identifying and documenting configuration items (software versions, hardware specs, documents)
Controlling changes to those items
Recording and reporting the status of changes
Verifying that products conform to their specifications

6.8.5 Suggestions for Performing Integrated Change Control







Recommendation
Explanation




View project management as communication and negotiation
Changes involve people; manage relationships proactively


Plan for change from the start
Build contingency reserves and define the change process early

Prevents ad-hoc changes that derail the project


Use configuration management
Maintains integrity of project deliverables and documents


Use performance reports to identify needed changes
Variance reports often reveal scope creep or needed adjustments


Focus on leading — don’t get lost in managing every change
Delegate detailed change tracking; focus on overall project direction

title: 6  Project Integration Management
text:
6.9 Closing Projects or Phases 📋 Required
Closing a project or phase involves finalising all activities and transferring the completed (or cancelled) work to the appropriate parties.

6.9.1 Key Outputs of Project Closing

Final Product TransitionOrganisational Process Asset UpdatesPost-Implementation Review


The sponsor receives the final product, service, or result as specified. For contracted work, this requires formal written acceptance. Internal projects often use a project completion form or client acceptance form.


The project team delivers: - Project documentation — all plans, reports, and records - Project closure document — formal sign-off that the project is complete - Final project report — summary of outcomes, costs, schedule performance, and a transition plan for ongoing operations - Lessons-learned report — captures what went right, what went wrong, and recommendations for future projects


Many organisations conduct a post-implementation review (also called a post-project audit) to: - Verify that the project achieved its stated objectives - Measure the benefits realised against the business case - Capture institutional knowledge for future projects









Note📖 Key Concept — Final Project Report Structure



A typical final project report includes:

Project Objectives — what the project set out to achieve
Summary of Project Results — what was actually delivered
Original vs. Actual Start/End Dates — schedule performance
Original vs. Actual Budget — cost performance
Project Assessment — was it a success? What went right and wrong?
Transition Plan — handover to operations; ongoing support requirements
Attachments — all key project management documentation (charter, scope statement, WBS, Gantt charts, risk register, lessons learned, acceptance form)

section: 7.1 What Is Project Scope Management? 📋 Required
text:
7.1 What Is Project Scope Management? 📋 Required
Project scope management includes the processes required to ensure that the project includes all the work required — and only the work required — to complete the project successfully.






Note📖 Key Concept — Product Scope vs. Project Scope











Term
Definition
Measurement




Product scope
The features and functions that characterise a product, service, or result
Measured against product requirements


Project scope
The work that must be done to deliver a product, service, or result with the specified features and functions
Measured against the project management plan






7.1.1 The Six Scope Management Processes

title: 7  Project Scope Management
text:
7.2 Planning Scope Management 📋 Required
The scope management plan is the first output of scope management. It documents how the project team will:

Define and develop project scope
Create, maintain, and approve the WBS
Formally accept completed deliverables (scope validation)
Handle requests for changes to scope (scope control)

The requirements management plan documents how project requirements will be:

Requirements management plan components


Aspect
Managed By




Analysed and documented
Requirements analysis process


Tracked and reported
Traceability matrix (RTM)


Prioritised
MoSCoW or weighted criteria


Managed through changes
Integrated change control


Verified
Acceptance testing

title: 7  Project Scope Management
text:
7.3 Collecting Requirements 📋 Required
Collecting requirements is often the most difficult step in scope management — and the most consequential. Research shows that rework from poor requirements can consume up to half of total project costs.

7.3.1 Why Requirements Are So Hard
Studies of software development projects found:

73% of teams said the most important challenge was gaining a clear understanding of what customers wanted
70% spent at least 10% of their time managing requirement changes
83% still used MS Word/Excel as the primary tool for communicating requirements



7.3.2 Cost of Late Requirements Changes
The later in the project lifecycle a requirement defect is found, the more expensive it is to fix:





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
xychart-beta
    title "Relative Cost to Correct a Requirements Defect"
    x-axis ["Requirements", "Design", "Code", "Test", "Operations"]
    y-axis "Relative Cost" 0 --> 120
    bar [1, 5, 10, 40, 100]


 Relative cost to fix a requirements defect by phase (after Grady, 1999) 









Warning⚠️ Common Mistake — Insufficient Requirements Gathering



Skipping thorough requirements gathering to “save time” is one of the most common — and costly — project mistakes. A defect found during operations costs 100× more to fix than the same defect found in the requirements phase.




7.3.3 Requirements Collection Techniques

InterviewsFocus Groups & WorkshopsQuestionnaires & SurveysObservationPrototypingDocument Analysis & Benchmarking


One-on-one discussions with key stakeholders.

Best for: Complex systems; senior stakeholders
Pros: Deep understanding; builds relationships
Cons: Time-consuming; expensive at scale



Facilitated group sessions (e.g., Joint Application Design — JAD) bring together sponsors, users, business analysts, and developers to jointly define requirements.

Best for: Consensus-building; resolving conflicting needs
JAD workshops are highly structured, intensive, typically 1–5 days
Produces detailed, agreed-upon requirements faster than one-on-one interviews



Structured questions sent to a large group of stakeholders.

Best for: Large user populations; geographic distribution
Pros: Efficient and scalable
Cons: Responses may be shallow; low return rates



Watching users perform their current work processes (also called job shadowing).

Best for: Process improvement projects; system replacement
Pros: Reveals actual vs. stated behaviour
Cons: Disruptive; requires significant analyst time



Developing a working replica or mock-up of part of the system for user feedback.

Best for: UI-heavy systems; unclear requirements
Can be throwaway (for learning only) or evolutionary (grows into final product)
Use case modelling is a related technique for identifying system interactions



Reviewing existing documentation (current systems, contracts, standards) and comparing to similar projects/products inside or outside the organisation.

Best for: System replacements; compliance-driven projects
Ensures continuity with existing processes

A Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) links each requirement to its source and tracks its status through implementation and testing.

title: 7  Project Scope Management
text:
7.4 Defining Scope 📋 Required
Defining scope provides a detailed description of the work required for the project. It is critical because:

It improves accuracy of time, cost, and resource estimates
It defines a baseline for performance measurement and project control
It aids in communicating clear work responsibilities to all stakeholders
It establishes the boundary between what is and what is not included in the project


7.4.1 The Project Scope Statement
The project scope statement is the primary output of scope definition. It should include at minimum:

Project scope statement components






Component
Description




Product scope description
Detailed description of the product, service, or result to be created


Product user acceptance criteria
The conditions that must be met for the customer to accept the deliverable


Project deliverables
A list of all outputs the project will produce


Project exclusions
Explicit statement of what is not included — prevents scope creep


Project boundaries
Interfaces with other projects or systems


Project constraints
Limitations on budget, schedule, resources, or technology


Project assumptions
Statements treated as true for planning purposes that have not been confirmed









Tip💡 Solved Example 5.2 — Project Scope Statement (Progressive Elaboration)



Project: Campus Network Upgrade
Version 1 (Charter-level, early in project): > “Upgrade the campus network to gigabit speeds for all buildings, including servers, switches, and wireless access points as needed.”
Version 2 (Detailed scope statement, after planning): > “Upgrade the campus network in 8 buildings (Buildings A–H) to support 1 Gbps wired connections and 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) wireless with coverage in all offices, classrooms, and common areas. The project includes replacing all existing Cat5 cabling with Cat6A, installing new Cisco Catalyst 9300 switches, deploying 120 Cisco 9130 Wi-Fi access points, and upgrading the core router. Excluded from scope: building G (under renovation), internet service provider (ISP) contract renegotiation, and end-user devices.”
The scope statement becomes more specific and detailed as the project progresses — this is called progressive elaboration.








Warning⚠️ Common Mistake — Vague Scope Statements



A scope statement like “Upgrade the IT infrastructure” is dangerously vague. Every stakeholder will have a different interpretation. Ambiguous scope is the leading cause of:

Scope creep (uncontrolled additions to the project)
Stakeholder dissatisfaction
Cost and schedule overruns

title: 7  Project Scope Management
section: 7.5 Creating the Work Breakdown Structure 📋 Required
text:
7.5 Creating the Work Breakdown Structure 📋 Required
A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) is a deliverable-oriented hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to be carried out by the project team.






Note📖 Key Concept — The WBS Is the Foundation of Project Planning



The WBS provides the basis for:

Scheduling — all activities in the project schedule come from the WBS
Cost estimating and budgeting — costs are estimated at work package level
Resource assignment — resources are assigned to work packages
Change control — work outside the WBS is considered out-of-scope


“Work should not be done on a project if it is not included in the WBS.” — PMI




7.5.1 WBS Structure and Levels





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart TD
    L1["**LEVEL 1**\nEntire Project\n(Project Name)"]
    L2A["**LEVEL 2**\nMajor Deliverable/Phase\n(e.g., Web Site Design)"]
    L2B["**LEVEL 2**\nMajor Deliverable/Phase\n(e.g., Web Site Development)"]
    L2C["**LEVEL 2**\nProject Management"]
    L3A["**LEVEL 3**\nSub-deliverable\n(e.g., Home Page)"]
    L3B["**LEVEL 3**\nSub-deliverable\n(e.g., Department Pages)"]
    L4A["**LEVEL 4 — Work Package**\n(e.g., Design graphics)"]
    L4B["**LEVEL 4 — Work Package**\n(e.g., Write content)"]

    L1 --> L2A & L2B & L2C
    L2A --> L3A & L3B
    L3A --> L4A & L4B

    style L4A fill:#15803d,color:#fff
    style L4B fill:#15803d,color:#fff


 WBS structure — levels and work packages 



Work packages are the lowest-level tasks in the WBS — they are the units at which: - Work time estimates are entered into project software - Resources and costs are assigned - The project manager monitors and controls progress


7.5.2 WBS Numbering
The PMI Practice Standard for Work Breakdown Structures defines a hierarchical numbering scheme:
1.0  Campus Network Upgrade Project
  1.1  Project Management
    1.1.1  Project charter
    1.1.2  Weekly status reports
    1.1.3  Project closure report
  1.2  Network Design
    1.2.1  Current state assessment
    1.2.2  Topology design
    1.2.3  Design review and approval
  1.3  Procurement
    1.3.1  Bill of materials
    1.3.2  Vendor selection
    1.3.3  Purchase orders
  1.4  Installation
    1.4.1  Cabling (Buildings A–D)
    1.4.2  Cabling (Buildings E–H)
    1.4.3  Switch configuration
    1.4.4  Wireless AP deployment
  1.5  Testing & Acceptance
    1.5.1  Performance testing
    1.5.2  Security testing
    1.5.3  User acceptance testing


7.5.3 Approaches to Developing a WBS

Using GuidelinesAnalogy ApproachTop-Down ApproachBottom-Up ApproachMind Mapping


Many organisations and government agencies prescribe WBS formats. Following guidelines ensures: - Consistency across projects - Easier evaluation of proposals - Reuse of templates from similar past projects
Example: The U.S. Department of Defense provides mandatory WBS structures for defence contracts. Contractors must follow these WBS formats in their cost proposals.


Use a WBS from a similar previous project as a starting template and adapt it.

Pros: Fast; based on real experience; less risk of omissions
Best for: Organisations that repeatedly do similar projects (e.g., building construction, system implementations)



Start with the overall project at Level 1, then progressively break it down into smaller pieces.

Natural approach for most projects
Works well when the project scope is well-understood at the start
Senior project managers and stakeholders drive the decomposition



Start by identifying all specific tasks that need to be done, then group them into higher-level categories.

Best for: Novel projects where the scope is not well-defined at a high level
More inclusive — team members contribute their own task lists
Results are then rolled up into a coherent WBS



Use a visual mind map to brainstorm all project deliverables and tasks without initially worrying about hierarchy.

Place the project name in the centre
Add branches for major deliverable areas
Add sub-branches for more detailed tasks
Convert the mind map to a formal WBS hierarchy

Mind mapping encourages creativity and helps capture ideas that linear outlining might miss.









Tip💡 Solved Example 5.3 — WBS for an Engineering IT Project



Project: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) Implementation for a Manufacturing Company
1.0  ERP Implementation Project
  1.1  Project Management
    1.1.1  Project charter approved
    1.1.2  Project management plan
    1.1.3  Weekly status reports
    1.1.4  Project closure
  1.2  Requirements & Design
    1.2.1  Business process analysis
    1.2.2  System requirements document
    1.2.3  Data migration plan
    1.2.4  System configuration design
  1.3  Software & Infrastructure

    1.3.2  Server hardware installed
    1.3.3  Network configuration
    1.3.4  ERP system configured
  1.4  Data Migration
    1.4.1  Legacy data extracted
    1.4.2  Data cleansed and transformed
    1.4.3  Data loaded into ERP
    1.4.4  Data validation and sign-off
  1.5  Testing
    1.5.1  Unit testing
    1.5.2  Integration testing
    1.5.3  User acceptance testing (UAT)
  1.6  Training
    1.6.1  Training materials developed
    1.6.2  End-user training delivered
    1.6.3  IT administrator training
  1.7  Go-Live & Support
    1.7.1  Go-live plan executed
    1.7.2  Post-go-live support (30 days)
    1.7.3  Project closure report
Work package example (1.5.3): User Acceptance Testing
Duration estimate: 15 days | Resources: 2 business analysts + 5 key users | Cost: $18,500

The WBS feeds directly into the project schedule:

text:
7.7 Validating Scope 📋 Required
Scope validation (also called scope verification) is the process of formally accepting completed project deliverables from the customer or sponsor.






Note📖 Key Concept — Scope Validation vs. Quality Control











Aspect
Scope Validation
Quality Control




Focus
Was the right work delivered?
Was the work done correctly?


Who performs it
Customer / sponsor / stakeholders
Project team / QA staff


Question asked
“Is this what we asked for?”
“Does this meet specifications?”


Output
Accepted deliverables / change requests
Verified deliverables


Timing
After QC has confirmed quality
During execution



Quality control is typically performed before scope validation. A deliverable should be verified as correct before presenting it to the customer for acceptance.



7.7.1 Scope Validation Process





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart TD
    QC["✅ Quality Control\nCompleted"] --> PRESENT["📤 Present Deliverable\nto Customer/Sponsor"]
    PRESENT --> REVIEW["🔍 Stakeholder\nInspection & Review"]
    REVIEW --> DEC{Accepted?}
    DEC -->|"✅ Yes"| ACCEPT["📝 Formal Acceptance\nDocument Signed"]
    DEC -->|"❌ No"| DEFECT["📋 Document Deficiencies\n& Change Requests"]
    DEFECT --> REWORK["🔧 Rework /\nCorrective Action"]
    REWORK --> PRESENT

    style ACCEPT fill:#15803d,color:#fff
    style DEFECT fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff


 Scope validation process flow

title: 7  Project Scope Management
text:
7.8 Controlling Scope 📋 Required
Scope control involves managing changes to the project scope while keeping the project on track toward its goals.

7.8.1 What Is Scope Creep?
Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of project scope — adding features, functions, or requirements without adjusting budget, schedule, or resources.






Warning⚠️ Common Cause — Scope Creep



Scope creep typically occurs because:

Requirements were not adequately defined or documented from the start
Stakeholders continuously request “small” additions that were never in scope
The project team accommodates informal requests without going through change control
There is no clear process for evaluating and approving changes to scope

Every scope addition — no matter how small — has an impact on cost, schedule, and resources.




7.8.2 Variance Analysis for Scope Control
An important tool for scope control is variance analysis — comparing planned vs. actual scope delivery:
\[\text{Scope Variance} = \text{Planned Deliverables} - \text{Actual Deliverables Completed}\]
If the variance is negative (less delivered than planned), the project manager must investigate the cause and take corrective action.


7.8.3 Best Practices for Scope Control

Keep Scope RealisticInvolve Users ActivelyReduce Changing RequirementsUse Off-the-Shelf TechnologyFollow Good PM Processes



Don’t make projects so large they can’t be completed
Break large projects into a series of smaller projects
Set a firm completion date — “May 1 was the drop-dead date, and everything else was backed into it”




Assign key users to the project team
Give users ownership of requirements definition and scope validation
Require users to sign off on key deliverables at review meetings
Deliver working software/hardware regularly for user feedback
Locate users near developers during the project




Use a formal requirements management process from the start
Apply prototyping, use case modelling, and JAD to thoroughly understand user needs
Put all requirements in writing and keep them current
Use a requirements management database (CASE tools, dedicated software)
Require all scope changes to include associated cost and schedule impacts




Avoid new/unproven technology unless its benefits clearly outweigh the risks
New technology introduces scope uncertainty — its capabilities are often unclear at the start




Establish formal change control procedures from the start (as part of integrated change control — Chapter 4)
Allocate dedicated resources for handling change requests
Use the WBS and scope statement as the authoritative definition of scope






7.8.4 IBM’s Rational Unified Process (RUP) Principles for Scope Management
The IBM Rational Unified Process provides these best-practice principles for software scope management:







Principle
Application




Adapt the process
Tailor scope management to project size and complexity


Balance competing stakeholder priorities
Negotiate scope trade-offs among stakeholders systematically


Collaborate across teams
Involve all affected parties in defining and approving scope


Demonstrate value iteratively
Deliver scope in increments to get early feedback


Elevate the level of abstraction
Use models and diagrams to communicate scope, not just text


Focus continuously on quality
Define acceptance criteria for each scope element

An IT project team has been working for three months when a senior manager requests that new functionality be added to the system. The team lead says “it’s a small change — we can just add it.” What is wrong with this approach, and what should happen instead?

title: 8  Project Planning & Work Breakdown Structure
text:
8.2 Requirements Collection 📋 Required
Before defining scope, the PM must understand what stakeholders need (requirements) vs. what they want (desires).

8.2.1 Requirements Elicitation Techniques

InterviewsWorkshopsSurveys & QuestionnairesObservation & Prototyping


One-on-one discussions with key stakeholders
Best for: Sponsors, senior users, technical experts
Tips: - Prepare open-ended questions - Ask “what does success look like to you?” - Probe: “What happens if we don’t do X?” - Document and validate responses after each interview


Structured group sessions to define requirements collaboratively
Best for: Large stakeholder groups with competing priorities
Techniques within workshops: - Brainstorming — generate ideas freely - Affinity diagramming — group related ideas - MoSCoW prioritisation — Must/Should/Could/Won’t - Impact mapping — how requirements link to goals


Structured data collection at scale
Best for: Large user bases, when in-person engagement is impractical
Tips: - Limit to 10-15 questions - Mix closed (rating) and open (text) questions - Always pilot test before sending


See the work being done or show a draft solution
Observation (Job Shadowing): - Watch end-users perform their current process - Identify pain points they can’t articulate - Document the “As-Is” process
Prototyping: - Build a low-fidelity mockup - Use it to validate requirements early - Cheaper to change a sketch than a built system





8.2.2 Requirements Documentation
Requirements should be documented using a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM). Before looking at the full matrix, let’s understand what each column means and why it matters:






Note📚 Understanding the RTM — Column by Column




RTM Column Guide








Column
What It Means
Example (R001)
Teaching Tip




Req ID (Requirement Identifier)
A unique code that identifies each requirement — think of it as a “fingerprint” for that requirement
R001
Encourage smart coding: use FUNC-001 for functional requirements and NFR-001 for non-functional ones


Requirement (Description)
A clear, testable sentence that starts with “The system shall…”
“The system shall process 500 data points/second”
Teach the SMART rule: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound


Source (Origin)
Who or what requested this requirement? (a person, document, or regulation)
User interviews
Always document the source — it protects the project from disputes later


Priority (Importance Level)
How critical is this requirement to project success?
Must
Introduce the MoSCoW model: ✅ Must — non-negotiable · 🔶 Should — important but deferrable · 🔹 Could — nice-to-have if time allows · ❌ Won’t — out of scope for this version


Acceptance Criteria (Verification Test)
How do we prove that the requirement has been met? A measurable, pass/fail test
“Processing test passing 500 data points/second”
Key message: “No acceptance criteria = no way to verify = the requirement is incomplete”


Linked Deliverable (Work Output)
Which project deliverable or work package fulfils this requirement?
Software v1.0
Helps the team distribute tasks and track accountability across the WBS


Status (Current State)
Where is this requirement in its lifecycle right now?
Approved
Suggested lifecycle: 📝 Draft → 🔍 Under Review → ✅ Approved → 🧪 In Testing → 🎯 Delivered

title: 8  Project Planning & Work Breakdown Structure
text:
8.3 The Scope Statement 📋 Required
The Project Scope Statement is the definitive document that describes what will be delivered and what will not:






Note📖 What a Good Scope Statement Contains




Project Scope Description — Detailed description of the product/service/result
Project Deliverables — All outputs the project must produce
Acceptance Criteria — How each deliverable will be measured and accepted
Project Exclusions — Explicitly what is NOT in scope
Constraints — Limiting factors (budget, time, regulatory, technical)
Assumptions — Conditions assumed to be true (must be validated)









Warning⚠️ The Single Most Dangerous Document Gap



The most common and costly scope error is failing to explicitly state exclusions.
Bad scope statement: “Design and construct a 500m pedestrian footbridge”
Good scope statement: “Design and construct a 500m steel-decked pedestrian footbridge between Points A and B. This project does NOT include: associated roadworks, lighting beyond the bridge deck, maintenance hangar, or path connections at either abutment.”
Undefined = In scope (in the client’s mind). If you don’t explicitly exclude it, you’ll be expected to deliver it.

“تصميم وإنشاء جسر مشاة بطول 500 متر”





الطرف
ما الذي يفهمه؟




✅
العميل
جسر + إنارة + طرق وصول + صيانة + تنسيق محيط


✅
فريق المشروع
فقط هيكل الجسر الأساسي


🎯
النتيجة
فجوة التوقعات — والعميل دائماً يتوقع الأكثر!



الدرس: كل ما لم يُستثنَ صراحةً في بيان النطاق، يُعدّ داخل النطاق في ذهن العميل.

8.4 Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) 📋 Required
The Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) is the most critical planning tool in project management. It is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work into manageable components called work packages.






Note📖 The 100% Rule




“The WBS includes 100% of the work defined by the project scope and captures ALL deliverables — internal, external, and interim — in terms of the work to be completed.”

Every element in the WBS must sum to 100% of the parent element’s work. Nothing is omitted; nothing is duplicated.

8.4.2 WBS Development Guidelines

Decomposition RulesWBS DictionaryWBS NumberingCommon WBS Mistakes


How to break down the WBS properly:

Decompose by deliverables, not by activities — the WBS is a things to be delivered structure, not a task list
Stop at the work package level — packages small enough to be: estimated, assigned to ONE person/team, and monitored
Apply the 80-Hour Rule — no work package should exceed 80 hours of effort (2 work weeks)
Apply the 100% Rule — each parent level = sum of all children (no gaps, no overlaps)
Use nouns, not verbs — “Foundation Concrete” not “Pour foundation concrete”



Each work package needs a WBS Dictionary entry:
The WBS Dictionary provides the definition for each element:







Field
Description




WBS Code
1.4.2


Work Package Name
Concrete Structures


Description
Supply and place all reinforced concrete for filter chambers, pump station walls, base slabs, and roof slabs. Excludes blinding concrete.


Responsible Party
Civil Contractor


Deliverables

Acceptance Criteria

Duration Estimate
8 weeks


Cost Estimate
$285,000


Dependencies

Standard WBS numbering convention:
1.0 Project
  1.1 Phase/Deliverable 1
    1.1.1 Sub-deliverable
    1.1.2 Sub-deliverable
      1.1.2.1 Work Package
      1.1.2.2 Work Package
  1.2 Phase/Deliverable 2
    1.2.1 Sub-deliverable
    ...
Numbers should: - Be unique (no two elements share a number) - Reflect hierarchy (depth of decomposition) - Be stable (don’t renumber if items are added)


Avoid these errors:
❌ Activities instead of deliverables — “Design the pump” should be “Pump Design Package”
❌ Missing the 100% rule — forgetting project management, testing, documentation
❌ Too much decomposition — breaking everything down to 1-hour tasks creates unmanageable complexity
❌ Unclear scope boundaries — work package descriptions that overlap with another package
❌ Skipping the WBS dictionary — the diagram alone is not enough; definitions are essential
❌ One person owns everything — each work package should have a single accountable owner

8.5 The Project Management Plan 📋 Required
The Project Management Plan (PMP) is the master document that describes how the project will be planned, executed, and controlled. It integrates all subsidiary plans:





mindmap
  root((📄 PROJECT<br/>MANAGEMENT<br/>PLAN))
    Subsidiary Plans
      Scope Management Plan
      Schedule Management Plan
      Cost Management Plan
      Quality Management Plan
      Resource Management Plan
      Communications Management Plan
      Risk Management Plan
      Procurement Management Plan
      Stakeholder Engagement Plan
    Baselines
      Scope Baseline<br/>= WBS + Dictionary
      Schedule Baseline<br/>= Approved Schedule
      Cost Baseline<br/>= Approved Budget
    Other Documents
      Change Management Plan
      Configuration Mgmt Plan
      Requirements Mgmt Plan
      Project Governance Plan


 Components of the Project Management Plan 









Warning⚠️ The PMP is Not the Project Schedule!



Many students (and some practitioners) confuse the Project Management Plan with the project schedule.
The PMP is the meta-document — it describes how the project will be managed in each knowledge area. The schedule is just ONE of many components of the PMP.
A complete PMP for a large engineering project may contain 200+ pages across all subsidiary plans.

section: 8.6 Scope Creep — The Silent Project Killer 📋 Required
text:
8.6 Scope Creep — The Silent Project Killer 📋 Required
Scope creep is the gradual, uncontrolled expansion of project scope without corresponding changes to budget, schedule, or resources.





sequenceDiagram
    actor Client
    actor PM
    actor Team

    Note over Client,Team: Project starts with defined scope
    
    Client->>PM: "Can we just add a small feature?" (No formal request)
    PM->>Team: "Sure, it's small, just do it"
    Note over Team: Work added without change control
    
    Client->>PM: "Can we extend to Building C?" (No formal request)
    PM->>Team: "OK, the client asked"
    Note over Team: Schedule starts slipping
    
    Client->>PM: "Why is the project late and over budget?"
    PM->>Client: "We added work without approving changes..."
    Note over Client,Team: Relationship damaged, claims possible


 How scope creep happens and its impact 




8.6.1 Change Control Process
Every project must have a formal change control process:

section: Case Study — Haramain High Speed Railway: WBS Coordination Across Borders
text:
Case Study — Haramain High Speed Railway: WBS Coordination Across Borders






Important🏭 Case Study: Haramain High Speed Railway — When Integration Fails at Scale



Background:
The Haramain High Speed Railway (قطار الحرمين السريع — HHR) connects the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah via Jeddah and King Abdullah Economic City, spanning 450 kilometres at speeds up to 300 km/h. This is the Arab world’s flagship rail project, operating in one of the most challenging environments on Earth — the Hejaz Mountains and the Arabian Desert.
Original Plan vs Actual: - Contract signed: 2009 - Original completion: 2013 - Actual opening: October 2018 (5 years late) - Budget: ~$16.5 billion (USD)
The WBS Problem:
The programme was divided between four major international consortia, each operating under different engineering standards and document management systems:








Consortium
Nationality
Scope




Al Shoula Group / Saudi Binladin Group
Saudi
Civil works — earthworks, structures, track foundation


Al Rajhi / China Railway Engineering
Chinese-Saudi
Northern civil works alignment


RENFE / CAF / Ineco
Spanish
Railway systems, signalling, rolling stock, operations


Siemens / Alstom
European
Electrification and E&M systems



Each consortium applied its own CAD standards, document numbering systems, and interface protocols — with no unified digital coordination environment across the programme.
What Happened:
- Civil works were substantially complete by 2013, but systems integration — connecting trains, signalling, electrification, and station systems — caused a further 5 years of delays - The interface between European-standard rail systems and Saudi civil infrastructure was managed informally, with no dedicated interface register - In 2016, a crisis at Saudi Binladin Group (the Kingdom’s largest contractor, suspended following safety incidents) forced urgent contractor replacement across 300+ km of residual civil works - Testing and commissioning of 40 stations required re-coordination of 12 separate sub-systems, each owned by a different consortium
Impact:







Factor
Effect




5-year programme delay
Billions in financing and standing costs


Contractor suspension (SBG)
6+ months for retendering and remobilisation


Signalling integration failures
18 additional months of testing and rectification


Interface ambiguity
300+ formal interface non-conformances logged



Project Management Root Causes:








Failure
Root Cause
PM Lesson




No unified interface register
Each consortium managed its own interfaces
Create a Programme Interface Register owned by an independent systems integrator


Four different CAD/document standards
No standardisation mandated at contract award
Mandate a single BIM/document management platform at programme initiation


Late commissioning focus
Testing planned as a single terminal activity
Overlap testing with construction using rolling section commissioning


Contractor financial collapse
No annual contractor capability re-assessment
Include contractor financial health reviews as a governance requirement in mega-contracts



The Achievement:
Despite its troubled delivery, the HHR now carries hundreds of thousands of pilgrims between Makkah and Madinah annually, reducing the historic 4–6 hour road journey to 2.5 hours by train — the Arab world’s first true high-speed railway.
Discussion Questions: 1. How should the WBS dictionary have addressed the interface between civil works (SBG scope) and railway systems (RENFE scope)? 2. What governance structure would you design to manage a four-consortium programme of this scale? 3. How does this case compare to the Airbus A380 integration failure? What structural similarities exist?
Sources: Saudi Railways Organisation (2018); Arab Union of Railways (2017)

Exercises






Caution✏️ Exercise 3.1 — Requirements Collection



You are PM for the design and construction of a new university engineering laboratory (1,500 m²).

Identify at least 8 categories of stakeholders who would have requirements for this lab
Write 3 specific requirements for each of 4 stakeholder groups (use the RTM format)
For each requirement, assign a priority (Must / Should / Could)
Identify 2 conflicting requirements and explain how you would resolve them









Caution✏️ Exercise 3.2 — Build a WBS



For the construction of a new community footbridge (80m span, steel throughtruss, timber deck, two abutments), develop a complete WBS that:

Has at least 4 levels of decomposition
Includes ALL project phases (from charter to closure)
Contains at least 30 work packages at level 4
Follows the 100% Rule (verify by checking each parent sums to 100%)
Includes a WBS Dictionary entry for 5 of the work packages

Hint: Consider these Level 1 categories: Project Management, Investigation, Design, Procurement, Construction, Commissioning, Closure








Caution✏️ Exercise 3.3 — Scope Statement Writing



A client has given you the following brief:

“We want you to fix our factory’s compressed air system. The compressors keep breaking down and it’s costing us $80,000 a year in repairs and lost production.”

Write a Scope Statement for this project that includes: 1. Project scope description 2. List of deliverables (minimum 6) 3. Acceptance criteria for at least 3 deliverables 4. Explicit exclusions (minimum 4 things that are NOT in scope) 5. Key assumptions (minimum 3) 6. Key constraints (minimum 2)








Caution✏️ Exercise 3.4 — Change Control Scenario



You are PM of a $3.5M road reconstruction project (12 months). You are in Month 4.
The client project manager calls you and says: > “We’ve had a great idea. While you’ve got the road dug up, can you install a new stormwater pipe underneath? The council surveyed it last week and it will need replacing in 3 years anyway. Saves us digging it up twice.”

Is this a reasonable request? Argue both for and against
Prepare an Impact Assessment covering: scope, schedule, cost, risk, and quality
What additional information would you need before completing the assessment?
Draft a Change Request Form (use the fields: ID, Date, Description, Requestor, Impact Summary, PM Recommendation)
How would you respond to the client verbally while the formal assessment is in progress?

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.2 Why Time Management Matters 📋 Required
Time management is frequently cited as the most challenging dimension of the triple constraint. Schedule issues are the primary source of conflict on IT and engineering projects — ahead of budget disputes or scope changes.






Warning⚠️ The Schedule Challenge




Time is the least flexible constraint: You can find extra budget; you can negotiate scope — but you cannot recover lost calendar time.
Schedule overruns are visible: Clients see delays immediately; cost overruns can be hidden longer.
IT projects are persistently late: Studies show the average IT project overruns its schedule by 70%; the Standish Group CHAOS Report consistently identifies schedule as the top failure dimension.




9.2.1 Individual and Cultural Differences
People’s relationship with time varies — this affects how teams approach schedules:








Dimension
Description
Scheduling Implication




Structured (J-type) — Myers-Briggs
Plans ahead, wants defined milestones, dislikes uncertainty
Follows schedules well; may over-engineer early planning


Flexible (P-type) — Myers-Briggs
Adapts as they go, resists rigid timelines, works under pressure
Tends to use up float; milestone reminders are essential


Monochronic cultures
Sequential focus; punctuality is a value; time is a resource
Will adhere to schedules; expect dates to be honoured


Polychronic cultures
Multiple simultaneous activities; relationships over deadlines
Need clearer milestone expectations and follow-up



Awareness of these differences helps PMs design realistic schedules and communicate deadlines effectively.
crumbs: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.3 Planning Schedule Management 📋 Required
Before defining any activities, the project team must agree on how scheduling will be done. This is captured in the Schedule Management Plan — a subsidiary plan within the overall Project Management Plan.






Note📖 Schedule Management Plan — Contents










Component
What It Defines




Scheduling methodology
CPM, critical chain, agile sprints, or a combination; which software tool


Level of accuracy
How precise must estimates be? (±10%, nearest hour, nearest day)


Units of measure
Hours, days, weeks, or calendar dates — consistent across all activities


Control thresholds
Acceptable variance before action is required (e.g., ±5% schedule variance)


Performance measurement rules
How progress is measured: % complete, milestone-based, or earned value


Reporting formats
What schedule reports go to whom, and how often (weekly Gantt to PM; monthly S-curve to sponsor)


Process descriptions
Who updates the schedule? Who approves changes? What is the change control process?





The schedule management plan is approved early in the project and defines the rules for all subsequent scheduling work.

section: 9.4 Activity Definition and Duration Estimating 📋 Required
text:
9.4 Activity Definition and Duration Estimating 📋 Required

9.4.1 From Work Packages to Activities
Work packages from the WBS must be further broken down into schedule activities — the individual tasks that can be tracked on a daily/weekly basis.







WBS Work Package
Schedule Activities




1.3.1 Foundation Design
A1: Geotechnical data review; A2: Foundation type analysis; A3: Structural calculations; A4: Foundation drawings; A5: Specification writing


1.4.2 Concrete Structures
B1: Formwork fabrication; B2: Reinforcement fixing; B3: Concrete pouring; B4: Curing; B5: Formwork striking; B6: Surface finishing





9.4.2 Activity List and Activity Attributes
The Activity List is a formal project document listing every schedule activity with its key attributes. Each entry contains enough information for planning and tracking:







Attribute
Description




Activity ID
Unique identifier (links back to WBS)


Activity Name
Short descriptive label


Activity Description
What work is being performed


Predecessor Activities
Which activities must finish/start before this one begins


Successor Activities
Which activities depend on this one


Leads and Lags
Any time offsets applied to dependencies


Resource Requirements
People, equipment, and materials needed


Constraints
Fixed dates, imposed deadlines, or resource restrictions


Assumptions
What is assumed to be true (affects duration and cost)









Tip💡 Who Should Estimate?



The people who will actually do the work should provide duration estimates — not the project manager alone. They have the most accurate knowledge of the effort involved, the risks, and the constraints. The PM’s role is to integrate estimates and challenge unrealistic ones.




9.4.3 Duration Estimation Methods

Analogous EstimatingParametric EstimatingThree-Point (PERT) EstimatingBottom-Up Estimating


Use historical data from similar projects

Fast and low effort
Less accurate
Best for early-stage estimates

Example: “Our last 50MW substation took 18 months, so this 60MW substation will take about 21 months”
Accuracy: ±25% to ±50%


Use statistical relationships between variables

Uses unit rates or formulas
More accurate than analogous
Requires reliable data

Example: “Excavation rate for this soil type is 120m³/day with a 20-tonne excavator. We have 2,400m³ to excavate, so: 2,400 ÷ 120 = 20 days”
Accuracy: ±10% to ±25%


Use optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates
Three estimates for each activity: - Optimistic (O): Best case, everything goes right - Most Likely (M): Most realistic estimate - Pessimistic (P): Worst case, everything goes wrong
PERT Expected Duration: \[t_E = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6}\]
PERT Standard Deviation: \[\sigma = \frac{P - O}{6}\]
PERT Variance: \[\sigma^2 = \left(\frac{P - O}{6}\right)^2\]


Estimate each activity individually, then aggregate

Most accurate method
Most time-consuming
Best for detailed planning

Process: 1. Identify all activities 2. Estimate each individually with subject matter experts 3. Sum all activities for total project duration 4. Add buffer/contingency
Accuracy: ±5% to ±15%

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.5 Effort, Duration, and Elapsed Time
These three terms are often confused but have distinct meanings:








Term
Definition
Example




Effort
The total amount of work required (person-hours)
A task requires 40 person-hours of work


Duration
The calendar time from start to finish
That same task takes 5 working days (8h/day × 5 = 40h)


Elapsed time
Calendar time including weekends, holidays, waiting
Concrete curing takes 7 elapsed days even if no one works









Note📖 Key Distinctions




A task that needs 40 hours of effort by one person at 8h/day = 5 working days of duration
The same task with two people = still 40 hours of effort, but ~2.5 days of duration (with coordination overhead)
A physical process like paint drying adds elapsed time (duration) with zero additional effort

Beware the common mistake of treating effort = duration. A PM who assigns two people to a 40-hour task and shows 2.5 days in the schedule must verify that the task is actually parallelisable — not all work can be divided.

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.6 Estimating Activity Resources 📋 Required
Before finalising duration estimates, the project manager must determine what resources are needed for each activity. Resources include:

Human resources — specific people, roles, or skill sets
Equipment — machinery, vehicles, test equipment, lab facilities
Materials — hardware, raw materials, software licences


9.6.1 Resource Breakdown Structure (RBS)
Just as the WBS breaks down the scope, the Resource Breakdown Structure (RBS) categorises all project resources hierarchically. It helps identify potential resource conflicts and ensures every activity has its resource needs documented.


9.6.2 The Resource-Duration Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Resource estimation and duration estimation are interdependent — which makes scheduling an iterative process:

Duration depends on how many resources are assigned
Resource availability depends on the schedule

The practical approach: estimate duration assuming a standard resource assignment, then level the resources (resolve over-allocations) afterwards.


9.6.3 Mythical Man-Month — Brooks’ Law






Warning⚠️ Adding People to a Late Software Project Makes It Later



Frederick Brooks in “The Mythical Man-Month” (1975) identified a counter-intuitive truth about software projects:

“Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.”

Why? Because: 1. New team members need ramp-up time (they consume effort from existing members) 2. Communication overhead increases with each additional person: \(n(n-1)/2\) communication channels for \(n\) people 3. Many software tasks are sequential, not parallel — a woman can have one baby in 9 months; nine women cannot have one baby in one month
Implication: Do not reflexively crash a software project by adding people. Better to focus existing team, reduce scope, or extend the deadline.




9.6.4 Resource Leveling
When the initial schedule creates resource over-allocations (a person assigned to more work than available hours allow), resource leveling resolves conflicts by:

Delaying non-critical activities within their available float
Shifting resources from non-critical to critical tasks
Extending the schedule when float is insufficient

In MS Project: Resource tab → Level Resources applies automatic leveling. The schedule end date will typically move later. The PM must then negotiate whether this is acceptable or whether additional resources must be sourced.

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.7 Activity Sequencing — Dependency Types 📋 Required
Activities must be sequenced based on their logical dependencies:


  
  
    
      Finish-to-Start (FS)
      Most Common
    
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot start until A finishes
    e.g. Excavation must finish before concrete pour starts
  

  
  
    Start-to-Start (SS)
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot start until A starts
    e.g. Training can begin once documentation starts
  

  
  
    Finish-to-Finish (FF)
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot finish until A finishes
    e.g. QA testing cannot end until development ends
  

  
  
    
      Start-to-Finish (SF)
      Rare
    
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot finish until A starts
    e.g. New system (A) starts → old system (B) can shut down
  



9.7.1 Lag and Lead Time

Lag: A delay after a dependency is satisfied

Example: Concrete curing — next activity starts 7 days after pouring finishes (FS + 7 days lag)

Lead: An overlap — the successor activity starts before the predecessor finishes

Example: Begin procurement drawings while detailed design is still 80% complete (FS - 2 weeks lead)




9.7.2 Types of Dependencies
Beyond the four relationship types (FS/SS/FF/SF), dependencies are also classified by their source:









Type
Also Called
Definition
Example




Mandatory
Hard logic
Inherent in the nature of the work — cannot be changed
Foundation must cure before walls are built (physics)


Discretionary
Soft logic, preferred logic
Based on best practice or preference — can be changed if needed
PMs prefer to complete testing before documentation, but could overlap


External
—
Depends on a party outside the project team
Regulatory approval must be received before construction begins









Warning⚠️ Be Careful with Discretionary Dependencies



Discretionary (soft) dependencies are often added out of habit or preference. They reduce scheduling flexibility — and under schedule pressure, teams may break them anyway (creating risk). Review all soft logic before baselineing the schedule. Only keep discretionary dependencies that are genuinely important.

section: 9.8 Network Diagrams — Activity on Arrow (AOA) 📋 Required
text:
9.8 Network Diagrams — Activity on Arrow (AOA) 📋 Required
The Activity on Arrow (AOA) method — also called the Arrow Diagramming Method (ADM) — places activities on arrows and uses numbered circles (nodes) to represent events (start/finish milestones):






Note📖 AOA Rules










Feature
Description




Activities
Represented by arrows (→); label shows the activity name and duration


Events / Nodes
Numbered circles (①②③…) at the tail (start) and head (finish) of each arrow


Node rule
An activity can only start after all activities arriving at its tail node are complete


Dummy Activities
Dashed arrows (- - ▶) with zero duration; used to show logic that cannot be expressed directly


Dependency type
Finish-to-Start (FS) only — AOA cannot represent SS, FF, or SF lags


Identification
Each activity is uniquely identified by its i-j node pair (e.g., activity 1-2)


Usage today
Less common than AON; still used in civil engineering, construction, and CPM/PERT exams







9.8.1 AOA Example — Software Release Project
We will use this five-activity software release as the running example for both AOA and AON (and the conversion between them):

Description
Predecessor(s)
Duration




A
Gather Requirements
—
3 days


B
Create UI Mockups
—
2 days


C
Develop Features
A and B
5 days


D
Write User Manual
B only
2 days


E
System Testing
C
3 days









Tip🔑 Key Logic to Represent




C needs both A and B before it can start
D needs only B — it does NOT need A
This split dependency is the classic situation requiring a dummy activity in AOA






9.8.2 AOA — Simple Sequential Example
Before tackling the split dependency, here is a simple purely sequential AOA to show the diagram conventions:



Activity
Description

A

Excavation and subgrade

    N1(["① Start"])
    N2(["②"])
    N3(["③"])
    N4(["④"])

    N1 -->|"A — 2d"| N2

 AOA — simple sequential project (road paving). Each activity is an arrow; circles are numbered events. 



Project duration = 2 + 5 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 16 days. No dummy needed — purely serial chain.



9.8.3 AOA Dummy Activities
A dummy activity is a dashed arrow with zero duration and zero cost. It represents a logical dependency only — it adds no real work.






Warning⚠️ Two Reasons You Need a Dummy



Reason 1 — Uniqueness constraint: Two real activities share the exact same start node and end node. In AOA every activity is identified by its i-j pair. If activity A and activity B both run from node ① to node ②, they are indistinguishable. A dummy gives one of them a unique node.
Reason 2 — Logic constraint: You need to express that activity C depends on both A and B, while activity D depends only on B — not on A. You cannot draw this correctly in AOA without a dummy.



Reason 1 — Uniqueness: Two Parallel Activities
Given activities:



Activity
Description

Duration




A

—

B

—

C
Develop Module
A and B
5 days




A and B both start independently and both must finish before C can begin. Because A and B share the same start node AND would share the same end node, they cannot be uniquely identified in AOA — a dummy is required.

Wrong (ambiguous — both are “activity 1-2”):

    N1(["①"])
    N2(["②"])
    N3(["③"])

    N1 -->|"A — 3d"| N2
    N1 -->|"B — 2d"| N2
    N2 -->|"C — 5d"| N3

    style N1 fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff


 WRONG: A and B both share nodes ①→②; they cannot be uniquely identified 



Correct (dummy gives B a unique i-j pair):

    N2(["②"])
    N3(["③"])
    N4(["④"])

    N1 -->|"A — 3d"| N2
    N1 -->|"B — 2d"| N3
    N3 -.->|"Dummy (0d)"| N2
    N2 -->|"C — 5d"| N4

    style N1 fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style N4 fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style N3 fill:#f59e0b,color:#fff


 CORRECT: dummy ③→② gives activity B the unique pair 1-3; C starts after both A and B are done 



Node ② now receives: A (from ①→②) AND the dummy (from ③→②, carrying B’s completion). So C waits for both A and B — correct logic, and every activity has a unique i-j identifier.



Reason 2 — Logic: Split Dependency (Software Release Example)
Given activities:



Activity
Description
Predecessor(s)
Duration




A

—
3 days


B

—

A and B
5 days


D

B only
2 days


E

3 days




The critical dependency: C needs both A and B, but D needs B only. Drawing D and C both starting from the same node would force D to also wait for A — a false dependency. A dummy is required to correctly isolate the split.

Requirement: C needs A and B; D needs B only.
Step-by-step AOA construction:

Since D needs only B, B must end at a node where only B arrives — that becomes D’s start node.
Since C needs both A and B, C must start from a node where both arrive.

A already ends at its own node. Add a dummy from B’s end-node to A’s end-node to carry B’s completion into C’s prerequisite check.

    N2(["②<br/>B done"])
    N3(["③<br/>A+B done"])
    N4(["④"])

    N6(["⑥ End"])

    N1 -->|"B — 2d"| N2
    N1 -->|"A — 3d"| N3

    style N2 fill:#0f766e,color:#fff


 AOA — Software Release Project with dummy activity. D starts from ② (only B flows in); C starts from ③ (A plus dummy-from-B flow in).

The dummy arrow ②→③ is the key: it carries B’s completion into node ③ without creating a false dependency between A and D.








Important❌ Common Mistake — Wrong Dummy Direction



If you draw the dummy as ②→③ where ② is A’s end and ③ is B’s end, then D (starting from ③) would also inherit A — giving D a false dependency on A. Always ensure D’s start node has only its required predecessors flowing into it.

Reading the diagram: - Activity B (2d) and Activity A (3d) start simultaneously from node ①
- D starts as soon as B finishes (node ②), independently of A
- C can only start after both A finishes (reaching ③ directly) and B finishes (reaching ③ via the dummy)
- E follows C; the project ends when both E and D are complete at node ⑥

text:
9.9 Network Diagrams — Activity on Node (AON) 📋 Required
The Activity on Node (AON) method — also called the Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM) — places activities inside boxes (nodes) and uses arrows to show dependencies:






Note📖 AON Rules










Feature
Description




Activities
Represented by boxes/rectangles; contain name, ID, and duration


Arrows
Show dependencies only — the arrow means “must finish before” (for FS)


Dependency types
FS, SS, FF, SF — all four types supported; lags and leads can be shown


Dummy activities
Never needed — every dependency is an explicit arrow


Start / End nodes
Optional “Start” and “End” milestone nodes used to clearly bound the network


Used by
All modern PM software: MS Project, Primavera P6, Oracle, etc.

9.9.2 AON Example — Road Paving (Sequential)
For comparison, the same sequential project from the AOA section:

Feature
AOA (Arrow Diagramming)
AON (Precedence Diagramming)




Activities represented as
Arrows
Boxes (nodes)


Nodes/circles represent
Events / milestones
Activities themselves


Dependencies shown by
Numbered node pairs (i-j)
Explicit arrows between boxes

FS only
FS, SS, FF, SF (with lags)


Dummy activities needed?
Sometimes (for logic and uniqueness)
Never


Reading complexity
Harder — must trace arrows through nodes

Rarely (legacy PERT tools)
Yes — MS Project, Primavera P6

In practice, AON is the standard for all modern project scheduling software. AOA is still examined in PMP/CAPM certification exams and appears in older construction scheduling literature.
