section: 9.10 Converting Between AOA and AON 📋 Required
text:
9.10 Converting Between AOA and AON 📋 Required
The same network can always be expressed in both notations. The Software Release example above will be used to demonstrate both directions.


9.10.1 Converting AOA → AON






Note📖 AOA → AON Conversion Rules




Each real activity arrow in AOA becomes a box (node) in AON.
Each dummy activity is discarded — it carries no real work.
For every two activities X and Y in AOA where X’s end-node is Y’s start-node (directly or via a dummy chain), draw an arrow from X’s box to Y’s box in AON.
If multiple activities feed into the same start node in AOA, all of them become incoming arrows to the same box in AON.
Add a START and END milestone box to bound the network.



Step-by-step conversion of the Software Release AOA → AON:







Step
Action




1
List all real activities: A, B, C, D, E


2
Identify the dummy: ②→③. Discard it, but remember what it implied: node ③ is reached by both A (directly) and B (via dummy from ②). So B is a predecessor of C (just like A).


3
Read predecessors from the AOA node logic: D starts from ② (only B); C starts from ③ (A and B); E starts from ④ (only C)


4
Draw boxes for A, B, C, D, E and connect with arrows








flowchart LR
    subgraph AOA["AOA (before)"]
        direction LR
        n1(["①"]) -->|"B—2d"| n2(["②"])
        n1 -->|"A—3d"| n3(["③"])
        n2 -.->|"Dummy"| n3
        n2 -->|"D—2d"| n5(["⑤"])
        n3 -->|"C—5d"| n4(["④"])
        n4 -->|"E—3d"| n6(["⑥"])
        n5 --> n6
    end

    subgraph AON["AON (after)"]
        direction LR
        S(["START"]) --> AA["A 3d"] & BB["B 2d"]
        AA --> CC["C 5d"]
        BB --> CC & DD["D 2d"]
        CC --> EE["E 3d"]
        EE --> EN(["END"])
        DD --> EN
    end

    style n1 fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style n6 fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style CC fill:#7c3aed,color:#fff


 AOA → AON conversion: dummy removed; all dependencies expressed as direct arrows. 






9.10.2 Converting AON → AOA






Note📖 AON → AOA Conversion Rules




Each activity box in AON becomes an arrow in AOA.
Assign numbered nodes (circles) at the start and end of each arrow.
If two or more activities share the same set of predecessors and the same set of successors, they may share start and/or end nodes — but only if this causes no false dependencies. If sharing a node would force an unintended dependency, add a dummy activity.
When activity Y has predecessors X₁ and X₂ in AON: X₁ and X₂ must both end at Y’s start node in AOA. If X₁ and X₂ already end at different nodes, add a dummy from one of those nodes to the other (or to a new merge node).
Check the uniqueness rule: no two real activities may share both the same start node and the same end node.



Step-by-step conversion of the Software Release AON → AOA:








Step
What we know from AON
AOA action




1
A: no predecessor, successor = C
Arrow A from a new start node ①


2
B: no predecessor, successors = C and D
Arrow B also from ①. B and A share the same start node (① — fine, different end nodes).


3
D: predecessor = B only
D can start from B’s end node. Let ② = B’s end. D: ②→⑤


4
C: predecessors = A and B
C must start from a node where both A and B are complete. A ends at ③. B ends at ②. Add Dummy ②→③ to carry B’s completion into ③. C: ③→④


5
E: predecessor = C only
E: ④→⑥


6
End: all paths converge at ⑥
D: ②→⑤→⑥ (add a final merge, or let ⑤ = ⑥ if D and E both end the project)








flowchart LR
    subgraph aon_side["AON (before)"]
        direction LR
        ST(["START"]) --> Ax["A 3d"] & Bx["B 2d"]
        Ax --> Cx["C 5d"]
        Bx --> Cx & Dx["D 2d"]
        Cx --> Ex["E 3d"]
        Ex --> EN2(["END"])
        Dx --> EN2
    end

    subgraph aoa_side["AOA (after)"]
        direction LR
        p1(["①"]) -->|"B—2d"| p2(["②"])
        p1 -->|"A—3d"| p3(["③"])
        p2 -.->|"Dummy (0d)"| p3
        p2 -->|"D—2d"| p5(["⑤"])
        p3 -->|"C—5d"| p4(["④"])
        p4 -->|"E—3d"| p6(["⑥"])
        p5 --> p6
    end

    style ST fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN2 fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style p1 fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style p6 fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style p3 fill:#7c3aed,color:#fff


 AON → AOA conversion: introducing a dummy to correctly represent that C needs both A and B while D needs only B. 









Tip💡 Key Insight — Why the Dummy Appears in AOA but Not AON



In AON, you simply draw two separate arrows into C (one from A, one from B) — no special mechanism needed.
In AOA, a node is a shared milestone. For C to need both A and B, both must arrive at the same node. But D must not see A — so D’s start node can only have B flowing in. The dummy is the only way to “route” B’s completion into the A+B merge node without forcing D to also wait for A.
The dummy solves the structural limitation that AOA can only merge dependencies at a single shared node.

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.11 Critical Path Method (CPM) 📋 Required
The Critical Path Method (CPM) identifies the longest path through the network — the sequence of activities that determines the minimum project duration.






Note📖 CPM Basic Terms & Formulas











Term
Formula
Meaning




ES — Early Start
\(ES = \max(EF \text{ of predecessors})\)
Earliest an activity can start


EF — Early Finish
\(EF = ES + Duration\)
Earliest an activity can finish


LF — Late Finish
\(LF = \min(LS \text{ of successors})\)
Latest it can finish without delaying the project


LS — Late Start
\(LS = LF - Duration\)
Latest it can start without delaying the project


Total Float
\(Float = LS - ES \;=\; LF - EF\)
Flexibility an activity has before it delays the project


Free Float
\(FF = ES_{successor} - EF\)
Flexibility before delaying the next activity


Critical Path
Activities where \(Float = 0\)
Longest path — determines total project duration


Critical Activity
\(Float = 0\)
Any delay on this activity delays the entire project

Step 1: Forward Pass (Calculate ES and EF)






Tip💡 Starting Convention



The first activity always has ES = 0 by convention — the project clock starts at zero. The formula \(ES = \max(EF \text{ of predecessors})\) only applies to activities that have predecessors. Similarly, in the backward pass, LF of the last activity = project duration (not calculated from successors).


\[ES_A = 0 \quad \text{(by convention — no predecessors)}, \quad EF_A = ES_A + Duration_A = 0 + 3 = 3\]
\[ES_B = EF_A = 3, \quad EF_B = 3 + 5 = 8\]
\[ES_C = EF_A = 3, \quad EF_C = 3 + 4 = 7\]
\[ES_D = EF_B = 8, \quad EF_D = 8 + 6 = 14\]
\[ES_E = \max(EF_B, EF_C) = \max(8, 7) = 8, \quad EF_E = 8 + 3 = 11\]
\[ES_F = \max(EF_D, EF_E) = \max(14, 11) = 14, \quad EF_F = 14 + 4 = 18\]
Project Duration = 18 days
Step 2: Backward Pass (Calculate LS and LF)
\[LF_F = 18 \quad \text{(by convention — equals project duration, no successors)}, \quad LS_F = LF_F - Duration_F = 18 - 4 = 14\]
\[LF_D = LS_F = 14, \quad LS_D = 14 - 6 = 8\]
\[LF_E = LS_F = 14, \quad LS_E = 14 - 3 = 11\]
\[LF_B = \min(LS_D, LS_E) = \min(8, 11) = 8, \quad LS_B = 8 - 5 = 3\]
\[LF_C = LS_E = 11, \quad LS_C = 11 - 4 = 7\]
\[LF_A = \min(LS_B, LS_C) = \min(3, 7) = 3, \quad LS_A = 3 - 3 = 0\]
Step 3: Calculate Float
\[Total\ Float = LS - ES = LF - EF\]

9.12.1 Gantt Chart Best Practices

What to IncludeMilestonesBaseline vs. Current

Planned vs. Actual tracking capability
Baseline vs. Current schedule view



Milestones are zero-duration events marking significant project achievements. On a Gantt chart, milestones appear as diamonds (◆).
What makes a good milestone? Use the SMART criteria:









Criterion
Meaning
Good Example
Poor Example




Specific
Clear, well-defined event
“100% design issued for construction”
“Design done”


Measurable
Can be objectively verified
Signed acceptance email received
“Mostly approved”


Assignable

Design Manager owns it
“The team”


Realistic

“Q2 sometime”




The pizza party test: If you sent stakeholders an invitation saying “We’re having a pizza party because we finished [milestone]”, would they say “Great, I’ll come!” — or “What is that?” If they wouldn’t understand why it matters, it probably isn’t a proper milestone.

Common engineering project milestones: - ✓ Project Kick-off - ✓ Investigations Complete - ✓ 30% Design Issue for Review - ✓ 60% Design Issue for Review - ✓ 100% Design Issue for Construction - ✓ Regulatory Approval Received - ✓ Construction Start - ✓ Structural Works Complete - ✓ Commissioning Complete - ✓ Practical Completion - ✓ Defects Liability Period End


A well-managed Gantt chart always shows:

Baseline (original approved schedule) — shown as the lower bar or grey shadow
Current (updated actual progress) — shown as the main coloured bar
% Complete — progress indicator on each bar

If Current = Baseline, the project is on track.
If Current extends beyond Baseline, analysis is needed.

section: 9.13 PERT Analysis — Handling Schedule Uncertainty 📋 Required
text:
9.13 PERT Analysis — Handling Schedule Uncertainty 📋 Required
PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique) extends CPM by acknowledging that activity durations are uncertain and modelling them probabilistically.

9.13.1 PERT Three-Point Estimating
For each activity, obtain three estimates and apply the PERT formulas:
\[t_E = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6} \qquad \sigma = \frac{P - O}{6} \qquad \sigma^2 = \left(\frac{P-O}{6}\right)^2\]
Where: - O (Optimistic) — best-case duration if everything goes perfectly - M (Most Likely) — the most realistic, expected duration under normal conditions - P (Pessimistic) — worst-case duration if most things go wrong - \(t_E\) (Expected Duration) — the weighted average; M is weighted 4× because it is the most likely outcome - \(\sigma\) (Standard Deviation) — how spread out the estimate is; large σ means high uncertainty - \(\sigma^2\) (Variance) — used when combining uncertainty across multiple activities on the critical path (variances add, standard deviations do not)

Tip💡 Reading the Table




Large gap between O and P (e.g., Approvals: 14 vs 56) → high uncertainty → large σ (7.00) → this activity dominates the project’s schedule risk
Small gap (e.g., Drawing Production: 6 vs 15) → lower uncertainty → σ = 1.50 → more predictable
\(t_E\) is always pulled toward P when P is far from M — the pessimistic tail has real weight
Add variances (not σ) when computing the overall project standard deviation: \(\sigma_{project} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma^2}\)









Note💡 ملاحظة



نشاط “الموافقات” له أكبر فجوة بين O و P (14 مقابل 56)، مما يعني عدم يقين عالٍ. هذا النشاط هو المصدر الرئيسي لمخاطر الجدول الزمني.


Project Expected Duration — sum all \(t_E\) values on the critical path:
\[T_E = 13.00 + 19.00 + 9.50 + 25.67 = \mathbf{67.17 \text{ days}}\]
Project Standard Deviation — sum the variances (not σ), then take the square root:
\[\sigma_{project} = \sqrt{\sigma^2_1 + \sigma^2_2 + \sigma^2_3 + \sigma^2_4} = \sqrt{5.44 + 9.00 + 2.25 + 49.00} = \sqrt{65.69} = \mathbf{8.11 \text{ days}}\]






Warning⚠️ Why Add Variances, Not Standard Deviations?



You cannot add σ values directly: \(2.33 + 3.00 + 1.50 + 7.00 = 13.83\) — this overstates uncertainty.
Variances add correctly because they measure independent squared spread. You take the square root after summing to get back to days: \[\sigma_{project} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma^2} <br/>eq \sum \sigma\]




9.13.2 Probability of Completion by Target Date
Using the normal distribution:
\[Z = \frac{T_{target} - T_{expected}}{\sigma_{project}}\]
Where \(T_{target}\) is the desired completion date and \(T_{expected}\) is the calculated expected completion.
The Z-score tells you how many standard deviations the target date is above the expected duration. You then look up that Z-score in the Standard Normal Distribution Table below to find the probability:

How to read: A Z-score of 1.645 means the target date is 1.645 standard deviations above the expected finish — and there is a 95% probability the project finishes by that date.








Note📖 Example PERT Probability Calculation



Using the values calculated above from our four activities:
Critical path expected duration: \(T_E = 67.17\) days
Project standard deviation: \(\sigma_{project} = 8.11\) days
Client deadline: 80 days
\[Z = \frac{80 - 67.17}{8.11} = \frac{12.83}{8.11} = 1.58\]
From Z-table: P(Z ≤ 1.58) ≈ 94%
There is a 94% probability of completing the project within 80 days.
To achieve 95% probability: Need Z = 1.645 → \(T = 67.17 + (1.645 \times 8.11) = 67.17 + 13.34 \approx \mathbf{80.5 \text{ days}}\)
To achieve 99% probability: Need Z = 2.326 → \(T = 67.17 + (2.326 \times 8.11) \approx \mathbf{86.1 \text{ days}}\)

9.14 Schedule Compression Techniques 📋 Required
When the calculated schedule exceeds the target date, two primary compression techniques are available:

  
    💰 CRASHING
    
      Add more resources to critical path activities
      Increases cost; may increase risk
      Use cost-slope to find cheapest compression per day
      Always crash the lowest cost-slope activity first
    
  
  
    ⚡ FAST-TRACKING
    
      Run sequential activities in parallel (using lead times)
      Increases risk of rework if earlier work changes
      No direct additional cost
      Requires close coordination and clear interfaces
    
  


9.14.1 Cost-Slope for Crashing
The cost-slope measures how much it costs to shorten an activity by one unit of time (one day). It lets you compare activities and always crash the cheapest one first.
\[\text{Cost Slope} = \frac{C_c - C_n}{T_n - T_c}\]

Tip💡 The Golden Rule of Crashing



Always crash the critical path activity with the lowest cost-slope first, then re-analyse.
Only critical path activities matter — crashing a non-critical activity saves zero project time.







Goal
Best choice




Save cost
Crash A or B ($2,000/day)


Save maximum time

Balanced — save 2 days cheapest
Crash A or B: 2 × $2,000 = $4,000 vs C or D: 2 × $3,000 = $6,000





Step-by-step crashing process:

Identify activities on the critical path only
Calculate cost-slope for each critical activity
Sort ascending by cost-slope (cheapest first)
Crash the cheapest activity — but do not exceed its maximum crash limit (\(T_n - T_c\))
Re-analyse the critical path — it may shift after crashing
Repeat until the target duration is reached







Warning⚠️ Crashing Cautions










Warning
Reason




Never crash non-critical activities
They don’t affect project end date


Always re-check the critical path after each crash
A new critical path may emerge


Respect each activity’s crash limit
Every activity has a minimum achievable duration


Watch for quality impact
Excessive acceleration increases error rates


Get budget approval first
Crash cost must be formally authorised





Quick example — save 3 days at minimum cost:
Activity A has a crash limit of 3 days (10 → 7) at $2,000/day:
\[\text{Additional cost} = 3 \times \$2{,}000 = \mathbf{\$6{,}000}\]
Alternatively, use Activity B (limit: 2 days) + Activity C (1 day):
\[2 \times \$2{,}000 + 1 \times \$3{,}000 = \$4{,}000 + \$3{,}000 = \mathbf{\$7{,}000}\]
✅ Optimal: Crash Activity A by 3 days for $6,000

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.15 Critical Chain Scheduling 📋 Required
Critical Chain Scheduling is an alternative to CPM developed by Eliyahu Goldratt based on his Theory of Constraints (from the novel “The Goal”, 1984). It focuses on managing buffers rather than individual activity floats.

9.15.1 The Problem with Traditional Scheduling
When PMs ask team members to estimate task durations, team members build in individual safety buffers — often doubling the realistic estimate. This leads to two dysfunctions:






Warning⚠️ Parkinson’s Law + Murphy’s Law = Schedule Disaster




Parkinson’s Law: “Work expands to fill the time available.” If an activity has 10 days in the schedule, it will take 10 days — even if it could be done in 6. People do not finish early; they use the buffer for other work or polishing.
Murphy’s Law: “Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong.” Problems arise anyway, consuming the individual buffers — and the project still runs late.

The result: individual padding doesn’t protect the project end date, but it does inflate the schedule and slow down the team.




9.15.2 The Multitasking Problem
Critical chain scheduling addresses the harm caused by excessive multitasking. Consider a team member assigned to three parallel tasks (A, B, C), each requiring 10 working days:









Approach
Task A finishes
Task B finishes
Task C finishes




Serial (one at a time)
Day 10
Day 20
Day 30


Parallel multitasking (one third each day)
Day 30
Day 30
Day 30



Parallel multitasking delays every task and adds context-switching overhead. The solution: focus — finish one task, then start the next.


9.15.3 How Critical Chain Scheduling Works





%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 20, 'rankSpacing': 45}}}%%
flowchart LR
    A["Task A<br/>(realistic)"] --> B["Task B<br/>(realistic)"] --> C["Task C<br/>(realistic)"] --> PB["PROJECT<br/>BUFFER<br/>🛡️"]
    
    F1["Feeding<br/>Chain 1"] --> FB1["Feeding<br/>Buffer 🛡️"] --> B
    F2["Feeding<br/>Chain 2"] --> FB2["Feeding<br/>Buffer 🛡️"] --> C

 Critical chain scheduling: buffers are consolidated, not distributed 



Steps in critical chain scheduling:

Remove individual safety buffers from activity estimates — use the 50% likely duration (not the padded estimate)
Identify the critical chain — the longest chain of dependent activities considering resource constraints (not just logic links)
Add a Project Buffer at the end of the critical chain before the project due date — this is where the removed padding goes
Add Feeding Buffers where non-critical chains feed into the critical chain — to protect the critical chain from delays on feeder paths
Manage the buffer — track what percentage of the buffer has been consumed vs. how much of the project is complete



9.15.4 Three Organisational Approaches to Buffers








Organisation Type
Behaviour
Outcome




Hard-nose
No buffers allowed; pressures people to commit to minimum durations
Team members hide buffers in their own work; no visibility


Lenient
Allows individual buffers in each task
Parkinson’s Law applies; project still runs late


Critical chain
Removes individual buffers; PM controls an aggregate project buffer
Buffer is visible; PM can see when project is truly at risk









Tip💡 Why Not Show the Buffer to the Team?



The project buffer should be managed by the PM, not consumed by the team. If team members know there is a 15-day buffer, they will use it. The buffer is a management reserve — not extra time for individual tasks.

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.16 Agile Time Management ➕ Extended
Traditional CPM scheduling assumes all work is defined upfront — you know every activity before the project starts. Agile projects take a fundamentally different approach.






Note📖 Agile Scheduling Principles




Don’t define all work before scheduling: Only plan in detail what will be done in the next sprint (1–4 weeks)
Product Backlog: A prioritised list of all desired features and work — managed by the Product Owner
Sprint Backlog: The subset of backlog items the team commits to completing in the current sprint
Velocity: The team’s average output per sprint (in story points or hours), used to predict future delivery
Responding to change over following a plan: The schedule adapts sprint-by-sprint based on what has been learned and what stakeholders now want




9.16.1 Agile vs. Traditional Scheduling








Dimension
Traditional (CPM)
Agile




Plan horizon
Full project upfront
Sprint-by-sprint (rolling wave)


Schedule document
Gantt chart + network diagram
Sprint board (Kanban/Scrum)


Change handling
Formal change control
Expected; backlog is re-prioritised


Progress measure
% of activities complete
Working product per sprint


Schedule owner
Project Manager
Team + Product Owner together



For engineering and construction projects, full CPM scheduling remains essential. For IT software development, agile or hybrid approaches are increasingly standard.

title: 9  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
9.17 Controlling the Schedule 📋 Required
Once the project is underway, the schedule must be monitored and controlled. The goals of schedule control are:

Know the current status of the schedule — what is on time, what is behind
Identify the factors causing schedule changes before they become delays
Determine whether the schedule has changed and by how much
Manage the actual changes when they occur


9.17.1 Tools and Techniques for Schedule Control







Tool
How It Helps




Progress reports
Team members report actual start, finish, and % complete for their activities


Schedule change control system
Defines the process for requesting, reviewing, and approving changes to the baseline


Tracking Gantt chart
Compares planned (grey bars) vs. actual (solid bars) progress visually


Variance analysis
Calculates schedule variance = \(SV = EV - PV\) (see Chapter 7 — Earned Value)


Float/slack monitoring
Activities with decreasing float are at risk; zero float means the critical path has shifted


PM software (MS Project, Primavera)
Recalculates CPM automatically when actuals are entered


Resource leveling
Resolves over-allocations that cause delays





9.17.2 Reality Checks and Best Practices






Tip💡 Schedule Control — Reality Checks




Do not plan everyone at 100% capacity. Real work includes email, meetings, administrative tasks, and unexpected interruptions. Planning at 80–85% capacity is more realistic.
Hold regular progress meetings with the team and stakeholders. Not to report blame, but to surface problems early when there is still time to respond.
Be honest with your sponsor when the schedule is slipping. Hiding a delay is worse than surfacing it early — sponsors can help (more resources, scope reduction, deadline extension) only if they know about the problem.
Use the buffer budgeting approach with senior management. Some PMs tell sponsors: “We have a 15-day buffer built in. I’ll report to you when we’ve consumed 25%, 50%, and 75% of the buffer — each level triggers a different response.” This gives management visibility without micromanagement.
Manage your own time. Project managers who are disorganised cannot manage their team’s schedule. Researcher Shawn Achor (Harvard) found that people who reduce the activation energy for productive habits are far more likely to sustain them — for example, keeping your schedule and tasks visible so the next step requires zero effort to identify.
Don’t just write lower numbers because someone pressured you. An unrealistic schedule does not make the project faster; it destroys credibility when the dates are missed. Use data and reasoning to defend your estimates — or formally document that the deadline was imposed.





9.17.3 Words of Caution on PM Software






Warning⚠️ PM Software Can Be Misused



Project scheduling software (MS Project, Primavera) is a powerful tool — but it is frequently misused:

You MUST enter dependencies for the software to calculate dates automatically. If you enter dates manually (manually scheduled tasks), the software cannot recalculate when things change. The whole benefit of CPM is lost.
You MUST enter actual data (actual start, actual finish, % complete) to compare planned vs. actual. A schedule that is never updated is just a picture of the original plan — not a management tool.
Many users don’t understand the CPM engine. They override the software’s logic and wonder why the dates don’t update. Proper scheduling software training is essential before relying on the output.

Treat the scheduling software as a CPM calculator and change-impact analyser — not just a Gantt drawing tool.

section: Case Study — Qatar FIFA World Cup 2022: Scheduling the Unschedulable
text:
Case Study — Qatar FIFA World Cup 2022: Scheduling the Unschedulable






Important🏭 Case Study: Qatar 2022 — When the Deadline Cannot Move



Background:
On 21 November 2022, the FIFA World Cup opened at Al-Bayt Stadium in Al-Khor, Qatar — the first World Cup hosted by an Arab nation. For Qatar’s Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (SC), the scheduling challenge was unique: the tournament date was set in December 2010 and could not shift by even a single day. This created a project scheduling environment where float on the critical path was, ultimately, zero.
The Scale: - 8 world-class stadiums built or substantially reconstructed (most World Cup hosts refurbish existing facilities) - Hard deadline: 21 November 2022 — fixed 12 years in advance - Construction workforce: 30,000+ workers across stadium sites simultaneously - Largest stadium: Lusail Stadium (88,966 capacity) — the centrepiece venue for the final
Scheduling Challenges:







Challenge
Response




Summer temperatures reaching 50°C made daytime work impossible June–September
Shifted all critical construction to mandatory night shifts (22:00–06:00); stadium cooling systems tested 18 months early to enable summer commissioning


COVID-19 pandemic (March 2020) halted construction for 4–6 weeks
Critical path reassessed immediately; non-critical works suspended; critical path workers resumed in isolated bubbles within 3 weeks


Lusail Stadium — largest design, started last
Assigned highest resource density of any stadium; 24-hour operations from 2018; Lusail became first stadium to complete trial events in 2021 despite being the last to start


Al-Thumama Stadium required partial structural redesign mid-construction
Design frozen at 60% completion; structural changes fast-tracked through review cycles; construction sequence reordered around the redesigned elements


All 8 stadiums required fully operational cooling systems before commissioning began
MEP commissioning placed on the critical path from contract start — 3 months bought back by accelerating installation sequence



CPM Application:
The SC’s scheduling team used Oracle Primavera P6 Enterprise with a master programme of 35,000+ activities. The critical path ran through Lusail Stadium’s seating bowl and roof structure — the most complex and the last to mobilise. Any activity reaching < 5 days of total float triggered an automatic Managing Director-level review within 24 hours.
The Fixed Deadline Strategy: 1. Each stadium committed to completion 6 months before the tournament — allowing full test event cycles 2. Three rounds of test events per stadium: Fan Experience Tests, Operational Readiness Tests, and FIFA Final Certification 3. A parallel maximum acceleration schedule was pre-approved and ready to activate — with pre-agreed resource profiles and contractor incentive payments — if the primary programme was ever threatened
Outcome:
All 8 stadiums were delivered on or before their committed test event dates. The tournament opened on its announced date. Qatar Stadium 974 — a temporary venue built from shipping containers — was delivered as a surprise late addition and met its commissioning deadline.
Key Scheduling Lessons: 1. When the deadline is absolute, schedule contingency must be proportionally large — planning to finish “just in time” is planning to fail 2. External disruptions (COVID, extreme heat) will invalidate sections of any schedule — the organisations that survived maintained pre-developed recovery plans 3. Risk-driven sequencing: the most complex activities (Lusail’s roof) were started earliest and given the most resources 4. Automatic escalation triggers on critical float are more reliable than human judgment — at 5 days of float with 30,000 workers in play, human review is too slow
Sources: Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (2022); Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (2023)

NoteMicrosoft Project: Applying Chapter 4 Concepts



Now that you understand activity sequencing, CPM, and Gantt charts, apply these directly in MS Project using the AAUP Wi-Fi Upgrade case study (Chapter 6) or your own project:

Expected outcome: Your MS Project schedule should match the CPM calculations you did by hand. If they differ, check for missing dependencies or manual scheduling overrides.

Resource LevellingResource SmoothingStrategies for Constrained Resources


Adjust the schedule to eliminate over-allocation

Can extend the project end date to resolve peaks
Activities are delayed into their float periods
Used when resource constraints are absolute (only 1 specialist available)
The project end date may slip

Example: If a structural engineer is needed 60 hrs/week for 2 weeks, but is only available 40 hrs/week, delay one set of activities by 2 weeks.


Smooth usage without changing the end date

Uses float to shift activities without extending the project
Cannot extend the project end date
Only non-critical activities can be moved
May leave some over-allocation if float is insufficient

Example: Move a non-critical design task from Week 3 to Week 5 to reduce the engineer’s peak load.


When you cannot add more resource:

Overtime — extend working hours (expensive, unsustainable)
Subcontract — outsource some activities
Reduce scope — remove lower-priority deliverables
Extend timeline — negotiate deadline relief with client
Cross-training — train team members to cover skill gaps
Shift scheduling — two shifts on critical path activities
Prioritise — focus the constrained resource on critical path only

10.5 Team Development — Tuckman’s Model
The most widely used model of team development, Tuckman’s Forming-Storming-Norming-Performing model:





%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 40, 'rankSpacing': 60}}}%%
flowchart LR
    F["🤝 FORMING<br/>Polite & cautious<br/>Roles unclear<br/>PM: Direct & guide"]
    S["⚡ STORMING<br/>Conflict & tension<br/>Power struggles<br/>PM: Coach & mediate"]
    N["🌱 NORMING<br/>Cohesion builds<br/>Roles clarify<br/>PM: Facilitate & support"]
    P["🚀 PERFORMING<br/>High effectiveness<br/>Autonomous team<br/>PM: Delegate & enable"]
    A["🏁 ADJOURNING<br/>Project ends<br/>Celebrate & reflect<br/>PM: Recognise & close"]

    F --> S --> N --> P --> A

    style F fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e40af
    style S fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#7f1d1d
    style N fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308,color:#854d0e
    style P fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166634
    style A fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#4c1d95


 Tuckman’s model of team development 









Warning⚠️ Common Mistake — Assuming Teams Start at “Performing”



One of the most common errors engineering PMs make is treating a newly assembled project team as if they are already high-performing. Even experienced professionals need time to develop working relationships, establish communication norms, and build trust.
Allow time in your schedule for team development. Teams that rush through Forming and Storming often cycle back through them at critical moments in the project.

title: 10  Resource Management
section: Case Study — Grand Egyptian Museum: Resource Management at Civilisational Scale
text:
Case Study — Grand Egyptian Museum: Resource Management at Civilisational Scale






Important🏭 Case Study: Grand Egyptian Museum, Cairo — Managing the World’s Largest Archaeological Museum



Background:
The Grand Egyptian Museum (المتحف المصري الكبير — GEM) near the Pyramids of Giza is the world’s largest archaeological museum, housing over 100,000 artefacts including the complete treasures of Tutankhamun’s tomb — displayed together for the first time. GEM is the most complex cultural construction project in the modern Arab world, requiring resource management across archaeological conservation, specialist construction, and international professional services simultaneously.
Scale: - Floor area: 93,000 m² - Construction cost: ~$1 billion (USD) - Construction started: 2002; Tutankhamun galleries opened: 2022 - Peak construction workforce: 12,000 workers on site simultaneously
Resource Management Challenges:
Labour Resources: - Specialist skills required: Conservation scientists, museum lighting engineers, acoustic designers, Egyptological curators — none available locally in sufficient numbers - Solution: International specialists hired on rotating 6-month contracts; partnership with Cairo University to provide 200+ trained conservators; national training programme created 800 Egyptian museum technicians who did not previously exist
Specialist Conservation Resource (The Parallel Programme): - The Tutankhamun galleries alone required 10 years of artefact conservation — a programme running parallel to construction - 5,000+ individual objects each required cataloguing, condition assessment, treatment, and custom display mount fabrication - Resource conflict: The same conservation scientists were needed by both the Tutankhamun programme and 90 other exhibition halls simultaneously - Solution: Conservation resource schedule maintained separately from construction programme with a dedicated 800m² on-site conservation laboratory
Equipment and Procurement Resources: - Main atrium roof: 24,000 m² of translucent alabaster panels — unique material requiring custom Italian fabrication equipment; 18-month delivery cycle - Atrium steel structure (5,000+ tonnes) required specialist cranes continuously in demand across 4 simultaneous erection zones - 300+ custom museum display cases designed and fabricated in Germany, Austria, and Italy — long-lead procurement that could not be accelerated
Multi-Cultural Team Integration: - Owner: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities - Construction Manager: Nippon Koei (Japan) + EHAF (Egypt)
- Main contractor: KRCC (Egyptian) with specialist packages from Italy, Japan, and Germany - Languages: Arabic, English, Japanese — creating documentation and communication challenges - PM Response: Trilingual coordination protocols; unified electronic document management; joint weekly progress meetings with all parties
Schedule Pressure from External Events: - The 2011 Egyptian Revolution and 2013 political transition caused 3 years of project suspension - Resource dispersal during suspension meant re-mobilisation phases lost key specialist personnel who had moved to other projects - Recovery required six months of intensive recruitment before construction could resume at full capacity
Outcome: The Tutankhamun galleries and Grand Hall opened in 2022 to international acclaim. Egypt’s heritage sector now has 800 trained museum technicians, a world-class conservation laboratory, and an institutional knowledge base that will support Egyptian museums for decades.
Key Resource Lessons: 1. Specialist resources for rare projects must be identified and secured years before they are needed — conservation scientists cannot be trained in 6 months 2. Multi-cultural teams with fundamentally different working standards require active management — language and documentation protocols must be agreed before work starts, not after problems emerge 3. Long-lead procurement must be on the critical path from day one — the alabaster panels nearly caused an 18-month delay 4. Political risk disperses resources faster than any technical problem — having a formal re-mobilisation plan is as important as the original resource plan
Sources: Grand Egyptian Museum Organisation (2022); Nippon Koei Co., Ltd. (2019)

With your schedule from Chapter 4’s practice complete, now add and manage resources:
Tasks to complete in MS Project:

Open the Resource Sheet (View → Resource Sheet) and enter all resources from your Resource Register:

Manual smoothing alternative: Instead of auto-levelling, manually split a task (Task tab → Split Task button) or reduce a resource’s units on a specific task to bring it within limits
Build a RACI view: Export the Task Usage view to Excel (File → Save As → Excel) and add a RACI column for each resource–task assignment

Expected outcome: After levelling, no resource should exceed their Max Units. The resource histogram should show all bars at or below the availability line. Compare the levelled finish date to the baseline — this is your resource-constrained schedule.

text:
11.1 Why Use MS Project?
Manual scheduling (spreadsheets, sticky notes, hand-drawn Gantt charts) becomes unmanageable once a project has more than 20–30 activities and multiple resources. Microsoft Project 2021 / Microsoft Project for Microsoft 365 automates:

Critical path calculation (updated instantly when you change a duration)
Resource allocation and over-allocation detection
Cost tracking against baseline
Earned Value analysis
Professional reporting







Note🖥️ Which Version Does This Chapter Target?



This chapter targets Microsoft Project 2021 (desktop, perpetual licence) and Microsoft Project Plan 3 / Plan 5 (Microsoft 365 subscription). The interface and ribbon are identical in both. Screenshots reference the dark ribbon theme but all steps apply to any colour theme.
Do NOT confuse with: Microsoft Planner (task management only, no scheduling engine) or Microsoft Project Online (web-only, simplified features).

text:
11.4 Step-by-Step: Creating a Project from Scratch
The following steps follow a logical sequence — do not skip steps or change the order, especially steps 5–6 (tasks before resources).

11.4.1 Step 1 — Create a New File

Open MS Project → File → New → Blank Project
Immediately save: File → Save As → choose location → name the file (e.g., CampusWiFi_v1.mpp)







Tip



File naming convention: [ProjectCode]_[Description]_v[version].mpp
Example: AAUP-IT-01_WiFiUpgrade_v1.mpp




11.4.2 Step 2 — Set Project Information
Go to Project tab → Project Information:



Field
Action




Start Date
Enter the project start date (e.g., 01 Sep 2025)


Schedule From
Leave as “Project Start Date” (forward scheduling)


Current Date
Today’s date (auto-filled)


Calendar
Select or create (see Step 3)


Priority
Leave at 500 (used for resource levelling)



Click Statistics button at any time to see summary: start, finish, duration, work, cost.


11.4.3 Step 3 — Create a Custom Calendar
Project tab → Change Working Time → Create New Calendar

Name it (e.g., “Palestine Standard”)
Set working days: Sunday to Thursday, 08:00–17:00 (with 1-hour lunch break)
Set Friday and Saturday as non-working days
Add exceptions (public holidays):

Select the date on the calendar
Click Exceptions tab → enter name → set as non-working




11.4.4 Step 4 — Set Up the WBS / Summary Tasks
In the Gantt Chart view, enter your WBS phases as Summary Tasks:

Type the Phase 1 name (e.g., Initiation) in the Task Name column → press Enter
Type sub-tasks below it
Select the sub-tasks → Task tab → Indent Task (or press Alt+Shift+Right arrow)
The parent row becomes a summary task (bold, with a collapse arrow)







Tip



Keyboard shortcut: Alt+Shift+→ to indent (make child), Alt+Shift+← to outdent (make parent)


Structure your task list to mirror the WBS numbering:
1. Project: Smart Campus Wi-Fi Upgrade          ← Project Summary (auto)
   1. Initiation                                 ← Summary Task
      1.1 Develop Project Charter
      1.2 Stakeholder Register
      1.3 Kick-off Meeting                       ← Milestone
   2. Planning                                   ← Summary Task
      2.1 Network Site Survey
      2.2 Equipment Specification
      ...


11.4.5 Step 5 — Enter Durations
Click the Duration column next to each task and type: - 5d = 5 days - 3w = 3 weeks - 0d = milestone (diamond on Gantt) - 1w 2d = 1 week + 2 days = 7 days






Important



Task Mode: Check the Task Mode column. Set to Manually Scheduled only for tasks with fixed dates (e.g., contractual milestones). All other tasks should be Auto Scheduled so MS Project recalculates the schedule automatically when dependencies change.




11.4.6 Step 6 — Set Dependencies (Predecessors)
In the Predecessors column, type the row number of the predecessor task:







To create this
Type in Predecessors column




Finish-to-Start (default)
3 (task 3 must finish before this starts)


Finish-to-Start + 2 day lag
3FS+2d


Start-to-Start
3SS


Finish-to-Finish
3FF


Start-to-Start + 1 week lag
3SS+1w


Multiple predecessors
3,5,7



Alternatively, in Gantt Chart view, drag from the end of one task bar to the start of another to create a FS dependency.






Warning



Critical Path Check: After entering all dependencies, go to View → Gantt Chart and check Format → Critical Tasks (check the box). All critical path tasks will turn red. If your entire project is red, you likely have no dependencies set.




11.4.7 Step 7 — Enter Resources
Switch to Resource Sheet view (View tab → Resource Sheet):
Fill in one row per resource:



Column
Guidance




Resource Name
Full name or role (e.g., “Network Engineer”)


Type
Work / Material / Cost


Material Label
(for materials only, e.g., “m²”, “units”)


Initials
Auto-filled; can customise


Group
Department or team (e.g., “IT”, “Civil”)


Max. Units
100% = full time; 50% = part time


Std. Rate
e.g., ₪120/h


Ovt. Rate
e.g., ₪180/h


Cost/Use
Fixed cost each time resource is used


Accrue At
Start / End / Prorated (how cost is recorded)


Base Calendar
Which working calendar applies to this person





11.4.8 Step 8 — Assign Resources to Tasks
Switch back to Gantt Chart view. For each task:

Double-click the task → Task Information dialog → Resources tab
Select the resource name from the dropdown
Set Units (e.g., 100% for full time on this task, 50% for half time)
Click OK

Or use the Assign Resources button (Resource tab) to drag and assign multiple resources at once.






Note



Over-allocation indicator: A red person icon appears in the Indicators column when a resource is assigned more than their Max. Units. Fix with: Resource tab → Level Resources or manually adjust assignments.




11.4.9 Step 9 — Set the Baseline
Before any work begins, freeze the plan:
Project tab → Set Baseline → Set Baseline
This saves the current schedule as Baseline 0. You can compare actual progress against this later. MS Project allows up to 11 baselines (Baseline 0–10).






Important



Set the baseline only when the plan is approved. Once work begins, do not reset the baseline unless formally approved through change control.




11.4.10 Step 10 — Track Progress
As work proceeds, update the schedule:

Mark % complete: Click a task → Task tab → Mark on Track (sets 100% on track) or type % in the % Complete column
Enter actual dates: Double-click task → Advanced tab → enter Actual Start / Actual Finish
Update remaining duration: In the Tracking Gantt, right-click a task → Update Task → enter remaining work

To see schedule variance: View → Tracking Gantt — the black baseline bar appears below the blue (current) bar.

title: 11  Microsoft Project — Practical Tool Guide
text:
11.8 Common Mistakes to Avoid






Warning⚠️ Top 10 MS Project Mistakes




Starting without a WBS — tasks entered randomly, no structure, impossible to track
All tasks manually scheduled — MS Project cannot recalculate; schedule is just a static table
No dependencies set — tasks float freely; critical path cannot be calculated
Assigning resources before entering all tasks — resource data becomes inconsistent
Never setting a baseline — no way to compare actual vs. planned
Ignoring over-allocation warnings — red resource icons are serious; they mean your plan is unrealistic
Updating % complete without entering actual dates — creates misleading tracking data
Not using a custom calendar — default calendar is Mon–Fri, which is wrong for regional projects
Using MS Project as a spreadsheet — typing static dates instead of letting the scheduling engine calculate them
One file for all versions — always version your file; never overwrite the baseline file

12.1 What is Risk?






Note📖 PMI Definition of Risk




“An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives such as scope, schedule, cost, or quality.” — PMBOK® Guide, 7th Edition

Key Insight: Risk ≠ Problem. A risk is a possibility, not a certainty. When a risk occurs, it becomes an issue that must be managed.

12.2 Risk Identification
Risk identification is an ongoing, collaborative process — not a one-time event at project start.

12.2.1 Risk Identification Techniques

BrainstormingRisk ChecklistsFMEA / HAZIDSWOT AnalysisAssumption and Constraint Analysis


Free-form group ideation in a risk workshop
Process: 1. Assemble cross-functional team (PM, engineers, client rep, external specialist) 2. Use structured prompts: “What could go wrong with…?” 3. Capture all ideas without judgment 4. Categorise and de-duplicate 5. Assess each identified risk
Tips: - Use an experienced facilitator, not the PM (who might inhibit responses) - Time-box: 30-60 minutes per major project phase - Anonymous input methods (sticky notes, digital tools) encourage candid responses


Use historical risk lists from similar projects
Industry-specific checklists exist for: - Civil/structural engineering - Process plant design - IT systems implementation - Environmental projects - Offshore/subsea projects
Checklists ensure common risks are not overlooked but must be supplemented with project-specific risks.


Failure Mode and Effects Analysis / Hazard Identification
Used in engineering and safety-critical industries:

For each component/process, ask: “How can this FAIL?”
For each failure mode: “What is the EFFECT of this failure?”
Assign: Severity, Occurrence probability, Detectability
Calculate Risk Priority Number (RPN): \[RPN = Severity \times Occurrence \times Detectability\]
Focus on highest RPN items

Challenge every assumption in the project plan
For each assumption: “What happens if this assumption is WRONG?”
Examples: - “We assumed excavation would encounter class 3 material — what if it’s class 5?” - “We assumed the supplier could deliver in 8 weeks — what if it takes 14?” - “We assumed EPA approval within 6 months — what if it takes 12?”

section: Case Study — Mecca Crane Collapse 2015: The Cost of Ignored Risk
text:
Case Study — Mecca Crane Collapse 2015: The Cost of Ignored Risk






Important🏭 Case Study: Masjid al-Haram Crane Collapse — Risk Management Under Deadline Pressure



Background:
On 11 September 2015 — just 11 days before Hajj was due to begin — a Liebherr LR 11350 crane collapsed at the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque of Mecca) construction site during a storm. The crane fell into the mosque’s northern courtyard, directly onto pilgrims performing prayers. The collapse killed 111 people and injured 394 others.
Saudi Binladin Group (SBG), one of the world’s largest construction contractors and the Kingdom’s most prestigious builder, was managing the largest ongoing expansion of Islam’s holiest site.
Risk Management Failures:








Risk Factor
What Should Have Happened
What Actually Happened




Crane securing protocol
Cranes must be secured in travel (free-slew) mode before storms; standards require de-rigging when wind exceeds 72 km/h
Wind reached 83 km/h; the crane remained rigged and unsecured in travel mode


Meteorological monitoring
48-hour advance weather monitoring with automatic crane protocols triggered at defined wind thresholds
A weather alert was issued but not formally communicated to crane operators


Public exclusion zones
Live construction adjacent to an occupied worship space — an extraordinary risk context requiring enhanced protocols
No enhanced exclusion zone protocol existed for public prayer areas below active cranes during extreme weather


Equipment condition
All cranes subject to regular third-party certification
Investigation indicated the crane’s luffing jib pin was in a degraded condition — a known maintenance concern


Risk culture
Supervisors must have authority to halt work for any safety concern
The 11-day countdown to Hajj created “normalisation of deviance” — routine shortcuts had accumulated over weeks without incident



The Normalisation of Deviance:
SBG had worked under intense Hajj-season deadline pressure for decades without a major fatal incident. Shortcuts that deviated from formal safety protocols had become routine because “nothing bad had happened before.” The 2015 collapse demonstrates that statistical tolerance of risk does not reduce the underlying probability of catastrophe — it merely delays it.
Financial and Operational Consequences: - Criminal investigation of SBG management; 13 individuals charged - Following the crane collapse and a separate Mina pilgrimage stampede (24 September 2015), SBG was suspended from all Saudi government contracts by end of 2015 - SBG had revenues exceeding $5 billion/year — the suspension was an existential business event - Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 subsequently restructured the Haramain and Haram construction contracting model entirely
Engineering and PM Lessons: 1. Deadline pressure is the greatest enemy of risk management — the closer the deadline, the more vigilantly risk protocols must be enforced, not relaxed 2. Known equipment deficiencies must be formally entered into the risk register — “we’ll fix it next month” is not a risk response 3. Public safety in and around construction exclusion zones is non-negotiable — it cannot be traded against schedule 4. Risk culture is built over years and destroyed in days — senior project leadership must model expected safety behaviour at peak pressure moments, not only in routine periods 5. “We have always done it this way without incident” is cognitive bias (normalisation of deviance), not a risk assessment
Discussion Questions: 1. Which of the six risk response strategies should SBG have applied to the crane stability risk during a known storm event at an occupied site? 2. What specific trigger events and thresholds should have been included in the risk register to prevent this incident? 3. How does schedule pressure influence risk decision-making on construction projects in the Arab world?
Sources: Al-Harthi and Al-Ghamdi (2016); MEED Projects (2016)

title: 12  Risk Management & Project Audit
text:
12.7 Project Audit
A project audit is a formal, independent assessment of a project conducted at a scheduled point during execution — not just at the end. The goal is to evaluate whether the project is performing as planned, identify corrective actions, and inform a formal go / no-go / restructure decision.






Note📖 Definition — Project Audit



A project audit is a structured, documented review of a project’s performance, processes, and compliance against its approved plan, governance requirements, and applicable standards. It is conducted by an independent reviewer or audit team — not the project team itself.

“The audit examines the reasons for success or failure and, more importantly, extracts lessons that can be applied to improve the management of future projects.” — Meredith & Mantel, Project Management: A Managerial Approach





12.7.1 Types of Project Audit

Types of project audit







Audit Type
Trigger
Focus




In-process Audit
Scheduled (e.g., end of each phase)
Is the project on track? Will it meet objectives?


Pre-completion Audit
Near project end
Are all deliverables complete? Is handover ready?


Termination Audit
When cancellation is being considered
Should the project continue, restructure, or terminate?


Post-project Audit
6–12 months after close
Did the project deliver the expected benefits?






12.7.2 The Audit Process

12.7.3 What the Audit Examines
A comprehensive project audit reviews six key dimensions:

Are all contracted deliverables on track to be completed?
Is there uncontrolled scope growth (scope creep)?

12.7.4 The Audit Report
The audit report is the formal output delivered to the project sponsor and steering committee. It must be honest, evidence-based, and actionable.

title: 13  Cost Management & Earned Value
section: 13.1 Basic Principles of Cost Management 📋 Required
text:
13.1 Basic Principles of Cost Management 📋 Required
Before estimating or controlling costs, project managers must understand the fundamental cost concepts that underpin financial decision-making:

13.1.1 What is Cost?
Cost is a resource sacrificed or foregone to achieve a specific objective — usually measured in monetary units. Project cost management encompasses all processes required to complete the project within an approved budget.


13.1.2 Key Cost Concepts

Types of CostsLife Cycle CostingFinancial Return ConceptsLearning Curve TheoryReserves



  


13.1.3 1. Direct vs. Indirect Costs








Note💼 Direct Costs



Expenses that can be attributed entirely and specifically to a single project. These do not exist if the project does not happen.







Example
Description




Specialized team salaries
Staff hired solely for this project


Project hardware/software licences
Purchased exclusively for project use


Raw materials
Consumed directly in deliverables


Contractor fees
Engaged specifically for project work













Tip🏢 Indirect Costs



Overhead or administrative costs that support general business operations rather than a specific project. Usually shared across multiple projects.



Example
Description




Office rent
Facility housing all teams


General utilities
Power, internet, water


Executive salaries
Leadership overseeing all projects


Insurance
Organisation-wide cover










13.1.4 2. Fixed vs. Variable Costs








Note📌 Fixed Costs



One-off or recurring expenses that remain constant regardless of the project’s production level, output, or timeframe.



Example
Description




Software subscriptions
Same monthly fee regardless of usage


Consultant retainers
Fixed monthly engagement fee


Equipment lease agreements
Fixed periodic payment













Tip📈 Variable Costs



Expenses that fluctuate or scale based on the level of project activity, resources used, or overall volume.



Example
Description




Temporary worker wages
More workers = higher cost


Materials consumed
Concrete, steel — quantity-driven


Shipping fees
Scales with volume and distance










13.1.5 3. Additional Cost Classifications








Cost Type
Definition
Key Rule / Example




Sunk Costs
Money already spent and unrecoverable
⚠️ Never let sunk costs influence future decisions — e.g. funds spent on a cancelled prototype or a failed software platform


Opportunity Costs
The potential value or revenue lost by choosing one project over an alternative
Choosing Project A means forgoing the benefit Project B would have delivered


Recurring Costs
Repetitive expenses incurred regularly
Weekly labour costs, monthly software subscriptions


Non-Recurring Costs
One-time upfront investments
Initial hardware setup, site mobilisation


Quality Costs
Expenses dedicated to ensuring quality standards are met
Prevention (training), Appraisal (testing), Failure (rework, warranty claims)


Contingency Reserves
Funds set aside for known risks or scope changes within the project’s baseline budget
Controlled by the PM; part of the cost baseline









Important⚠️ The Sunk Cost Trap



A common decision-making error is allowing sunk costs to drive future spending. The fact that ₪500,000 has already been spent on a failing system is irrelevant to the question of whether to continue — only the future costs and benefits of each option should guide the decision.





Life cycle costing (LCC) considers the total cost of ownership across the asset’s entire life — not just the capital construction cost:
\[LCC = C_{initial} + C_{operations} + C_{maintenance} + C_{disposal} - C_{salvage}\]






Important⚠️ Why LCC Matters



A pump that costs $8,000 to purchase but \(3,000/year to maintain over 20 years has a life cycle cost of:\)\(LCC = \$8,000 + (20 \times \$3,000) = \$68,000\)$
A $12,000 pump requiring only \(1,200/year has:\)\(LCC = \$12,000 + (20 \times \$1,200) = \$36,000\)$
The “cheaper” pump costs 89% more over its service life. LCC prevents false economy in procurement.




Senior management and clients evaluate projects using financial metrics. Project managers must speak this language:








Term
Definition
Formula




Revenue
Income generated from the project’s outputs
—


Profit
Revenue minus all expenditures
\(Profit = Revenue - Cost\)


Profit margin
Ratio of profit to revenue (expressed as %)
\(PM = \frac{Profit}{Revenue} \times 100\)


Return on Investment (ROI)
Benefit of investment relative to its cost
\(ROI = \frac{(Benefits - Costs)}{Costs} \times 100\%\)


NPV
Net Present Value — sum of discounted future cash flows
\(NPV = \sum \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}\)


Payback Period
Time to recover initial investment
\(PP = \frac{Initial\ Investment}{Annual\ Net\ Benefit}\)



A positive NPV means the project creates value. A higher ROI indicates better return per dollar invested.


Learning curve theory states that as workers gain experience producing a product, unit cost decreases in a predictable pattern. Each time cumulative output doubles, cost per unit falls by a fixed percentage.
\[Unit\ Cost_n = Unit\ Cost_1 \times n^b \quad \text{where } b = \frac{\log(learning\ rate)}{\log(2)}\]



Learning Rate
Meaning




80%
Each time production doubles, unit cost = 80% of previous


90%
Unit cost = 90% of previous each doubling



Example: If the first unit costs $100,000 and the learning rate is 80%, the 2nd unit costs $80,000; the 4th unit costs $64,000; the 8th costs $51,200.
Project implication: Software development, prefabrication, and repetitive construction activities all exhibit learning curve effects — factor this into estimates for repetitive work.


Reserves are funds included in a cost estimate to mitigate risk:








Reserve Type
Purpose
Who Controls




Contingency Reserve
Known-unknowns — identified risks with probability and impact
Project Manager


Management Reserve
Unknown-unknowns — unforeseeable events
Senior Management / Sponsor



Contingency is part of the cost baseline; management reserve is NOT in the cost baseline but IS in the project budget.

title: 13  Cost Management & Earned Value
text:
13.2 Cost Estimation 📋 Required
Cost estimation is the process of predicting the financial cost of completing project work.

13.2.1 Estimation Classes (فئات تقدير التكلفة) — AACE International Standard
The AACE International Cost Estimate Classification System categorises capital project cost estimates into five distinct classes (Class 1 through 5) based on the maturity of project definition deliverables (نضج مخرجات تعريف المشروع) — not merely elapsed time or estimate purpose. It provides a standardised stage-gate framework that aligns estimate accuracy and methodology with the degree of project scope development.






Note📌 Three Key Rules of the System




Primary determinant is scope maturity — the class assigned depends on how complete the project definition deliverables are, not the phase name or calendar date.
Accuracy ranges (نطاق الدقة) are not universal — they depend on technological complexity, quality of historical data, and defined risk levels.
Scope changes are excluded — accuracy percentages represent normal variation within a defined scope; they do not cover scope growth.

Classifications scale from early conceptual approximations (Class 5) up to highly detailed final construction tenders (Class 1). As scope definition matures (نضج المشروع), accuracy improves and methodology shifts from stochastic models to fully quantified take-offs.






Tip📖 Key Vocabulary (المصطلحات الأساسية)

13.2.2 Estimation Techniques (أساليب تقدير التكلفة)

Analogous (Top-Down)ParametricBottom-UpThree-Point (PERT)



13.2.3 التقدير بالمقارنة / التناظري (Analogous — Top-Down)
Based on historical data from similar past projects — الاعتماد على البيانات التاريخية لمشروع سابق مماثل لتقدير تكلفة أو مدة المشروع الحالي.
\[Cost_{new} = Cost_{historical} \times Adjustment\ Factor\]







When to use
Very early project stages — Class 5 / Class 4 — when design details are almost non-existent (المراحل الأولية جداً عندما تكون التفاصيل شبه معدومة)


Advantages (المميزات)
Very fast · Low cost · Requires minimal engineering effort


Disadvantages (العيوب)
Very low accuracy — assumes similar conditions, location, and inflation rates, which rarely holds true (يفترض تشابه الظروف والموقع والتضخم، وهو ما لا يحدث غالباً)









Tip💡 Simple Example — Painting a School Classroom



Situation: You need to estimate the cost of painting a new classroom (60 m²). You have no detailed plans yet — only the room size.
Historical data: Last year you painted a similar classroom of 50 m² for ₪2,500.
Step 1 — Calculate the historical unit rate: \[Unit\ Rate = \frac{\text{₪}2{,}500}{50\ m^2} = \text{₪}50\ per\ m^2\]
Step 2 — Apply to the new project: \[Cost_{new} = \text{₪}50/m^2 \times 60\ m^2 = \mathbf{\text{₪}3{,}000}\]

Interpretation: Based on the last job, painting this classroom should cost around ₪3,000. This took 2 minutes to calculate — but accuracy is only ±30% to ±50%. The real cost could be anywhere from ₪1,500 to ₪4,500 depending on paint quality, number of coats, and labour rates. Use this number only for early budget screening.



Cost Capacity Factor — Six-Tenths Rule (قاعدة الأعشار الستة): \[Cost_B = Cost_A \times \left(\frac{Capacity_B}{Capacity_A}\right)^{0.6}\]
Engineering example: A 50 ML/day desalination plant cost \(85M. Estimating a 65 ML/day plant:\)\(\$85M \times (65/50)^{0.6} = \$85M \times 1.21 \approx \$103M\)$
Accuracy (نطاق الدقة): ±25% to ±50%




13.2.4 التقدير البارامتري / الإحصائي (Parametric)
Uses a statistical relationship between historical data and project parameters to calculate cost — استخدام علاقة إحصائية بين البيانات التاريخية والمتغيرات الأخرى (البارامترات) لحساب التكلفة، مثل: تكلفة المتر المربع × المساحة الكلية.
\[Cost = Unit\ Rate \times Quantity\ of\ Parameter\]







When to use
Early to mid stages — Class 4 / Class 3 — e.g. estimating hospital construction costs based on number of beds (تقدير تكلفة بناء المستشفيات بناءً على عدد الأسرة)


Advantages (المميزات)
More accurate than analogous estimating · Easy to adjust and scale using software


Disadvantages (العيوب)
Entirely dependent on model quality — if historical data or equations are wrong, the result will be incorrect (إذا كانت البيانات القديمة أو المعادلات خاطئة، ستكون النتيجة غير صحيحة)









Tip💡 Simple Example — Painting a School (Multiple Classrooms)



Situation: You need to paint an entire school — 12 classrooms, a corridor, and a staff room. You now have the floor plan (areas known) but no detailed specifications. You use published unit rates from similar school projects.

You can see where costs come from — and changing one rate (e.g. if corridor paint is more expensive) instantly updates the total. 13.2.5 التقدير من أسفل إلى أعلى (Bottom-Up)
Bottom-up estimating builds the total project estimate by estimating each individual task, activity, or work package separately — then rolling all those estimates upward into a project total.

Time-consuming · Very costly to prepare · Requires complete engineering documents (يستهلك وقتاً طويلاً، مكلف جداً لإعداده، ويتطلب وثائق هندسية مكتملة)

Comparison: The analogous estimate gave ₪3,000 for the same 60 m² room. The bottom-up estimate gives ₪599 — a massive difference showing how inaccurate rough top-down estimates can be without scope detail. Scale this up across 12 classrooms + corridor + staff room and the bottom-up total would be far more reliable than ₪48,950 from the parametric approach.




The 4-Step Process (خطوات التطبيق)








Step
Action
What to Do




1 — Break Down (تفكيك المشروع)
Create a WBS (هيكل تقسيم العمل)
Split the project into work packages — the road map of individual tasks to estimate


2 — Estimate Each Package (تقدير كل حزمة)
Consult team & experts
For each work package, determine time, cost, and resources. Consult developers, engineers, designers


3 — Aggregate (التجميع التصاعدي)
Sum all estimates
Add all work package estimates to produce the total project cost


4 — Review & Refine (المراجعة والتحسين)
Validate with stakeholders
Adjust using historical data or expert judgement; confirm with sponsor



For each work package — مكوّنات تكلفة كل حزمة عمل:

Materials (المواد): Quantity × Unit rate
Labour (العمالة): Hours × Hourly rate
Equipment (المعدات): Hours/days × Hire rate
Overheads (المصاريف العامة): (L + M + E) × OH%
Profit/margin (الربح) — for contractors



Benefits (المميزات)







Benefit
Explanation




High accuracy (دقة عالية)
No big assumptions — every task is individually examined


Better risk identification (كشف المخاطر مبكراً)
Task-level breakdown exposes cost and schedule risks before they escalate


Stakeholder confidence (ثقة أصحاب المصلحة)
Detailed, evidence-based estimates are far easier to defend and gain buy-in for





Drawbacks (العيوب)







Drawback
Impact




Time-consuming (يستغرق وقتاً طويلاً)
Estimating every task separately is a project in itself for large programmes


Requires many inputs (يحتاج مدخلات كثيرة)
Coordination across team members, experts, and stakeholders adds overhead


Risk of over-detailing (خطر الإفراط في التفصيل)
Too deep a WBS decomposition makes estimates hard to track and maintain



Accuracy (نطاق الدقة): ±5% to ±15%





13.2.6 التقدير ثلاثي النقاط (Three-Point Estimation — PERT)
A technique to reduce risk and uncertainty by considering three scenarios instead of a single fixed number — تقنية لتقليل المخاطر وعدم اليقين عبر أخذ ثلاثة سيناريوهات في الاعتبار بدلاً من رقم واحد ثابت.









Scenario
Symbol
Arabic
Description




Optimistic
O
المتفائل
Best-case scenario — everything goes perfectly


Most Likely
M
الأكثر احتمالاً
Realistic scenario under normal conditions


Pessimistic
P
المتشائم
Worst-case scenario — major risks materialise



PERT Weighted Average Formula (المعادلة الموزونة):
\[CE = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6}\]
The Most Likely estimate is weighted four times more than the Optimistic or Pessimistic — reflecting that realistic conditions are far more probable than extremes.
Standard Deviation (الانحراف المعياري) — measure of uncertainty:
\[\sigma = \frac{P - O}{6}\]
A large \(\sigma\) means high uncertainty; a small \(\sigma\) means the three estimates are close together and the outcome is more predictable.






Tip💡 Simple Example — Painting a Classroom: How Long Will It Take?



Situation: You are planning to paint the classroom but you are unsure how many days it will take. You ask your painter, who gives you three honest answers:









Scenario
Symbol
Days
Reasoning




Optimistic
O
2 days
Surface is clean, paint arrives on time, no interruptions


Most Likely
M
4 days
Normal conditions — some prep work, one afternoon break


Pessimistic
P
10 days
Wall cracks found, paint delivery delayed, extra coats needed



Step 1 — PERT weighted average: \[CE = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6} = \frac{2 + (4 \times 4) + 10}{6} = \frac{2 + 16 + 10}{6} = \frac{28}{6} \approx \mathbf{4.67\ days}\]
Step 2 — Standard deviation (how uncertain is this estimate?): \[\sigma = \frac{P - O}{6} = \frac{10 - 2}{6} = \frac{8}{6} \approx \mathbf{1.33\ days}\]

Interpretation: Rather than simply saying “4 days” (most likely), the PERT estimate gives 4.67 days — pulled upward by the pessimistic scenario. The standard deviation of 1.33 days tells you there is meaningful uncertainty: plan for 5–6 days to be safe. If the painter said O=3, M=4, P=5, the σ would be only 0.33 — very predictable. The wider the gap between O and P, the riskier the estimate.

Apply to cost: Using the bottom-up rate of ₪25/hr × 8 hrs/day: \[CE_{cost} = 4.67\ days \times 8\ hrs \times \text{₪}25/hr = \mathbf{\text{₪}934}\]
vs. the most-likely-only estimate of 4 × 8 × ₪25 = ₪800 — the PERT approach adds ₪134 as implicit risk buffer.


Used to build cost contingency (ميزانية الطوارئ) from risk analysis.
Accuracy (نطاق الدقة): ±10% to ±15% (when combined with realistic risk data)

title: 13  Cost Management & Earned Value
text:
13.5 Earned Value Management (EVM) 📋 Required
Earned Value Management (EVM) integrates scope, schedule, and cost into a single measurement system — giving you an objective view of project status at any point.

13.5.1 The Three Core EVM Values






Note📖 The Three Fundamental EVM Metrics












Metric
Acronym
Old Name
Question it Answers




Planned Value
PV
BCWS
How much work was planned to be done (in $)?


Earned Value
EV
BCWP
How much work has actually been accomplished (in $)?


Actual Cost
AC
ACWP
How much have we actually spent (in $)?







13.5.2 Rate of Performance (RP)
Rate of Performance (RP) is a practical alternative to the standard EV calculation when the precise % complete of an activity is uncertain. It compares actual work completed to the work that should have been done by now:
\[RP = \frac{\text{Actual work completed}}{\text{Work planned to be completed}} \times 100\%\]
\[EV = RP \times PV\]






Tip💡 RP Example



Activity A is planned to take 10 days and is budgeted at $5,000. After 5 days (50% of planned time), the team has completed 3 days of work (30% of the planned work).
\[RP = \frac{3}{5} = 60\%\]
\[EV = 60\% \times \$2,500 = \$1,500\]
(Note: $2,500 = PV at status date = 50% of $5,000)
RP is especially useful for activities where measuring % complete is subjective — it grounds the earned value calculation in planned vs. actual work quantities.

section: 🚗 EVM Made Intuitive — The Tulkarem to Jenin Road Trip
text:
🚗 EVM Made Intuitive — The Tulkarem to Jenin Road Trip






Note🗺️ Before the Numbers: A Story First



EVM can feel like a wall of formulas — until you tie each one to something real. Imagine you are driving from Tulkarem to Jenin — two cities in the West Bank, roughly 60 km apart. You planned the trip carefully, estimated fuel, food, and tolls, and set a budget of ₪10 per km. You are the project manager of this journey.
\[\text{Budget at Completion (BAC)} = 60\ \text{km} \times \text{₪}10/\text{km} = \text{₪}600\]



  
    🚗 Tulkarem → Jenin
    
      60 kmTotal Distance
      ₪10/kmBudget Rate
      ₪600BAC
    
  


13.5.4 Step 1 — Planning the Trip (PV, EV, AC)
By midday you had planned to cover 24 km of the route. That is your Planned Value (PV) — the budgeted cost of work you planned to accomplish by this point.
\[PV = 24\ \text{km} \times \text{₪}10 = \text{₪}240\]
But in reality, checkpoints and traffic on Road 60 slowed you down. You have only driven 20 km so far. That is your Earned Value (EV) — the value of work you actually completed, expressed in budget terms.
\[EV = 20\ \text{km} \times \text{₪}10 = \text{₪}200\]
Now check your wallet. Fuel, a snack at a roadside stand, and a parking fee at the checkpoint total ₪180 spent. That is your Actual Cost (AC).
\[AC = \text{₪}180\]






Tip📌 Quick Recap — The Three Core Values











Metric
What It Represents
Value




PV — Planned Value
Work you planned to do by now
₪240 (24 km planned)


EV — Earned Value
Work you actually completed
₪200 (20 km driven)


AC — Actual Cost
Money you actually spent
₪180 spent



On paper you should be at 24 km, but you are only at 20 km — yet you have spent less than expected. Let’s see what the numbers tell us.





13.5.5 Step 2 — Are You On Schedule? On Budget? (SV & CV)

Schedule Variance (SV)
SV tells you whether you are ahead or behind your travel plan.
\[SV = EV - PV = \text{₪}200 - \text{₪}240 = \mathbf{-\text{₪}40}\]
A negative SV means you are behind schedule — you are 4 km (₪40 worth of distance) behind where you planned to be.


Cost Variance (CV)
CV tells you whether you are spending more or less than expected for the work done.
\[CV = EV - AC = \text{₪}200 - \text{₪}180 = \mathbf{+\text{₪}20}\]
A positive CV means you are under budget — you spent ₪20 less than the budget for the 20 km you have completed. Your roadside snack cost less than expected!






Important⚠️ Variance Summary












Variance
Formula
Result
Meaning




SV (Schedule Variance)
EV − PV
−₪40
🟠 Behind schedule (4 km behind plan)


CV (Cost Variance)
EV − AC
+₪20
🟢 Under budget (₪20 saved so far)



Rule: Negative = Bad · Positive = Good · Zero = Exactly on plan






13.5.6 Step 3 — How Efficiently Are You Travelling? (SPI & CPI)
Variances tell you the gap in money terms. Performance indices tell you the ratio — how efficiently you are working compared to the plan. They are unit-free numbers that allow comparisons across projects of any size.

Schedule Performance Index (SPI)
\[SPI = \frac{EV}{PV} = \frac{\text{₪}200}{\text{₪}240} = \mathbf{0.833}\]
An SPI of 0.833 means you are completing 83.3% of the planned distance for every kilometre planned. For every 10 km you should drive, you are only covering about 8.3 km. You are running at 83% of your planned pace.


Cost Performance Index (CPI)
\[CPI = \frac{EV}{AC} = \frac{\text{₪}200}{\text{₪}180} = \mathbf{1.111}\]
A CPI of 1.111 means for every ₪1 you spend, you get ₪1.11 worth of distance. Your driving is cost-efficient — you are stretching the budget beyond what was planned.






Note📊 Index Interpretation Guide












Index
Value
Condition
Plain English




SPI
0.833
< 1 ⚠️ Behind schedule
Driving slower than planned — arrive late


CPI
1.111
> 1 ✅ Under budget
Spending less per km than budgeted — saving money



EVM tells two stories at once: How fast you are going (SPI) and how wisely you are spending (CPI). Here you are running late but saving money — a common real-world situation.






13.5.7 Step 4 — How Will the Whole Trip End? (EAC Forecasts)
So far you have driven 20 km and spent ₪180. You still have 40 km left to Jenin. What will the total trip cost be? EVM offers four forecasting methods, each reflecting a different assumption about your future behaviour.

  Known values going into the forecast:
  BAC = ₪600 · EV = ₪200 · AC = ₪180 · CPI = 1.111 · SPI = 0.833


EAC Formula 1 — Current efficiency continues

“I have been driving efficiently and plan to keep it that way — same fuel habits, same stops, all the way to Jenin.”

\[EAC_1 = \frac{BAC}{CPI} = \frac{\text{₪}600}{1.111} = \mathbf{\text{₪}540}\]
If you maintain your current cost efficiency for the remaining 40 km, you will arrive in Jenin having spent only ₪540 — saving ₪60 against the original budget.


EAC Formula 2 — Early savings were temporary

“I was frugal at the start, but from here I will drive at exactly the original budgeted rate — ₪10 per km for the remaining distance.”

\[EAC_2 = AC + (BAC - EV) = \text{₪}180 + (\text{₪}600 - \text{₪}200) = \text{₪}180 + \text{₪}400 = \mathbf{\text{₪}580}\]
You will finish the trip spending ₪580 — still ₪20 under the original budget, but you gave up most of your early savings.


EAC Formula 3 — Both schedule and cost delays continue

“Checkpoints and slow traffic will follow me all the way. My CPI and SPI will remain the same — I am both slow and (luckily) cost-efficient.”

\[EAC_3 = AC + \frac{BAC - EV}{CPI \times SPI} = \text{₪}180 + \frac{\text{₪}400}{1.111 \times 0.833}\]
\[= \text{₪}180 + \frac{\text{₪}400}{0.925} = \text{₪}180 + \text{₪}432.4 = \mathbf{\text{₪}612.4}\]
Even though you are spending efficiently, being delayed stretches the trip — extra waiting time at checkpoints means more fuel idling, more snacks, more cost. You will arrive ₪12.4 over budget.


EAC Formula 4 — Fresh estimate from this point forward

“I will stop at Sebastia ruins on the way — a complete re-plan of the remaining journey. I estimate the rest will cost ₪450 from here.”

\[EAC_4 = AC + ETC_{new} = \text{₪}180 + \text{₪}450 = \mathbf{\text{₪}630}\]
A detour and longer journey means arriving ₪30 over budget — but with memories of an ancient Roman city. This is the bottom-up ETC method: ignore past performance and estimate remaining work fresh.






Tip💡 All Four EAC Forecasts Compared












Formula
Assumption
EAC
vs. BAC (₪600)




EAC₁ = BAC / CPI
Same cost efficiency to end

✅ ₪60 under


EAC₂ = AC + (BAC − EV)
Rest at original budgeted rate

✅ ₪20 under


EAC₃ = AC + (BAC−EV)/(CPI×SPI)
Same cost and schedule delays

🟠 ₪12 over


EAC₄ = AC + New ETC
Complete re-estimate from now

🔴 ₪30 over



Which formula should you use? In practice, EAC₁ is the most common (current efficiency is the best predictor of future efficiency). EAC₄ is used after major scope or route changes.






13.5.8 Step 5 — What’s Left and What’s the Final Verdict? (ETC & VAC)
Using EAC₁ = ₪540 (assuming cost efficiency continues):

Estimate to Complete (ETC)
How much money do you still need to reach Jenin?
\[ETC = EAC - AC = \text{₪}540 - \text{₪}180 = \mathbf{\text{₪}360}\]
You have ₪360 left to spend to complete the remaining 40 km of your journey.


Variance at Completion (VAC)
What will your final saving (or overrun) be compared to the original budget?
\[VAC = BAC - EAC = \text{₪}600 - \text{₪}540 = \mathbf{+\text{₪}60}\]
A positive VAC means you will finish ₪60 under budget. That is ₪60 saved — enough for a warm meal in Jenin when you arrive! 🍽️

Important🏁 Trip Conclusion



You are on your way from Tulkarem to Jenin. Halfway through the journey, the EVM dashboard tells you:

You are 4 km behind schedule (SPI = 0.833) — checkpoints slowed you down
You are spending efficiently (CPI = 1.111) — fuel and food cost less than planned
If you keep this cost efficiency, you will arrive ₪60 under budget (VAC = +₪60)
The only scenario that puts you over budget is if you continue to be delayed and those delays add cost — or if you change the route entirely

This is the power of EVM. At any moment on the trip — or on any real project — you can answer three fundamental questions objectively:

Are we on schedule? → SPI = 0.833 → No, slightly behind
Are we on budget? → CPI = 1.111 → Yes, actually ahead
How will it end? → EAC₁ = ₪540 → Under budget if we maintain efficiency

    style M fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6

 Cost control cycle 




13.8.1 Cost Control Techniques

EVM TrendingCost ForecastingChange ControlRecovery Strategies


Monitor CPI and SPI trends weekly: - Is CPI improving or deteriorating? - Historical research shows: CPI rarely improves by more than 10% from its value at 20% project completion - Early warning: CPI < 0.9 at 20% completion = high overrun risk


Review EAC regularly and communicate honestly: - EAC = BAC/CPI — if current cost performance continues (most common) - EAC = AC + (BAC−EV) — if remaining work will be done at original budget - EAC = AC + ETC — if an independent re-estimate of remaining work is done
Compare all three forecasts monthly — divergence signals problems.


All cost changes must go through formal change control: 1. Identify cost trending beyond threshold (typically ±5%) 2. Issue early warning notice to client 3. Raise formal change request 4. Get written approval before spending additional funds


When the project is over budget: 1. Value Engineering — achieve same outcome at lower cost 2. Scope reduction — formally remove lower-priority deliverables 3. Productivity improvement — identify and remove bottlenecks 4. Procurement re-negotiation — re-tender over-budget packages 5. Request Management Reserve — request release from sponsor
